59539.q: On which curve is the Gini coefficient based graphically?
59539.e: The Lorenz curve shows what share of the population has what share of income; Gini measures how far it is from the line of equal distribution.
59539.m: The Gini coefficient is derived from the Lorenz curve.

59540.q: The area between the line of equal distribution and the Lorenz curve is 0.15, the area under the line is 0.5. What is the Gini coefficient?
59540.m: The Gini coefficient is the ratio of the inequality area to the whole triangle.

59541.q: According to the World Bank, which country has had one of the highest income Gini values in the world for years?
59541.e: South Africa is at the top with values around 0.63; causes include the effects of apartheid and high unemployment.
59541.m: South Africa is considered one of the most unequal countries in the world.

59542.q: In Switzerland, how is wealth distributed compared with income?
a: Wealth is much more unequally distributed
Both are distributed exactly the same
59542.e: In Switzerland, the Gini value for wealth is far above that for disposable income, which is around 0.3.
59542.m: In Switzerland, wealth is much more unequally distributed than income.

59543.q: What can the Gini coefficient on its own NOT show?
a: How high the level of income is
Whether everyone has the same amount
How far the Lorenz curve deviates
59543.e: A poor country and a rich country can have the same Gini value; it only measures distribution, not the level.
59543.m: The Gini coefficient says nothing about a country's prosperity.

59544.q: How do taxes and social benefits typically change the Gini coefficient?
59544.e: Progressive taxes and benefits redistribute income; the Gini of disposable income is therefore lower than that of market income.
59544.m: Redistribution by the state lowers the Gini coefficient.

59545.q: Which ratio does the S80/S20 quintile ratio describe as an addition to the Gini?
a: Income of the richest 20 % compared with that of the poorest 20 %
Income of men compared with that of women
Income of cities compared with that of villages
Income of the young compared with that of the old
59545.e: The quintile ratio shows how many times more income the richest fifth has than the poorest fifth.
59545.m: The S80/S20 ratio compares the richest fifth with the poorest fifth.

59546.q: How many main goals does the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development include?
59546.e: The 17 main goals are divided into 169 targets. Their predecessors, the Millennium Goals, numbered only eight.

59547.q: In which year did the UN General Assembly adopt the 2030 Agenda?
59547.e: The countries adopted the 2030 Agenda in September 2015 in New York.

59548.q: What were the eight predecessor goals of the SDGs for the years 2000 to 2015 called?
59548.e: The Millennium Development Goals were aimed mainly at developing countries; the SDGs apply to all countries.
59548.m: The Millennium Goals were the predecessors of the SDGs.

59549.q: What is an important difference between the SDGs and the Millennium Goals?
a: They apply to all countries, including Switzerland
They can be enforced in court
59549.e: The 2030 Agenda is universal; industrialised countries such as Switzerland must also report on their progress.
59549.m: The SDGs are goals for the whole world.

59550.q: What is the topic of SDG 1?
59550.e: Goal 1 is: end poverty in all its forms everywhere.
59550.m: The first sustainability goal is ending poverty.

59551.e: SDG 13 calls for urgent action to combat climate change and its effects.
59551.m: Climate action is the 13th sustainability goal.

59552.q: Which guiding principle stands above the whole 2030 Agenda?
a: Help only in return for reforms
59552.e: Under “Leave no one behind”, the most disadvantaged are to be reached first.
59552.m: The 2030 Agenda aims to leave no one behind.

59553.q: Which SDG deals with gender equality?
59553.e: SDG 5 aims to achieve gender equality and empower all women and girls.
59553.m: Gender equality is the fifth SDG.

59554.q: How does the World Bank decide whether someone lives in extreme poverty?
a: With an amount of money available per person per day
With the size of their home
With the number of years at school
With whether they own a car
59554.e: The international poverty line is an amount of money per day, adjusted for purchasing power. Since 2025 it has been 3 dollars.
59554.m: Extreme poverty is measured by an amount of money per day.

59555.q: Which organisation decides which countries count as Least Developed Countries (LDCs)?
59555.e: The UN has used the category since 1971; the Committee for Development Policy reviews the list every three years.
59555.m: The LDC list is a UN category.

59556.q: Which three criteria decide LDC status?
59556.e: The criteria used are GNI per head, the Human Assets Index and the Economic and Environmental Vulnerability Index.
59556.m: An LDC is poor, has few human assets and is economically vulnerable.

59557.q: How many countries did the UN count as Least Developed Countries at the end of 2024?
59557.e: After São Tomé and Príncipe graduated in December 2024, 44 LDCs remained.
59557.m: At the end of 2024 there were 44 least developed countries.

59558.q: On which continent are most of the Least Developed Countries?
59558.e: About three quarters of the LDCs, namely 32 countries, are in Africa.

59559.q: Which country is the only LDC in the Americas?
59559.e: Haiti is the poorest country in the Americas and the only one there on the LDC list.
59559.m: Haiti is the only LDC in the Americas.

59560.q: Which country was the first to leave the LDC category, in 1994?
59560.e: Botswana made the step up thanks to diamond revenues and stable government.
59560.m: Botswana was the first country to leave the LDC list.

59561.q: Which Asian country graduated from the LDC group in December 2023?
59561.e: After a transition period, Bhutan was removed from the list in December 2023.
59561.m: Bhutan has no longer been an LDC since the end of 2023.

59562.q: In which city was the fifth UN Conference on the Least Developed Countries held in March 2023?
59562.e: The conference in Qatar adopted the Doha Programme of Action for the LDCs for the years 2022 to 2031. The previous conference had taken place in Istanbul in 2011.
59562.m: The fifth UN LDC conference took place in Doha in 2023.

59563.q: What problem can leaving the LDC category bring?
59563.e: After graduation, preferential tariffs and cheap loans end after a transition period; that is why there are transition strategies.
59563.m: Leaving the LDC group ends some advantages.

59564.q: Who coined the abbreviation BRIC in 2001?
59564.e: The economist Jim O'Neill grouped Brazil, Russia, India and China together as economies that would become important.
59564.m: The term BRIC comes from a bank economist.

59565.q: Which international organisation do the BRICS countries want to counterbalance with their joint currency reserve fund from 2014?
59565.e: The Contingent Reserve Arrangement is meant to help members with foreign currency in the short term when they have balance of payments problems, similar to the IMF. In this way the BRICS want to become more independent of Western-dominated institutions.
59565.m: The BRICS have their own emergency fund for foreign currency.

59566.q: Which bank did the BRICS countries found in 2014?
59566.e: The New Development Bank finances infrastructure and sustainability projects in the member countries. It is meant to offer an alternative to the World Bank.
59566.m: The BRICS countries have their own development bank.

59567.q: In which city does the BRICS New Development Bank have its headquarters?
59567.e: The bank was agreed at the Fortaleza summit in 2014 and has its headquarters in Shanghai.
59567.m: The BRICS bank is based in China.

59568.q: Which of these countries joined the BRICS at the beginning of 2024?
59568.e: In 2024, Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates joined; Argentina turned down the invitation.
59568.m: Egypt has belonged to the BRICS since 2024.

59569.q: Which Southeast Asian country became a full member of the BRICS in January 2025?
59569.e: In January 2025, Indonesia became the first country in Southeast Asia to join.
59569.m: Indonesia has been a BRICS member since 2025.

59570.q: Which goal do the BRICS countries pursue together?
a: More weight for the South in the world economy
A customs union like the EU
59570.e: The group wants to form a counterweight to the G7, the IMF and the World Bank, but it is not a formal organisation with a treaty.
59570.m: The BRICS demand more influence for emerging economies.

59571.q: What is typical of an emerging economy?
a: It is on the way from a developing country to an industrialised one
It lies on a national border
It is a rich oil country
59571.e: Emerging economies are industrialising rapidly, but often still have big social and regional differences.
59571.m: An emerging economy is on the threshold of becoming an industrialised country.

59572.q: Which English abbreviation is often used for emerging economies?
59572.e: NIC stands for Newly Industrialised Countries. LDC, on the other hand, refers to the least developed countries.
59572.m: Emerging economies are often called Newly Industrialised Countries.

59573.q: What is the group of eleven countries called that Goldman Sachs chief economist Jim O'Neill named in 2005 as the next rising economies after the BRICs?
59573.e: The Next Eleven include Mexico, Indonesia, Nigeria, Vietnam and South Korea, among others. Because of their populations and growth, they were seen as important emerging economies of the future.
59573.m: The Next Eleven are eleven rising countries after the BRICs.

59574.q: Which strategy did many Latin American countries follow from the 1950s?
59574.e: They used tariffs to protect their own industry, which was meant to replace imported goods.
59574.m: Import substitution means replacing imports with your own production.

59575.q: What do you call the danger that an emerging economy gets stuck at a middle level of income?
59575.e: When wages rise but innovation is lacking, a country loses its cost advantage without being able to keep up with high-wage countries.
59575.m: Many emerging economies get stuck in the middle-income trap.

59576.q: Which countries make up the MINT group, which the economist Jim O'Neill made well known?
59576.e: The investment firm Fidelity coined the term in 2011, and O'Neill made it popular from 2013. They are four populous, rising countries.
59576.m: The MINT countries are seen as possible successors to the BRICS.

59577.q: Which Latin American emerging economy joined the OECD in 1994?
59577.e: Mexico became a member in 1994, the same year the NAFTA free trade agreement came into force.
59577.m: Mexico has been in the OECD since 1994.

59578.q: What does the term “economic dualism” describe in emerging economies?
59578.e: Next to ultra-modern industrial zones there are poor rural regions and a large informal sector.
59578.m: In emerging economies, modern life and poverty exist side by side.

59579.q: Which emerging economy is often called the “workshop of the world”?
59579.e: Thanks to export zones and cheap labour, China became the world's largest industrial producer and exporter of goods.
59579.m: China is known as the workshop of the world.

59580.q: What was the fairer world economic order called that developing countries pushed through in the UN General Assembly in 1974?
59580.e: On 1 May 1974, the General Assembly adopted a declaration on establishing a New International Economic Order. Demands included better raw material prices and control over their own natural resources.
59580.m: With the New International Economic Order, the South demanded fairer trade rules in 1974.

59581.q: Which countries south of the equator still count as part of the Global North?
59581.e: North and South are economic, not geographical terms; Australia and New Zealand are industrialised countries.
59581.m: Global North and South are not just compass directions.

59582.q: Where does the term “Third World” originally come from?
a: From the Third Estate before the French Revolution
From the number of continents in the South
From third place in a UN ranking
From the third wave of colonisation
59582.e: In 1952, the demographer Alfred Sauvy compared the poor countries with the Third Estate, which had few rights before 1789. Later the term also referred to countries outside the Western and Eastern blocs.
59582.m: The term Third World refers to the Third Estate.

59583.q: Which group did developing countries found in 1964 at the first UNCTAD in Geneva?
59583.e: The G77 represents the interests of the South at the UN and today has over 130 members.
59583.m: The Group of 77 is the voice of the developing countries at the UN.

59584.q: Why are many countries that mainly export raw materials at an economic disadvantage?
a: Raw material prices fall over the long term compared with manufactured goods
Raw materials may not be traded across borders
Manufactured goods keep getting cheaper than raw materials
Raw materials are only exchanged for other raw materials
59584.e: For the same amount of coffee or copper, a country often gets fewer machines or medicines over time. This is called worsening terms of trade.
59584.m: Raw material exporters often lose purchasing power over the long term.

59585.q: What were the reform conditions called that the IMF and the World Bank imposed on indebted countries of the South in the 1980s and 1990s?
59585.e: To get new loans, the countries had to cut government spending, privatise state companies and open their markets, for example. Critics accused the programmes of making poverty worse in some cases.
59585.m: Structural adjustment programmes linked loans to economic reforms.

59586.q: Which economist described five stages of economic growth, including the “take-off”, in 1960?
59586.e: Rostow's model belongs to modernisation theory: every country goes through the same stages up to mass consumption.
59586.m: Rostow saw development as a series of stages.

59587.q: Which conference of 1955 is seen as the forerunner of the Non-Aligned Movement?
59587.e: In Bandung (Indonesia), 29 Asian and African countries met to position themselves between the power blocs. The movement itself was founded in Belgrade in 1961.
59587.m: Cooperation between the non-aligned countries began in Bandung.

59588.q: What is the south of Italy called, which stands for a north-south divide within a country?
59588.e: The south of Italy has much lower incomes and higher unemployment than the industrialised north.
59588.m: There are north-south divides within countries, too.

59589.q: Which federal office in the Federal Department of Foreign Affairs is responsible for development cooperation?
59589.e: The Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation belongs to the Federal Department of Foreign Affairs.
59589.m: The SDC is the Swiss agency for development cooperation.

59590.q: Besides the SDC, which federal office is responsible for Switzerland's economic development cooperation?
59590.e: The State Secretariat for Economic Affairs promotes trade, the private sector and good economic policy in partner countries, among other things.
59590.m: Besides the SDC, SECO also carries out development cooperation.

59591.q: According to the UN target, what share of gross national income should rich countries spend on development aid?
59591.e: The target was agreed at the UN in 1970; only a few countries reach it consistently.
59591.m: Official development aid should be 0.7 per cent of GNI.

59592.q: A country has a GNI of 800 billion francs. How much would it have to spend on development aid under the 0.7 per cent target?
59592.m: To work out 0.7 per cent, you multiply by 0.007.

59593.q: Which OECD committee decides what counts as official development assistance (ODA)?
59593.e: The Development Assistance Committee (DAC) defines ODA and reviews the donor countries.
59593.m: The OECD's DAC decides what counts as development aid.

a: Aid with the obligation to buy in the donor country
Aid in the form of loans
59594.e: With tied aid, goods or services must be bought from the donor country, which often makes them more expensive.
59594.m: Tied aid often also benefits the donor country's economy.

59595.q: Which principle of the Paris Declaration of 2005 stresses the leading role of partner countries?
59595.e: Under “ownership”, partner countries are meant to decide their development strategies themselves; donors follow them.
59595.m: Partner countries should steer their own development.

59596.q: What does the Swiss organisation Helvetas, founded in 1955, mainly work for?
59596.e: Helvetas was founded in Zurich in 1955 as one of the first private Swiss organisations for development cooperation. It supports projects for drinking water, education and farming, for example.
59596.m: Helvetas is a Swiss organisation for development cooperation.

59597.q: What distinguishes development cooperation from humanitarian aid?
a: It works on structures over the long term
59597.e: Humanitarian aid saves lives in emergencies; development cooperation aims to fight the causes of poverty over many years.
59597.m: Development cooperation aims for long-term change.

59598.q: Where does the name of the Fairtrade label Max Havelaar come from?
a: From a Dutch novel against colonial injustice
From the founder of a Swiss coffee company
59598.e: The novel “Max Havelaar” by Multatuli (1860) denounced the exploitation of the people in the Dutch East Indies. The label took the name of the main character.
59598.m: Max Havelaar is a character in a novel who fights against colonial injustice.

59599.q: In which country was the Max Havelaar label introduced in 1988?
59599.e: The first label was for coffee from Mexico; the Swiss foundation followed in 1992.
59599.m: The Max Havelaar label comes from the Netherlands.

59600.q: Which two instruments does Fairtrade guarantee to producer organisations?
59600.e: The minimum price protects against price crashes; the premium pays for community projects such as schools or wells.
59600.m: Fairtrade guarantees a minimum price and a premium.

59601.q: What did the “banana women” from Frauenfeld campaign for from 1973?
59601.e: The group around Ursula Brunner drew attention to the low wages and prices in the banana trade and was willing to pay more. This led to the organisation Gebana.
59601.m: The banana women are seen as pioneers of fair trade in Switzerland.

59602.q: When is World Fair Trade Day celebrated?
a: On the second Saturday in May
On the first Sunday in December
59602.e: World Fair Trade Day takes place each year on the second Saturday in May.
59602.m: Fair Trade Day is celebrated in May.

59603.q: Which umbrella organisation awards the Fairtrade label internationally?
59603.e: Fairtrade International, based in Bonn, sets the standards; certification is checked by the independent FLOCERT.
59603.m: Fairtrade International sets the standards for the label.

59604.q: Which criticism is often made of fair trade?
a: It only reaches a small share of farmers
59604.e: Critics complain that minimum prices only benefit certified cooperatives and that hired workers gain little.
59604.m: Fair trade helps many producers, but not all.

59605.q: Which product was the first fresh product with the Max Havelaar label in Switzerland, in 1997?
59605.e: Max Havelaar bananas have been sold in Switzerland since 1997. Because large retailers stocked them, they reached a market share of over 50 per cent.
59605.m: Fairtrade bananas are very common in Switzerland.

59606.q: What is a typical difference between fair trade shops and fair products in the supermarket?
a: Fair trade shops sell only fairly traded goods
Fair trade shops sell only organic products
Supermarkets may not stock Fairtrade goods
Fair trade shops are state-run businesses
59606.e: Fair trade shops, in Switzerland often “claro” shops, stock only fairly traded goods and give information about the background.
59606.m: Fair trade shops are specialist shops for fair trade.

59607.q: Which economist founded the Grameen Bank in Bangladesh?
59607.e: Muhammad Yunus started giving small loans in 1976; in 1983 Grameen became an independent bank.
59607.m: Muhammad Yunus is seen as the father of microcredit.

59608.q: What did Muhammad Yunus and the Grameen Bank receive the Nobel Prize for in 2006?
59608.e: The Nobel Committee honoured their work promoting economic and social development from below.
59608.m: Yunus received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2006.

59609.q: Who traditionally receives the large majority of loans from the Grameen Bank?
59609.e: Women usually repay loans reliably and often invest in their family and children.

59610.q: What replaces missing collateral for many microloans?
59610.e: Small groups of borrowers vouch for each other; social pressure ensures high repayment rates.
59610.m: With microloans, the group is often jointly liable.

59611.q: A woman borrows 200 francs at 20 per cent interest a year. How much does she pay back after one year?
59611.e: Interest: 200 × 0.20 = 40 francs; she has to pay back 200 + 40 = 240 francs.
59611.m: Interest is calculated as a percentage of the amount borrowed.

59612.q: Which term covers savings accounts and insurance for poor people as well as small loans?
59612.e: Microfinance offers various financial services to people on low incomes who have no access to banks.
59612.m: Microfinance is more than just microcredit.

59613.q: Which risk did the microfinance crisis of 2010 in India reveal?
a: Borrowers fall into a debt trap
The banks had too few customers
The loans were interest-free and unprofitable
Women were no longer allowed to get loans
59613.e: Aggressive lending and high interest rates meant that many people took out several loans at the same time and could no longer repay them. The government then heavily restricted the lenders.
59613.m: Microloans can also become a debt trap.

59614.q: In which city was OPEC founded in 1960?
59614.e: OPEC was founded in September 1960 at a conference in Baghdad. The five founding countries wanted more control over their oil prices in relation to the big Western oil companies.
59614.m: OPEC was founded in Baghdad in 1960.

59615.q: In which European city has OPEC had its headquarters since 1965?
59615.e: OPEC moved its headquarters from Geneva to Vienna in 1965. As a neutral country, Austria offered favourable conditions for the organisation.

59616.q: Which Latin American country is one of the five founding members of OPEC?
59616.e: The founding members were Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela. The Venezuelan minister Juan Pablo Pérez Alfonzo is seen as one of the fathers of the organisation.
59616.m: Venezuela is the only Latin American founding member of OPEC.

59617.q: What is OPEC's main tool for trying to influence the price of oil?
a: A joint oil price at petrol stations
59617.e: OPEC sets production amounts for its members. If less is produced, supply becomes scarcer and the price tends to rise.
59617.m: OPEC controls the supply of oil through production quotas.

59618.q: Which term from economics describes OPEC as an agreement between suppliers on quantities and prices?
59618.e: A cartel is an agreement between independent suppliers to limit competition. That is why OPEC is often called the oil cartel.
59618.m: In economics, OPEC is described as a cartel.

59619.q: Which country is OPEC's most important partner in the “OPEC+” group, which has existed since 2016?
59619.e: In OPEC+, the OPEC countries coordinate with other producing countries. Russia is by far the largest producer among them.
59619.m: In OPEC+, OPEC works together mainly with Russia.

59620.q: Which Gulf country left OPEC at the beginning of 2019 to concentrate more on natural gas?
59620.e: Qatar left OPEC in January 2019. The country is mainly a big exporter of liquefied natural gas and produced comparatively little oil.
59620.m: Qatar left OPEC in 2019 because natural gas is more important for the country.

59621.q: Which African country left OPEC at the beginning of 2024 in a dispute over production quotas?
59621.e: Angola left on 1 January 2024 because it did not agree with the production quota it had been given. Nigeria, Algeria and Libya are still members.
59621.m: Angola left OPEC in 2024 because of a quota dispute.

59622.q: Which OPEC country is known as the “swing producer” because it can raise or cut its production sharply and quickly?
59622.e: Saudi Arabia has large unused production capacity. This lets it adjust supply at short notice and strongly influence the world market.
59622.m: Saudi Arabia is the most important swing producer on the oil market.

59623.q: What did Switzerland introduce during the oil crisis in autumn 1973 to save fuel?
59623.e: After the oil embargo by Arab producing countries in connection with the Yom Kippur War, the Federal Council ordered three car-free Sundays in November and December 1973. Within a few months the price of oil rose to about four times its previous level.
59623.m: The oil crisis of 1973 brought Switzerland car-free Sundays.

59624.q: What is the name of the largest conventional oil field in the world?
59624.e: The Ghawar field lies in eastern Saudi Arabia and is about 280 km long. For decades it supplied a large share of Saudi production.
59624.m: Ghawar in Saudi Arabia is the largest conventional oil field in the world.

59625.q: Why did Saudi Arabia build an oil pipeline across the country from the Persian Gulf to the Red Sea?
a: To be able to avoid the Strait of Hormuz
59625.e: Almost all tankers from the Gulf have to pass through the narrow Strait of Hormuz off Iran. The East-West Pipeline takes oil to the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea in case this strait is blocked.
59625.m: The East-West Pipeline takes Saudi oil to Yanbu on the Red Sea.

59626.q: Which emirate has by far the largest share of the oil reserves of the United Arab Emirates?
59626.e: About 95 per cent of the Emirates' oil reserves are in Abu Dhabi. Dubai produced comparatively little oil and focused early on trade, tourism and finance.
59626.m: Abu Dhabi holds almost all of the Emirates' oil reserves.

59627.q: Where was the first economically important oil found in the Middle East in 1908?
59627.e: The find at Masjed Soleyman in present-day Iran led to the founding of the Anglo-Persian Oil Company, the forerunner of BP. This began the oil age in the Gulf.
59627.m: The oil age in the Middle East began in Persia in 1908.

59628.q: In which Gulf state is the Burgan field, one of the largest oil fields in the world?
59628.e: The Burgan field in southern Kuwait was discovered in 1938. For decades it has supplied most of Kuwait's oil production.
59628.m: The Burgan field is the heart of Kuwait's oil production.

59629.q: On which island in the Persian Gulf was oil found in 1932, the first place on the Arab side?
59629.e: Oil was struck in Bahrain in 1932, a few years before Saudi Arabia and Kuwait. The find encouraged the search on the nearby Arabian mainland.
59629.m: In 1932, Bahrain was the first oil find on the Arab side of the Gulf.

59630.q: According to most estimates, which Gulf country has the largest proven oil reserves in the region?
59630.e: Saudi Arabia has about 260 billion barrels of proven reserves. Depending on the source, this puts it in second place worldwide behind Venezuela.
59630.m: Saudi Arabia has the largest oil reserves on the Persian Gulf.

59631.q: Which geological structure often forms a trap around the Persian Gulf in which oil collects?
59631.e: In an anticline, rock layers arch upwards. Light oil and gas rise and collect under an impermeable cap layer at the top.
59631.m: Oil often collects at the top of anticlines.

59632.q: What did the Iraqi army set on fire when it withdrew from Kuwait in 1991?
a: The tankers in the port of Dubai
59632.e: During the withdrawal at the end of the Gulf War, Iraqi troops set fire to hundreds of Kuwaiti oil wells. The fires raged for months and caused severe air and soil pollution.
59632.m: In 1991, hundreds of oil wells burned in Kuwait.

59633.q: What is the name of Saudi Arabia's state oil company?
59633.e: Saudi Aramco grew out of the Arabian American Oil Company and was fully nationalised by 1980. ADNOC belongs to Abu Dhabi, QatarEnergy to Qatar.
59633.m: Saudi Aramco is Saudi Arabia's state company.

59634.q: In which Canadian province are the largest oil sands deposits in the world?
59634.e: The Athabasca, Cold Lake and Peace River deposits are in Alberta. They are among the largest known oil resources of all.
59634.m: The world's largest oil sands are in Alberta.

59635.q: What is the thick, tar-like oil substance called that sticks to grains of sand in oil sand?
59635.e: Oil sand is a mixture of sand, clay, water and bitumen. The bitumen is so thick that it does not flow out of a borehole like normal crude oil.

59636.q: How is bitumen extracted that lies too deep for open-pit mining?
a: By flushing it out with seawater
59636.e: In the SAGD process (Steam Assisted Gravity Drainage), steam is pumped into a well. The heated bitumen becomes runnier and flows to a deeper production well.
59636.m: Deep oil sand is made runny with hot steam.

59637.q: Which town is the centre of the oil sands industry in the Athabasca area?
59637.e: Fort McMurray lies in the middle of the mining area on the Athabasca River. Calgary is home to many oil companies, but it is far from the oil sands.
59637.m: Fort McMurray is the oil sands town.

59638.q: What forced almost the entire population of Fort McMurray to evacuate in 2016?
a: A dam failure at a tailings pond
59638.e: In May 2016, a huge wildfire reached the town. About 88,000 people had to flee, and oil sands production was cut sharply for a while.
59638.m: A wildfire drove the people out of Fort McMurray in 2016.

59639.q: Why is bitumen mixed with lighter hydrocarbons before being transported through pipelines?
a: So that it is runny enough
So that it is not radioactive
So that it weighs less than water
So that it does not freeze
59639.e: Pure bitumen is almost solid at normal temperatures. Adding diluents creates so-called “dilbit” (diluted bitumen), which can be pumped through pipes.
59639.m: Bitumen has to be diluted to flow through pipelines.

59640.q: What are the huge ponds called in which the polluted process water with sand and clay residues is stored in oil sands mining?
59640.e: After bitumen and sand are separated, a sludge of water, fine clay and leftover oil remains. These tailings ponds cover large areas in Alberta and endanger migrating birds and groundwater, for example.
59640.m: Oil sands mining leaves behind huge tailings ponds.

59641.q: Why does oil from oil sand usually cause more greenhouse gases per barrel than conventional oil?
a: Extracting it takes a great deal of energy
It is only transported using coal
59641.e: A lot of natural gas is burned to make steam, mine and process the material. That is why emissions from extraction to refinery are much higher than for oil that is easy to extract.
59641.m: Oil sands oil is worse for the climate because extracting it uses so much energy.

59642.q: Which pipeline project for transporting oil sands oil to the USA was finally abandoned in 2021?
59642.e: Keystone XL was meant to carry oil from Alberta to the Gulf of Mexico. After the US government withdrew the permit in 2021, the operator ended the project.

59643.q: In which country is the Orinoco Belt, one of the largest heavy oil deposits in the world?
59643.e: The Orinoco Belt north of the Orinoco River contains huge amounts of extra-heavy oil. That is why Venezuela officially reports the largest oil reserves in the world.
59643.m: Venezuela's heavy oil lies in the Orinoco Belt.

59644.q: What job does the sand in fracking fluid do?
a: It keeps the cracks that are created open
59644.e: Fine cracks are forced into the rock under high pressure. The sand acts as a proppant so that the cracks do not close again when the pressure is released, allowing gas or oil to flow out.
59644.m: In fracking, grains of sand keep the cracks in the rock open.

59645.q: Which drilling technique makes fracking in thin shale layers economical in the first place?
59645.e: The well is first drilled vertically and then horizontally through the layer. This way a long section is in contact with the rock and can be fracked in many places.
59645.m: Fracking only pays off with horizontal drilling.

59646.q: In which type of rock are the deposits found that are called unconventional gas and oil and are extracted by fracking?
59646.e: Shale is very dense and hardly permeable. Gas and oil stay trapped in it and only flow to the well after the rock has been artificially broken open.
59646.m: Shale gas is trapped in dense shale.

59647.q: What was the result of the shale revolution for the USA?
a: It became the world's largest oil producer
It banned the export of natural gas
59647.e: Thanks to fracking, US production rose sharply after 2010. Since 2018, the USA has been the world's largest producer of crude oil, ahead of Saudi Arabia and Russia.
59647.m: Fracking made the USA the largest oil producer.

59648.q: Which basin in Texas and New Mexico is the most important shale oil area in the USA?
59648.e: The Permian Basin supplies most of America's shale oil. It is named after rocks from the Permian period.
59648.m: The Permian Basin is the heart of US shale oil production.

59649.q: In which US state did the Bakken Formation trigger an oil boom?
59649.e: The Bakken Formation lies mainly in North Dakota. After 2008, fracking made the state one of the largest oil producers in the USA.
59649.m: Fracking brought North Dakota an oil boom.

59650.q: What is considered the main cause of the sharp increase in small earthquakes in Oklahoma after 2009?
59650.e: Oil and gas production produces a lot of salty formation water. If it is pumped deep underground, the pressure can activate old faults and trigger earthquakes.

59651.q: Which European country was the first to ban fracking by law, in 2011?
59651.e: In July 2011, France banned hydraulic fracturing for extracting oil and gas. In Germany, too, unconventional fracking has been largely banned since 2017.
59651.m: France banned fracking as early as 2011.

59652.q: How does the output of a shale oil well typically develop over time?
a: It falls sharply in the first few years
It only begins after ten years
59652.e: Shale wells often lose a large part of their initial output in the very first year. That is why new wells have to be drilled all the time to keep production up.

59653.q: Why is fracking controversial in many countries?
a: It can endanger groundwater and trigger earthquakes
It only works under the seabed
It needs no water at all
59653.e: In fracking, large amounts of water with sand and chemicals are pumped into the ground. Critics fear polluted groundwater, and injecting wastewater can trigger earthquakes.
59653.m: Fracking is controversial because of risks to groundwater and earthquakes.

59654.q: To roughly what temperature must natural gas be cooled for it to become liquid?
59654.e: Methane, the main component of natural gas, boils at about -162 °C. It is kept liquid at this temperature in insulated tanks.
59654.m: Liquefied natural gas is about minus 162 degrees cold.

59655.q: By roughly what factor does the volume of natural gas shrink when it is liquefied?
59655.e: Liquefied natural gas takes up only about one six-hundredth of the volume of natural gas as a gas at normal pressure. Only this makes transport by ship economical.
59655.m: Liquefied natural gas takes up about 600 times less space.

59656.q: Which country was the largest exporter of liquefied natural gas in 2023?
59656.e: Thanks to shale gas and new export terminals on the Gulf Coast, the USA overtook Qatar and Australia in 2023. A large share went to Europe.
59656.m: In 2023, the USA became the largest LNG exporter.

59657.q: Which small country on the Persian Gulf is one of the largest exporters of liquefied natural gas?
59657.e: Qatar shares one of the largest gas fields in the world with Iran. It liquefies the gas at Ras Laffan and ships it to Asia and Europe.
59657.m: Qatar is one of the largest LNG exporters in the world.

59658.q: What does an LNG terminal in the importing country do with the liquefied natural gas it receives?
a: It turns it back into gas
It burns it directly to make electricity
It compresses it into solid ice
59658.e: In the terminal, the ultra-cold LNG is warmed up and regasified. It is then fed into the pipeline network as normal natural gas.
59658.m: An import terminal turns liquefied natural gas back into gas.

59659.q: What is an FSRU, like the one Germany used in Wilhelmshaven from the end of 2022?
a: A floating terminal for storage and regasification
A drilling platform for shale gas
A power station for liquid hydrogen
59659.e: FSRU stands for Floating Storage and Regasification Unit. Such ships can be put into use faster than a fixed terminal on land.
59659.m: An FSRU is a floating LNG terminal.

59660.q: What do you call the gas that evaporates from the cargo during an LNG voyage despite the insulation?
59660.e: Because some heat always gets into the tanks, a small part of the cargo evaporates. Many LNG tankers use this boil-off gas as fuel for their engines.
59660.m: On LNG tankers, some boil-off gas evaporates all the time.

59661.q: Why does Japan depend almost entirely on liquefied natural gas for its natural gas?
a: It has no pipeline connection to producing countries
It bans gas pipelines because of earthquakes
It has its own large LNG fields
It only uses natural gas for ships
59661.e: As an island nation without gas pipelines to other countries, Japan has to import natural gas by ship. For decades it has been one of the largest LNG importers in the world.
59661.m: Japan imports natural gas almost only as LNG.

59662.q: How does natural gas mainly reach Switzerland?
a: In LNG tankers along the Rhine
From its own gas fields in the Central Plateau
59662.e: Switzerland has no access to the sea and no LNG terminal of its own. The gas comes through high-pressure pipelines such as the Transitgas pipeline, but it can also come from LNG landed in neighbouring countries.
59662.m: Switzerland gets its natural gas through pipelines.

59663.q: How does LPG (liquefied petroleum gas) differ from LNG?
a: LPG consists mainly of propane and butane
LPG is only made from coal
59663.e: LNG is liquefied natural gas, so mainly methane. LPG is a mixture of propane and butane that becomes liquid under low pressure and is used, for example, in gas bottles for barbecues.
59663.m: LNG is mainly methane, LPG mainly propane and butane.

59664.q: Roughly what share of the world's coal production comes from China (as of 2023)?
59664.e: In 2023, China produced over 4 billion tonnes of coal, about half of world production. India follows in second place, a long way behind.
59664.m: China produces about half of the world's coal.

59665.q: Which northern Chinese province is traditionally known as China's “coal province”?
59665.e: Shanxi has huge hard coal deposits and has depended heavily on mining for decades. Guangdong, Yunnan and Hainan are in the south and hardly play a role.
59665.m: Shanxi is China's classic coal province.

59666.q: Besides Shanxi, which autonomous region is one of China's two largest coal mining areas?
59666.e: Inner Mongolia and Shanxi together supply over half of China's coal. There are large open-pit mines especially in Inner Mongolia.
59666.m: Inner Mongolia is one of China's coal giants.

59667.q: Roughly how large was coal's share of China's electricity generation in 2023?
59667.e: Despite the rapid expansion of wind and solar power, about 60 per cent of China's electricity still came from coal-fired power stations in 2023. Twenty years earlier it had been about 80 per cent.
59667.m: Coal still supplies most of China's electricity.

59668.q: Which country was the largest supplier of imported coal to China in 2023?
59668.e: China is both the largest producer and the largest importer of coal. The most important supplier in 2023 was Indonesia, followed by Russia, Mongolia and Australia.
59668.m: China buys most of its imported coal from Indonesia.

59669.q: Which problem in China's cities was strongly linked to burning coal in the 2010s?
59669.e: Coal-fired power stations and coal heating release fine dust and sulphur dioxide. In winter 2013, smog in Beijing reached extreme levels, after which China introduced stricter clean air programmes.
59669.m: Burning coal contributed heavily to smog in China's cities.

59670.q: What is a coal seam fire, like the ones near Wuda in China?
a: A fire burning in coal layers underground
A fire in a coal-fired power station
A fire on a coal freighter
A forest fire above a mine
59670.e: In Wuda in Inner Mongolia, some coal seams have been burning underground for decades. Such fires destroy coal and release a lot of carbon dioxide and pollutants.
59670.m: Coal seam fires are fires in coal layers underground.

59671.q: According to its own announcement in 2020, by when does China want to be climate-neutral (CO2-neutral)?
59671.e: In 2020, President Xi Jinping announced that China's CO2 emissions would peak before 2030 and that the country would become CO2-neutral by 2060. For this, coal use must fall sharply.
59671.m: China wants to be CO2-neutral by 2060.

59672.q: Why does China run long coal railways such as the Daqin Railway?
a: Coal is mined in the north and inland but used mainly on the coast
Coal may not be transported by ship in China
There are no roads in southern China
The trains heat the cities on their way
59672.e: The big coal areas are in Shanxi and Inner Mongolia, while industry and many power stations are on the coast. The Daqin Railway takes coal from Datong to the port of Qinhuangdao.
59672.m: Long railway lines carry coal from inland China to the coast.

59673.q: What happens in coal liquefaction, as China carries it out in Ordos, for example?
a: Liquid fuels are made from coal
Coal is mixed with water to make sludge
Coal is dissolved underground with acid
59673.e: Chemical processes turn coal into diesel and other liquid hydrocarbons. China wants to reduce its dependence on imported oil this way, but accepts high CO2 emissions.
59673.m: Coal liquefaction turns coal into liquid fuel.

59674.q: Which country has been the world's largest uranium producer since 2009?
59674.e: Kazakhstan supplies about 40 per cent of the world's uranium production. It is followed by Canada, Namibia and Australia, among others.

59675.q: By which method is most of the uranium in Kazakhstan extracted?
59675.e: In in-situ leaching, a solution is pumped into the deposit through boreholes. It dissolves the uranium out of the rock, and then the solution is pumped back up.
59675.m: Kazakhstan extracts uranium by leaching underground.

59676.q: In which Canadian province are Cigar Lake and McArthur River, the uranium deposits with the highest ore grades in the world?
59676.e: In Saskatchewan's Athabasca Basin, some of the ore contains over ten per cent uranium. That is many times the world average.
59676.m: The world's richest uranium ore is in Saskatchewan.

59677.q: What is the yellow uranium concentrate called that is produced after the ore has been processed?
59677.e: Yellowcake consists mostly of uranium oxide (U3O8). It is the product that uranium mines sell, and it is then processed further and enriched.
59677.m: Uranium ore is turned into yellowcake.

59678.q: Roughly what percentage of the fissile isotope uranium-235 does natural uranium contain?
59678.e: Natural uranium is over 99 per cent uranium-238. For most nuclear power stations, the share of uranium-235 is enriched to about 3 to 5 per cent.
59678.m: Natural uranium contains only about 0.7 per cent uranium-235.

59679.q: Which country has the largest known uranium resources in the world, including the Olympic Dam deposit?
59679.e: Australia has about a quarter of the world's economically recoverable uranium resources. Olympic Dam in South Australia is a copper, gold and uranium mine.
59679.m: Australia has the largest uranium resources in the world.

59680.q: Which company mined uranium on a large scale for the Soviet Union in the Ore Mountains and Thuringia in East Germany?
59680.e: SDAG Wismut mined uranium for the Soviet nuclear programme from 1946 to 1990. Cleaning up the spoil heaps and sludge ponds later cost billions.
59680.m: Wismut mined uranium in East Germany for the Soviet Union.

59681.q: In which country is the uranium mining town of Arlit in the Sahara?
59681.e: Uranium has been mined around Arlit since the 1970s, for a long time mainly by French companies. Uranium is one of Niger's most important exports.

59682.q: Which radioactive gas is a particular health hazard in underground uranium mining?
59682.e: Radon is produced when uranium decays and collects in tunnels. Breathing it in increases the risk of lung cancer, which is why mines have to be well ventilated.
59682.m: Radon is the invisible danger in uranium mining.

59683.q: Why does uranium, strictly speaking, not count as a fossil energy resource?
a: It was not formed from living things
It is only found in seawater
It is not burned but evaporated
59683.e: Fossil resources such as coal, oil and natural gas formed from dead plants and tiny organisms. Uranium is an element that was already present when the Earth formed.
59683.m: Uranium is a non-renewable resource, but not a fossil one.

59684.q: Which geologist predicted in 1956 that US oil production would reach its peak around 1970?
59684.e: Marion King Hubbert worked for Shell and presented his model in 1956. Conventional US production did indeed reach its maximum in 1970.
59684.m: Hubbert correctly predicted the US production peak for 1970.

59685.q: What shape is the Hubbert curve, which describes how production from an oil region develops?
59685.e: According to Hubbert, production first rises, reaches a maximum and then falls again about as quickly. This creates a bell-shaped curve.
59685.m: The Hubbert curve is shaped like a bell.

59686.q: In resource geography, what distinguishes “reserves” from “resources”?
a: Reserves can be extracted economically with today's technology
Reserves are only suspected, not proven
Reserves only lie under the sea
Reserves are amounts that have already been extracted
59686.e: Reserves are proven deposits that can be extracted profitably at today's prices with today's technology. Resources also include suspected amounts or amounts that are currently uneconomic.
59686.m: Reserves are the part of resources that can be extracted economically today.

59687.q: A country has 1,750 billion barrels of reserves and produces 35 billion barrels a year. What is the static range?
59687.e: The static range is reserves divided by annual production, so 1,750 ÷ 35 = 50 years. It takes into account neither new finds nor changes in consumption.
59687.m: The static range divides the reserves by annual production.

59688.q: What does the figure EROI stand for in the energy industry?
a: Ratio of energy gained to energy used
Annual profit of an oil company
Share of renewable energy in consumption
Price of a barrel in euros
59688.e: EROI means Energy Return on Investment. The harder oil is to extract, for example from oil sand or the deep sea, the smaller this ratio becomes.
59688.m: EROI shows how much energy you get back for the energy you put in.

59689.q: Which report by the Club of Rome made the limited supply of raw materials a worldwide topic in 1972?
59689.e: The report “The Limits to Growth” used computer models to study population, production and the use of raw materials. It sparked a worldwide debate about resource scarcity.
59689.m: “The Limits to Growth” was published in 1972 for the Club of Rome.

59690.q: What is meant by “peak demand”, in contrast to peak oil?
a: Demand for oil peaks before production reaches its limits
Production falls because fields are exhausted
The oil price reaches a record high
The refineries are working at full capacity
59690.e: With peak oil, geology limits production. With peak demand, the need for oil falls first, for example because of electric cars, efficiency and climate policy, even though there would still be enough oil.
59690.m: With peak demand, the demand for oil falls first.

59691.q: Why has oil production in the British North Sea been falling since the end of the 1990s?
a: The big oil fields are largely exhausted
The North Sea freezes over in winter
The oil is now pumped to Norway
59691.e: British production reached its maximum in 1999. Since then the ageing fields have produced less and less, and new finds are smaller.
59691.m: The British North Sea passed its production peak in 1999.

59692.q: Which development disproved the assumption that US oil production would fall permanently after 1970?
a: The discovery of oil in Switzerland
59692.e: Thanks to fracking, US production exceeded the 1970 record for the first time in 2018. This shows that technology and prices can greatly change reserves.
59692.m: Shale oil pushed US production above the 1970 record.

59693.q: Production from an oil field falls by 5 per cent every year. What percentage of the original amount is still being produced after two years?
59693.e: After one year, 95 per cent remains; after two years, 0.95 × 0.95 = 0.9025, which is 90.25 per cent. Percentage decreases are multiplied, not added.
59693.m: Annual percentage decreases work by multiplying.

59694.q: What are diamonds called whose sale is used to finance civil wars?
59694.e: In countries such as Sierra Leone or Angola, armed groups financed their wars with diamonds. This is an example of the resource curse.
59694.m: Blood diamonds show how raw materials can fuel conflicts.

59695.q: Which technical term describes a raw materials boom raising the value of the currency and thereby weakening industry and the exports of other sectors?
59695.e: The term arose after the discovery of the large Groningen gas field in the Netherlands in 1959. The rise in the value of the guilder then harmed the rest of the export industry.
59695.m: Dutch disease weakens industry through a raw materials boom.

59696.q: What do you call a state that is financed mainly by income from raw materials rather than by taxes?
59696.e: A rentier state lives on so-called rents, meaning income from selling raw materials. Because it hardly collects any taxes, it depends less on the approval of its people.
59696.m: A rentier state lives on income from raw materials instead of taxes.

59697.q: How does Norway protect itself against the resource curse?
a: It invests oil income in a sovereign wealth fund abroad
It bans the export of oil
It nationalises all the country's companies
It keeps its oil production secret
59697.e: The state pension fund, often called the oil fund, invests the income in foreign shares and bonds. It is one of the largest sovereign wealth funds in the world and protects the domestic economy from overheating.
59697.m: Norway saves its oil money in a sovereign wealth fund.

59698.q: Which country with the largest oil reserves in the world fell into a severe economic crisis after the oil price collapse from 2014?
59698.e: Venezuela financed its state budget almost entirely through oil. When the price collapsed, there was hyperinflation, shortages of supplies and large-scale emigration.
59698.m: Venezuela's dependence on oil led to the crisis after 2014.

59699.q: What is the aim of the EITI initiative, which Switzerland also supports?
a: Transparency about payments in the raw materials sector
A worldwide maximum price for oil
59699.e: The Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative requires governments and companies to disclose their payments from oil, gas and mining. This is meant to make corruption harder.
59699.m: EITI makes money flows in the raw materials sector visible.

59700.q: Which Swiss city is one of the most important trading centres for oil in the world?
59700.e: Many large commodity trading firms are based in Geneva and handle a significant share of the world's traded oil. Zug and Lugano are also important commodity locations.
59700.m: Geneva is a centre of the world's oil trade.

59701.q: Under which English expression is the resource curse also known?
59701.e: “Paradox of Plenty” refers to the idea that an abundance of raw materials does not automatically lead to prosperity.
59701.m: The resource curse is also called the Paradox of Plenty.

59702.q: What is the name of the plan with which Saudi Arabia wants to make its economy less dependent on oil?
59702.e: Vision 2030 was presented in 2016 and is meant to promote tourism, industry and services. The country wants to cushion the effects of falling oil income in this way.
59702.m: With Vision 2030, Saudi Arabia wants to move away from oil.

59703.q: Why do state budgets that depend on raw materials suffer particularly from the resource curse?
a: Because raw material prices fluctuate strongly
Because raw materials may not be taxed
Because raw materials are only paid for in dollars
Because raw material prices stay the same every year
59703.e: When prices rise, spending and debt often grow quickly. When they fall, income is suddenly missing, which can lead to austerity programmes, crises and unrest.
59703.m: Fluctuating raw material prices make state budgets unstable.

59704.q: Why does the Niger Delta have many poor communities despite large oil deposits?
a: The profits go mainly to companies and the state
The oil is used only in the delta
The oil is of too poor quality to sell
59704.e: Oil has been produced in the delta since 1956. The local people hardly benefit, but they suffer from polluted soils, water and air.
59704.m: In the Niger Delta, oil wealth is very unequally distributed.

59705.q: Which Ogoni writer and environmental activist was executed by Nigeria's military regime in 1995?
59705.e: Ken Saro-Wiwa campaigned non-violently against the environmental destruction caused by oil production in Ogoniland. His execution after a disputed trial sparked protests worldwide.
59705.m: Ken Saro-Wiwa was executed for his campaign for Ogoniland.

59706.q: What does “gas flaring”, which is widespread in the Niger Delta, mean?
a: Associated gas from oil production is burned off
Natural gas is filled into bottles
Gas is used to generate electricity
Gas is pumped back into the ground
59706.e: The natural gas that escapes during oil production is often simply burned because there are no pipelines. This wastes energy, pollutes the air and harms the people living nearby.
59706.m: In gas flaring, associated gas is simply burned.

59707.q: Which important type of ecosystem in the Niger Delta is particularly affected by oil pollution?
59707.e: The Niger Delta has one of the largest mangrove areas in Africa. Spilled oil coats the roots and kills trees, fish and crabs on which many people depend.
59707.m: Oil pollution destroys the mangroves of the Niger Delta.

59708.q: Which port city is the centre of the oil industry in the Niger Delta?
59708.e: Port Harcourt is the capital of Rivers State and home to many oil companies and refineries. Lagos is Nigeria's largest city, but it lies west of the delta.
59708.m: Port Harcourt is the oil city of the Niger Delta.

59709.q: According to the UNEP report of 2011, how long is the clean-up of Ogoniland expected to take?
59709.e: The UN Environment Programme found extremely high oil levels in some soils and drinking water. It estimated that a full clean-up could take 25 to 30 years and recommended a start-up fund of one billion US dollars.
59709.m: Cleaning up Ogoniland will take decades.

59710.q: What is the name of the militant group that, from 2006, demanded a bigger share of the oil wealth in the Niger Delta with attacks on pipelines and kidnappings?
59710.e: The Movement for the Emancipation of the Niger Delta attacked production facilities and kidnapped oil workers. The attacks at times reduced Nigeria's oil production considerably.
59710.m: MEND used violence in its fight over the delta's oil wealth.

59711.q: What is meant by “oil bunkering” in the Niger Delta?
a: Building protective walls around oil fields
59711.e: Gangs tap into pipelines and sell the oil or process it in illegal refineries. This causes large leaks, fires and environmental damage.
59711.m: Oil bunkering is stealing oil from pipelines.

59712.q: Where did residents of the Niger Delta successfully sue Shell for compensation for oil pollution?
a: In courts in Europe, for example in London
At the International Court of Justice in The Hague as a state
59712.e: The Bodo community sued in London and received 55 million pounds in compensation in 2015. Shell was also ordered to pay in the Netherlands, because the company had its headquarters there.
59712.m: People affected in the Niger Delta sued Shell in Europe.

59713.q: As one of Africa's largest oil producers, which organisation does Nigeria belong to?
59713.e: Nigeria has been a member of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries since 1971. OPEC tries to influence the oil price through production amounts.
59713.m: Nigeria is a member of OPEC.

59714.q: What is the rare earth metal dysprosium used for in neodymium magnets?
a: It stops electricity in the magnet
59714.e: Adding dysprosium prevents neodymium magnets from losing their magnetism at high temperatures, for example in electric motors.

59715.q: Which country dominates (as of 2023) both the mining and especially the processing of rare earths?
59715.e: China mines most of the rare earths and, with about 90 per cent, controls an even larger share of their separation and processing.
59715.m: In processing rare earths, China is almost a monopoly.

59716.q: Why are rare earths considered “rare”, even though some are more common in the Earth's crust than lead?
a: They are rarely concentrated enough to be worth mining
They break down quickly in air
They are only found in meteorites
They only lie in the Earth's mantle
59716.e: The elements are widespread in the Earth's crust, but almost never in such high concentrations that mining them is worthwhile.
59716.m: Rare earths are widespread, but rarely concentrated.

59717.q: For which use is neodymium especially important?
59717.e: Neodymium-iron-boron magnets are the strongest permanent magnets and are found in the electric motors of electric cars and in many wind turbines.
59717.m: Neodymium makes magnets in electric motors and wind turbines especially strong.

59718.q: Which Chinese deposit in Inner Mongolia is considered the largest known deposit of rare earths?
59718.e: Bayan Obo near Baotou is an iron and rare earth deposit and supplies a large share of world production.
59718.m: Bayan Obo in Inner Mongolia is the largest rare earth deposit.

59719.q: After which Swedish place are as many as four chemical elements named, including yttrium and ytterbium?
59719.e: In a mine near Ytterby, close to Stockholm, the mineral was found from which yttrium, ytterbium, terbium and erbium were isolated.
59719.m: Four elements carry the name of the village of Ytterby.

59720.q: Why is separating the individual rare earths from each other so technically difficult?
a: Their chemical properties are very similar
They do not dissolve in any acid
59720.e: The lanthanides hardly differ chemically, so many stages of liquid-liquid extraction are needed to separate them.
59720.m: Because rare earths are chemically alike, separating them is difficult.

59721.q: Which radioactive element is often produced as a by-product when mining the rare earth mineral monazite?
59721.e: Besides rare earths, monazite often contains thorium, which is why mining produces radioactive residues that must be stored safely.

59722.q: What is the group of 15 chemical elements called that, together with scandium and yttrium, make up the rare earths?
59722.e: In the periodic table, the lanthanides range from lanthanum to lutetium. Together with scandium and yttrium, they are counted as rare earth metals.

59723.q: Which country adopted a national lithium strategy in 2023 that is meant to secure the state a majority in new lithium projects through the company Codelco?
59723.e: In 2023, President Gabriel Boric presented the Estrategia Nacional del Litio, after which Codelco agreed a partnership with the producer SQM in the Salar de Atacama.
59723.m: With its lithium strategy, Chile wants more state control over lithium.

59724.q: In what form is lithium mainly extracted in the Lithium Triangle?
59724.e: Lithium-rich salt water is pumped up from under the salt flats and evaporated in ponds.
59724.m: In the Lithium Triangle, lithium comes from the brine of the salt flats.

59725.q: How is the brine in the evaporation ponds of the salt flats mainly concentrated?
59725.e: The dry, sunny high altitude makes the water evaporate over many months until the lithium concentration is high enough.
59725.m: Sun and wind evaporate the brine over months.

59726.q: Which salt flat in Bolivia is the largest salt pan on Earth?
59726.e: The Salar de Uyuni in south-west Bolivia covers over 10,000 square kilometres and is the largest salt flat in the world.
59726.m: The Salar de Uyuni is the largest salt pan on Earth.

59727.q: Which environmental problem is most often criticised in lithium mining in the salt flats?
a: High water use in a dry region
59727.e: Pumping out and evaporating large amounts of brine can lower the water table and endanger wetlands and the farming of Indigenous communities.
59727.m: Lithium mining in salt flats uses a lot of water in dry areas.

59728.q: Which country was the world's largest lithium producer (as of 2023), mainly thanks to hard rock mining?
59728.e: Australia extracts lithium from the mineral spodumene and was at the top ahead of Chile in 2023, while Bolivia produced little despite huge resources.
59728.m: Australia is the largest lithium producer; Bolivia has large unused reserves.

59729.q: Which lithium product is typically made from the evaporated brine and sold to battery manufacturers?
59729.e: Adding soda ash to the concentrated brine makes lithium carbonate settle out, an important raw material for battery cathodes.
59729.m: Lithium carbonate is the most important product traded from brine.

59730.q: What is the process called in which lithium is filtered directly out of the brine without large evaporation ponds?
59730.e: In direct lithium extraction (DLE), adsorbents or membranes bind the lithium, and the remaining brine can be pumped back.
59730.m: Direct lithium extraction is meant to save water and time.

59731.q: Which property makes lithium especially suitable for rechargeable batteries?
59731.e: Lithium has a density of only about 0.53 grams per cubic centimetre and a very negative electrode potential, which allows high energy densities.
59731.m: Lithium is the lightest metal and stores a lot of energy per kilogram.

59732.q: Where does by far the largest share of the world's mined cobalt come from (as of 2023)?
59732.e: In 2023, the Democratic Republic of the Congo supplied about three quarters of the world's cobalt production.
59732.m: About three quarters of cobalt comes from the Congo.

59733.q: In which region of the Democratic Republic of the Congo are the most important cobalt mines?
a: In the Congo Basin around Kisangani
59733.e: The rich copper and cobalt deposits are in the south of the country, in the Central African Copperbelt around Kolwezi and Lubumbashi.
59733.m: Cobalt comes from the Copperbelt in the south of the Congo.

59734.q: Cobalt is usually obtained as a by-product of which metals?
59734.e: Cobalt is rarely mined on its own; it is mostly produced along with copper and nickel.
59734.m: Cobalt is usually a by-product of copper and nickel.

59735.q: What is a large share of cobalt used for today?
59735.e: Cobalt stabilises the cathodes of many lithium-ion batteries, for example in mobile phones and electric cars.
59735.m: A lot of cobalt is in the batteries of mobile phones and electric cars.

59736.q: What is small-scale mining called, in which people in the Congo dig cobalt ore with simple tools?
59736.e: In artisanal small-scale mining, thousands of people often work without protection, some of them children, which is sharply criticised internationally.
59736.m: Artisanal mining is manual work with great health risks.

59737.q: Which commodities company based in the canton of Zug runs large copper and cobalt mines in the Congo?
59737.e: Glencore, with its headquarters in Baar in the canton of Zug, runs the Kamoto (KCC) and Mutanda mines in the Congo, among others.
59737.m: The Zug company Glencore is a big cobalt producer in the Congo.

59738.q: Which battery technology needs no cobalt at all and is therefore used in many electric cars?
59738.e: LFP batteries use iron phosphate as the cathode and need neither cobalt nor nickel, but they have a somewhat lower energy density.

59739.q: Where does the name “cobalt” come from?
a: From the Greek word for blue
From a town in the Congo
59739.e: Miners believed goblins had bewitched the ore, because it gave off poisonous arsenic fumes when smelted and produced no usable metal.
59739.m: Cobalt is named after the miners' goblin, the kobold.

59740.q: In which country is most of the cobalt from the Congo refined?
59740.e: The cobalt ore or intermediate product is mostly shipped to China, where most of the world's cobalt refining takes place.
59740.m: China refines most of the world's cobalt.

59741.q: Which country is the world's largest copper producer (as of 2023)?
59741.e: Chile mines about a quarter of the world's copper, ahead of Peru and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
59741.m: Chile is the largest copper producer in the world.

59742.q: Which copper mine in the Atacama is the largest in the world by output?
59742.e: The Escondida mine east of Antofagasta, run by BHP, produces more copper than any other mine.
59742.m: Escondida is the copper mine with the highest output in the world.

59743.q: Which state company runs the famous Chuquicamata mine?
59743.e: Codelco is the Chilean state copper company and one of the largest copper producers in the world.
59743.m: Codelco is Chile's state copper company.

59744.q: In which year was copper mining in Chile nationalised under President Salvador Allende?
59744.e: In 1971, parliament unanimously decided to nationalise the big copper mines, which had previously belonged mainly to US firms.
59744.m: Chile nationalised its big copper mines in 1971.

59745.q: Which problem do many copper mines in the Atacama solve with seawater desalination?
a: Lack of water in the desert
Ore temperatures that are too high
59745.e: The Atacama is the driest non-polar desert on Earth, so desalinated seawater is pumped through pipelines to heights of over 3,000 metres.
59745.m: In the Atacama, water for the mines often comes from the sea.

59746.q: With which process is ground copper ore usually concentrated, by making copper minerals stick to air bubbles?
59746.e: In flotation, chemicals make the copper sulphides water-repellent, so they stick to air bubbles and rise as froth.
59746.m: Flotation separates copper minerals from waste rock using air bubbles.

59747.q: How high is the copper content of the ore in large Chilean porphyry deposits typically?
59747.e: Porphyry copper ores usually contain only about 0.5 to 1 per cent copper, so huge amounts of rock have to be moved.
59747.m: Copper ore usually contains less than one per cent copper.

59748.q: Why is demand for copper rising sharply because of the energy transition?
a: Copper stores heat in the battery
Copper replaces silicon in solar cells
59748.e: Electric cars, wind turbines, solar installations and power grids need a lot of copper for cables, windings and lines.
59748.m: The energy transition needs a lot of copper because it conducts electricity so well.

59749.q: Which large mine was switched from open-pit to underground mining in 2019?
59749.e: The huge Chuquicamata open pit near Calama had become too deep and uneconomic, so Codelco has been mining underground since 2019.
59749.m: Chuquicamata has been an underground mine since 2019.

59750.q: What does the ore coltan mainly consist of?
59750.e: The name coltan is short for columbite and tantalite, two minerals that contain niobium and tantalum.
59750.m: Coltan is a mixture of columbite and tantalite.

59751.q: For which component in smartphones and laptops is tantalum from coltan mainly used?
59751.e: Tantalum capacitors store a lot of charge in a tiny space and are very reliable.
59751.m: Tantalum from coltan is found in tiny capacitors.

59752.q: In which region is a particularly large amount of coltan mined under disputed conditions?
59752.e: In the provinces of North and South Kivu, armed groups partly finance themselves through the coltan trade.
59752.m: In eastern Congo, coltan is often linked to conflicts.

59753.q: Which four raw materials are internationally known as “conflict minerals” (3TG)?
59753.e: 3TG stands for tin, tantalum, tungsten and gold.
59753.m: Conflict minerals are tin, tantalum, tungsten and gold.

59754.q: Since when has the EU regulation on due diligence for importers of conflict minerals applied?
59754.e: The EU Conflict Minerals Regulation came fully into force on 1 January 2021 and concerns importers of tin, tantalum, tungsten and gold.
59754.m: The EU Conflict Minerals Regulation has applied since 2021.

59755.q: What has the US Dodd-Frank Act required of listed companies regarding conflict minerals since 2010?
a: They must disclose whether the minerals come from the Congo or neighbouring countries
They may no longer buy minerals from Africa
They must pay a special tax on every smartphone
They must run their own mines in the USA
59755.e: Section 1502 of the Dodd-Frank Act requires reports on whether conflict minerals come from the Congo or neighbouring countries. It does not include a ban.
59755.m: The Dodd-Frank Act brought a duty to disclose conflict minerals in the USA.

59756.q: Since when have Swiss companies had legal due diligence obligations for minerals and metals from conflict areas?
59756.e: With the indirect counter-proposal to the Responsible Business Initiative, due diligence and reporting obligations on conflict minerals and child labour have applied since 1 January 2022.
59756.m: In Switzerland, due diligence obligations for conflict minerals have applied since 2022.

59757.q: Where does the element tantalum get its name from?
a: From the Latin word for hard
From the village where it was discovered
59757.e: Tantalum hardly absorbs anything, even in acid, just as Tantalus in Greek legend could not drink despite standing in water up to his chin.
59757.m: Tantalum is named after thirsty Tantalus.

59758.q: Which second metal is obtained from coltan besides tantalum and used in high-strength steel?
59758.e: Columbite supplies niobium, which in small amounts makes steel for pipelines and bridges stronger.
59758.m: Besides tantalum, coltan also supplies niobium.

a: Diamonds whose proceeds finance armed conflicts
59759.e: Rebel groups sold rough diamonds to finance weapons and wars against governments.

59760.q: Since which year has the Kimberley Process certification scheme for rough diamonds applied?
59760.e: The Kimberley Process Certification Scheme came into force in 2003 and requires certificates of origin for traded rough diamonds.
59760.m: The Kimberley Process has applied since 2003.

59761.q: Which town is the Kimberley Process named after?
59761.e: In 2000, diamond-producing countries met in Kimberley in South Africa, a historic centre of diamond mining.
59761.m: The Kimberley Process began in Kimberley in South Africa.

59762.q: In which West African country did the rebel group RUF finance its civil war (1991 to 2002) with diamonds?
59762.e: The Revolutionary United Front controlled diamond fields in eastern Sierra Leone and financed its war that way.
59762.m: In Sierra Leone, diamonds financed a civil war.

59763.q: In which country did the rebel movement UNITA finance its fight with diamonds for decades?
59763.e: In the Angolan civil war, UNITA controlled diamond areas and sold rough stones worth billions of dollars.
59763.m: In Angola, UNITA financed its war with diamonds.

59764.q: What is often criticised about the Kimberley Process?
a: It does not cover violence by states
It only applies to cut stones
It is only applied by Switzerland
59764.e: The definition of conflict diamonds only covers rebels, which is why human rights abuses by governments, for example in Marange in Zimbabwe, are not covered.
59764.m: The Kimberley Process ignores violence by governments.

59765.q: Why are diamonds in Sierra Leone particularly easy for rebels to exploit?
a: They lie as placer deposits in river sediments
They are firmly enclosed in granite
59765.e: Many diamonds lie in alluvial land (alluvial deposits) and can be obtained with a shovel and sieve, without expensive technology.
59765.m: Alluvial diamonds can be obtained with simple tools.

59766.q: In which volcanic rock are primary diamond deposits found?
59766.e: Diamonds form deep in the Earth's mantle and are carried to the surface in pipes of kimberlite.
59766.m: Diamonds reach the surface in kimberlite pipes.

59767.q: Which African country is seen as an example of how diamond income can contribute to development?
59767.e: Botswana uses its diamond income, through the joint company Debswana with De Beers, for schools, health and infrastructure.
59767.m: Botswana is seen as a success story for diamond income.

59768.q: How does a concentrated solar power station (CSP) differ from a photovoltaic installation?
a: It focuses sunlight into heat for a turbine
It does not need the sun
59768.e: CSP power stations concentrate sunlight with mirrors, heat a medium and generate electricity using steam and a turbine.
59768.m: Concentrated solar power stations first turn sunlight into heat.

59769.q: How can concentrated solar power stations still supply electricity after sunset?
a: With heat stores made of molten salt
With pumped storage lakes in the desert
59769.e: Hot molten salt stores heat for several hours, so that the steam turbine can keep running at night.
59769.m: Molten salt storage lets solar thermal power work at night.

59770.q: In which country is the Noor Ouarzazate solar complex on the edge of the Sahara?
59770.e: Noor Ouarzazate is one of the largest concentrated solar power complexes in the world and combines parabolic troughs, a solar tower and photovoltaics.
59770.m: Noor Ouarzazate in Morocco is one of the largest solar power stations in the world.

59771.q: Which problem regularly reduces the output of solar installations in deserts?
a: Dust and sand on the panels
59771.e: Layers of dust block the light, so panels in deserts are often cleaned with robots or water.
59771.m: Dust is a main enemy of desert solar installations.

59772.q: How does great heat affect the efficiency of silicon solar panels?
59772.e: As the cell temperature rises, the voltage of the solar cells falls, so panels deliver a little less power in great heat.
59772.m: Heat lowers the efficiency of solar cells.

59773.q: What was the concept called that was meant to deliver electricity from desert power stations in North Africa to Europe?
59773.e: From 2009, the Desertec initiative wanted to bring solar and wind power from North Africa and the Middle East to Europe through high-voltage lines.
59773.m: Desertec wanted to bring desert electricity to Europe.

59774.q: In which Indian state is the huge Bhadla Solar Park in the Thar Desert?
59774.e: The Bhadla Solar Park in Rajasthan has a capacity of over 2 gigawatts and is one of the largest photovoltaic parks in the world.
59774.m: The Bhadla Solar Park lies in the Thar Desert in Rajasthan.

59775.q: What is the type of solar power station called in which many mirrors (heliostats) direct light onto a central tower?
59775.e: In a solar tower power station, thousands of heliostats follow the sun and focus the light onto a receiver at the top of the tower.
59775.m: In a solar tower power station, heliostats direct the light onto a tower.

59776.q: Why are deserts in the subtropics especially well suited to solar power stations?
a: Lots of sunshine and few clouds
Lots of rain cools the panels
59776.e: Under the subtropical high-pressure zones, the sky is usually cloudless, so the yearly solar radiation is very high.
59776.m: Subtropical deserts offer lots of sun and few clouds.

59777.q: Why do wind turbines at sea usually produce more electricity than on land?
a: The wind blows more strongly and more evenly
The salt water cools the generator
59777.e: Over the sea, there are no hills, trees or houses to slow the wind down, so it is stronger and steadier.
59777.m: Offshore, the wind blows more strongly and evenly.

59778.q: In which country was Vindeby, the world's first offshore wind farm, built in 1991?
59778.e: The Vindeby wind farm off the Danish island of Lolland was connected to the grid in 1991 with eleven turbines.
59778.m: The first offshore wind farm was built in Denmark in 1991.

59779.q: Which type of foundation is most common for offshore wind turbines in shallow water?
59779.e: A monopile is a single large steel tube driven into the seabed. It is suitable for water depths of up to about 30 to 40 metres.
59779.m: In shallow water, most offshore turbines stand on monopiles.

59780.q: What is the advantage of floating wind turbines, like those running in the Hywind Scotland farm since 2017?
a: They can stand in deep water
59780.e: Floating foundations are attached to the seabed with anchor chains and allow wind farms where the sea is too deep for fixed foundations.
59780.m: Floating wind turbines open up deep sea areas.

59781.q: Why is electricity from distant offshore wind farms often transmitted as high-voltage direct current?
a: The losses over long undersea cables are smaller
Direct current is harmless to fish
Alternating current does not flow in water
Direct current does not need a cable
59781.e: Over long undersea cables, alternating current causes high reactive power losses; with HVDC the electricity can be brought ashore more efficiently.
59781.m: Long undersea cables often use high-voltage direct current.

59782.q: To which country does the Hornsea wind farm, one of the largest offshore wind farms in the world, belong?
59782.e: Hornsea lies in the North Sea off the coast of Yorkshire, England; Hornsea 1 and 2 together have a capacity of about 2.5 gigawatts.
59782.m: Hornsea off England is one of the largest offshore wind farms.

59783.q: Which country has the largest installed offshore wind capacity in the world (as of 2023)?
59783.e: China overtook Great Britain in 2021 and has installed the most offshore wind turbines since then.
59783.m: China has the largest offshore wind capacity in the world.

59784.q: Why are many German offshore wind farms far out in the North Sea, often out of sight of the coast?
a: To protect the Wadden Sea and because the winds are stronger
Because there is no wind at all near the coast
Because the sea there is over 1,000 m deep
Because long undersea cables make electricity cheaper
59784.e: The Wadden Sea off the coast is a national park and World Heritage Site. Further out, the wind is also stronger. The first German test farm, alpha ventus, began operating in 2010 about 45 km off Borkum.
59784.m: German offshore wind farms are usually far out in the North Sea.
