59785.q: Which marginal sea is considered Europe's most important offshore wind area because of its shallow water and strong winds?
59785.e: In many places the North Sea is only 20 to 50 metres deep and has strong westerly winds, ideal conditions for fixed foundations.
59785.m: The North Sea is Europe's most important offshore wind area.

59786.q: In which geological structure are Kenya's geothermal fields?
59786.e: In the East African Rift, plates are drifting apart, which brings hot magma close to the surface.
59786.m: Kenya's geothermal heat comes from the East African Rift.

59787.q: What is the name of Kenya's most important geothermal field near Lake Naivasha?
59787.e: The Olkaria power stations, the largest geothermal complex in Africa, are in Hell's Gate National Park near Naivasha.
59787.m: Olkaria is Africa's largest geothermal complex.

59788.q: Roughly what share of Kenya's electricity generation comes from geothermal energy (as of 2023)?
59788.e: With almost half of the electricity generated, geothermal energy is Kenya's most important source of electricity, ahead of hydropower and wind.
59788.m: Almost half of Kenya's electricity comes from geothermal heat.

59789.q: Which advantage of geothermal energy is especially important for Kenya?
a: It supplies steady power regardless of the weather
It needs no water and no drilling
It only works in the rainy season
It only produces electricity during the day
59789.e: Unlike hydropower, which collapses in years of drought, geothermal energy supplies steady electricity around the clock.
59789.m: Geothermal energy supplies base-load power regardless of the weather.

59790.q: What is the name of the state company that runs the Olkaria power stations?
59790.e: The Kenya Electricity Generating Company (KenGen) is Kenya's largest electricity producer and runs most of the geothermal plants.
59790.m: KenGen runs Kenya's large geothermal power stations.

59791.q: Which country has the largest installed geothermal capacity in Africa (as of 2023)?
59791.e: Kenya has installed almost 1,000 megawatts of geothermal capacity, far ahead of all other African countries.
59791.m: Kenya is Africa's leader in geothermal energy.

59792.q: In which decade did Kenya's first geothermal power station go into operation at Olkaria?
59792.e: The first unit of Olkaria I went into operation in 1981.
59792.m: Kenya has used geothermal energy since 1981.

59793.q: In which Swiss city was a geothermal project stopped after a noticeable earthquake in 2006?
59793.e: While injecting water at a depth of about 5 kilometres, the Deep Heat Mining project triggered an earthquake of magnitude 3.4.
59793.m: In Basel, an earthquake stopped a geothermal project in 2006.

59794.q: How is the hot steam in a geothermal power station used to generate electricity?
a: It drives a turbine with a generator
It makes solar cells light up
It is burned to make hydrogen
59794.e: Steam from the boreholes flows through a turbine that turns a generator; afterwards the cooled water is usually pumped back.

59795.q: On which river is the Itaipú Dam?
59795.e: Itaipú dams the Paraná on the border between Brazil and Paraguay.

59796.q: Which two countries run the Itaipú hydroelectric power station together?
59796.e: The power station belongs half to Brazil and half to Paraguay, as set out in the Itaipú Treaty of 1973.
59796.m: Itaipú belongs half to Brazil and half to Paraguay.

59797.q: What is the installed capacity of the Itaipú power station?
59797.e: Itaipú has 20 generators of 700 megawatts each, so 14,000 megawatts in total.
59797.m: Itaipú has a capacity of 14,000 megawatts.

59798.q: Why do ten generators at Itaipú run at 50 hertz and ten at 60 hertz?
a: Paraguay and Brazil have different grid frequencies
Half of them are only a reserve
The river flows at different speeds
59798.e: Paraguay uses 50 hertz and Brazil 60 hertz, so each half of the generators supplies electricity at the right frequency.
59798.m: Itaipú serves two grids with 50 and 60 hertz.

59799.q: Which power station set a new world record for annual electricity production in 2020, replacing Itaipú as the record holder?
59799.e: Itaipú held the record with about 103 terawatt hours in 2016. China's Three Gorges Dam generated about 112 terawatt hours in 2020, beating this figure.
59799.m: The Three Gorges Dam has replaced Itaipú as the record holder.

59800.q: What was the consequence for nature on the Paraná when the Itaipú reservoir was filled in 1982?
a: Huge waterfalls disappeared into the reservoir
The river dried up completely downstream
The sea pushed up as far as the dam
59800.e: The Guaíra Falls (Sete Quedas), once one of the largest waterfalls in the world by volume of water, were flooded. Large areas of forest were also lost.
59800.m: The Itaipú reservoir flooded the Guaíra Falls.

59801.q: What does Paraguay use most of its share of Itaipú electricity for?
59801.e: Paraguay only needs part of its half itself and sells the surplus to Brazil under the treaty.
59801.m: Paraguay sells surplus Itaipú electricity to Brazil.

59802.q: From which Indigenous language, an official language in Paraguay alongside Spanish, does the name Itaipú come?
59802.e: Guaraní is spoken by a majority of the population in Paraguay. Itaipú means something like “singing stone”, after an island in the river.
59802.m: Itaipú is a word from Guaraní.

59803.q: Which border towns are near the Itaipú Dam?
a: Foz do Iguaçu and Ciudad del Este
59803.e: The dam lies north of Foz do Iguaçu (Brazil) and Ciudad del Este (Paraguay), in the area where the borders with Argentina meet.
59803.m: Itaipú lies near Foz do Iguaçu and Ciudad del Este.

a: Recovering raw materials from waste, devices and buildings
Building cities on raw material deposits
59804.e: In urban mining, the city with its buildings, devices and landfills is seen as a store of raw materials from which secondary raw materials are recovered.
59804.m: Urban mining sees the city as a mine of raw materials.

59805.q: Why are old smartphones considered a “gold mine”?
a: They contain more gold per tonne than many ores
They are made mainly of gold
Gold is produced when the battery is charged
They are made in gold mines
59805.e: A tonne of mobile phones contains many times more gold than a tonne of typical gold ore, which often contains only a few grams per tonne.
59805.m: Electronic waste often contains more gold than natural ore.

59806.q: How much electronic waste was produced worldwide in 2022 (Global E-waste Monitor 2024)?
59806.e: According to the UN report, about 62 million tonnes of electronic waste were produced in 2022, of which less than a quarter was documented as properly recycled.
59806.m: The world produces over 60 million tonnes of electronic waste every year.

59807.q: How is the recycling of electrical devices in Switzerland mainly financed?
a: With a tax on household rubbish
59807.e: When you buy a device, you pay an advance recycling fee (vRG), which covers its later disposal through Swico or SENS.
59807.m: The advance recycling fee finances e-waste recycling in Switzerland.

59808.q: What must shops in Switzerland do with old electrical devices of the same type they sell?
a: Take them back free of charge
59808.e: The Ordinance on the Return, Taking Back and Disposal of Electrical and Electronic Equipment (VREG) obliges shops to take back devices from their range free of charge.
59808.m: Swiss shops take back old electrical devices for free.

59809.q: What do you call raw materials obtained from recycling instead of mining?
59809.e: Secondary raw materials come from waste and old products and replace material that would otherwise have to be newly mined.

59810.q: Which recycled product made from demolition material is increasingly used in building construction in Switzerland?
59810.e: Concrete from demolished buildings and mixed rubble are processed and used as aggregate in recycled concrete, which saves gravel.
59810.m: Recycled concrete saves gravel from pits.

59811.q: Why has recycling rare earths from electronic waste been difficult so far?
a: They are built in firmly in small amounts
They evaporate when the device is taken apart
59811.e: Rare earths are often found in tiny amounts in magnets and phosphors that are hard to separate, which is why the recycling rate is very low.
59811.m: Rare earths are hard to recover from devices.

59812.q: What do you call digging up old rubbish tips to recover the valuable materials in them?
59812.e: In landfill mining, landfills are dug up, metals and other valuable materials are sorted out, and the rest is treated again.
59812.m: Landfill mining gets valuable materials out of old landfills.

59813.q: Which Swiss organisation organises the return of IT, consumer electronics and telecommunications devices?
59813.e: Swico Recycling runs a take-back system for computers, mobile phones, televisions and office equipment, financed by the advance recycling fee.
59813.m: Swico takes back old computers and mobile phones.

59814.q: Which US agricultural scientist is known as the “father of the Green Revolution” and received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970?
59814.e: Norman Borlaug bred high-yielding, disease-resistant varieties of wheat that helped prevent famines in Mexico, India and Pakistan. For this he received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970.
59814.m: Norman Borlaug was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for breeding wheat.

59815.q: Which feature made the high-yielding varieties of wheat and rice in the Green Revolution so productive?
a: Growing for several years without new sowing
High yields with no fertiliser at all
59815.e: The semi-dwarf varieties do not fall over even with heavy ears of grain. So they could turn a lot of fertiliser into grain instead of collapsing.
59815.m: Short stalks allowed the new varieties to carry heavy ears of grain.

59816.q: In which region of the world did the “miracle rice” of the Green Revolution spread especially quickly from 1966?
59816.e: The rice variety IR8 from the International Rice Research Institute produced many times the traditional yields with fertiliser and irrigation. It was grown mainly in South and Southeast Asia.
59816.m: The miracle rice of the Green Revolution spread mainly in Asia.

59817.q: In which country does the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI), founded in 1960, have its headquarters?
59817.e: IRRI was founded in 1960 in Los Baños in the Philippines with support from the Ford and Rockefeller Foundations. It played a key role in breeding new rice varieties.
59817.m: The International Rice Research Institute is in Los Baños in the Philippines.

59818.q: Which Indian state is the classic example of the Green Revolution in wheat?
59818.e: In irrigated Punjab, high-yielding varieties, fertiliser and wells were introduced especially quickly from the mid-1960s. The state became India's breadbasket.
59818.m: Thanks to the Green Revolution, Punjab became India's breadbasket.

59819.q: Which inputs did the high-yielding varieties of the Green Revolution need to reach their potential?
a: Green manure, mixed cropping and fallow
Dung, draught animals and their own seed
59819.e: The new varieties only gave top yields if they were grown with lots of mineral fertiliser, reliable irrigation and pesticides. This “package” was expensive.
59819.m: The high-yielding varieties depended on a whole package of inputs.

59820.q: Which social criticism is often made of the Green Revolution?
a: Larger farms benefited more than poor smallholders
Grain yields in Asia fell permanently
It led to a ban on mineral fertiliser
It stayed limited to Europe and North America
59820.e: Those who had capital and land could buy seed, fertiliser and pumps more easily. As a result, the differences between rich and poor farmers grew in some regions.
59820.m: The Green Revolution increased yields, but partly increased social inequality.

59821.q: Why was the sharp increase in farm yields from the 1960s called the “Green Revolution”?
a: It changed farming quickly and without a violent overthrow
It banned the use of mineral fertiliser
Green parties pushed it through in Europe
59821.e: The term comes from a speech by the US official William Gaud in 1968. He deliberately contrasted the rapid, peaceful change in farming with a “red” revolution.
59821.m: The Green Revolution was a rapid change in farming without an overthrow.

59822.q: In which country did Norman Borlaug begin breeding wheat in the 1940s, work that later led to the CIMMYT research centre?
59822.e: From 1944, Borlaug worked in a Rockefeller Foundation programme in Mexico. This led in 1966 to the International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center CIMMYT near Mexico City.
59822.m: The wheat breeding of the Green Revolution began in Mexico.

59823.q: What is typical of plantation farming?
a: Large farms with monoculture for export
Small farms with mixed crops for their own needs
Nomadic herders with herds on common land
Cooperatives growing vegetables for local markets
59823.e: Plantations are capital-intensive large farms that usually grow a single permanent crop. The harvest is often processed on site and exported.
59823.m: Plantations are export-oriented large farms with monoculture.

59824.q: Which plantation crop shaped the Caribbean from the 17th century and was closely linked to the transatlantic slave trade?
59824.e: Millions of enslaved people from Africa were forced to work on the sugar cane plantations of the Caribbean. Sugar was one of the most important goods in the triangular trade.
59824.m: Sugar cane growing in the Caribbean was based on the work of enslaved people.

59825.q: Which country is the largest cocoa producer in the world (as of 2023)?
59825.e: Côte d'Ivoire supplies about 40 per cent of the world's cocoa beans, followed by Ghana. Cocoa there is grown mainly by smallholders, but for export.
59825.m: Côte d'Ivoire is the world's most important cocoa country.

59826.q: Which crop has shaped the plantations in the highlands of Sri Lanka since the 19th century?
59826.e: After a fungus (coffee rust) destroyed the coffee plantations of the British colony of Ceylon, the planters switched to tea. Ceylon tea is still an important export today.
59826.m: In Sri Lanka's highlands, tea replaced coffee in the 19th century.

59827.q: What lies behind the insulting term “banana republic” for countries in Central America?
a: The great political influence of foreign fruit companies
A ban on banana exports to Europe
A currency linked to the price of bananas
The banana originally coming from Central America
59827.e: US companies such as the United Fruit Company owned huge banana plantations and had strong influence on governments. The writer O. Henry coined the term in 1904.
59827.m: The term banana republic refers to the power of fruit companies in Central America.

59828.q: Which banana variety dominates world trade today and is threatened by the fungal disease TR4 (Panama disease)?
59828.e: From the 1950s, the Cavendish replaced the Gros Michel, which was wiped out by an earlier form of Panama disease. Because all the plants are almost genetically identical, the new pathogen TR4 spreads easily.
59828.m: Genetically uniform plantations are especially vulnerable to disease.

a: Plants grown for the farmers' own needs
Catch crops to improve the soil
59829.e: Cash crops such as coffee, cocoa, cotton or tea are grown to earn money, often for export. They are typical of plantations.
59829.m: Cash crops are grown for sale, not for eating at home.

59830.q: Which plantation crop comes from the Amazon region but is grown mainly in Southeast Asia today?
59830.e: Seeds of the Pará rubber tree were taken from Brazil to London in 1876, and from there to British colonies in Asia. Today most natural rubber comes from Southeast Asia, above all from Thailand and Indonesia.
59830.m: The rubber tree moved from the Amazon to the plantations of Southeast Asia.

a: Producing mainly for your own needs
Producing mainly for the world market
Producing on behalf of a large company
59831.e: In subsistence farming, a household produces most of what it needs to live itself. Money and markets play only a small role.
59831.m: Subsistence farmers produce first and foremost for their own family.

59832.q: What do you call a type of farming in which farmers use most of what they produce themselves but sell surpluses at local markets?
59832.e: Many smallholders around the world live by semi-subsistence farming. They first cover their own needs and then sell surpluses to get money for school fees or tools.
59832.m: Most of the world's smallholders combine feeding themselves with some selling.

59833.q: Which three crops are traditionally grown together in the Mesoamerican milpa?
59833.e: The maize gives the beans something to climb, the beans fix nitrogen, and the large squash leaves shade the soil. These “three sisters” also complement each other in the diet.
59833.m: In the milpa, maize, beans and squash grow together as the three sisters.

59834.q: Which root crop is a staple food on many subsistence farms in Africa because it grows even on poor soils and in drought?
59834.e: Cassava (manioc) comes from South America and produces starchy root tubers. The tubers can stay in the ground for a long time and so serve as a reserve for hard times.
59834.m: Cassava is an important reserve for many smallholders in the tropics.

59835.q: According to the FAO, how big are most of the world's farms?
59835.e: According to an FAO study from 2021, about 84 per cent of all farms work less than 2 hectares. But they use only about 12 per cent of the farmland.
59835.m: The great majority of the world's farms are very small.

59836.q: Why are households in subsistence farming especially vulnerable to hunger crises?
a: Without money, failed harvests can hardly be made up for by buying food
They are not allowed to eat their own harvest
They only grow plants for export
They receive fixed deliveries from the state every year
59836.e: Anyone with hardly any cash or stores cannot bridge a drought or a pest attack by buying food. A single bad harvest can then mean hunger.
59836.m: Without money and stores, a failed harvest quickly becomes an emergency for subsistence farmers.

59837.q: Why do subsistence farmers often rely on mixed cropping rather than monoculture?
a: It spreads the risk of crop failure
It gets them higher export prices
It makes harvesting with machines easier
It means they need more mineral fertiliser
59837.e: If one type of plant fails because of drought or pests, the others still provide food. Mixed crops also make varied use of soil and light.
59837.m: Mixed crops are a kind of insurance against failed harvests for smallholders.

59838.q: On many subsistence farms south of the Sahara, who does a large part of the field work and food supply?
59838.e: In many regions of Africa, women farm the fields for staple foods, fetch water and process the harvest. Even so, they often have fewer rights to land than men.
59838.m: In many African smallholdings, women carry the main burden of food production.

59839.q: Why are rice fields flooded in wet rice farming?
a: The water suppresses weeds, which the rice itself can tolerate
Rice can only germinate and flower under water
The water protects the ears from birds
The flooding replaces harvesting the grains
59839.e: Rice has air-conducting tissue and survives in standing water, but most weeds do not. The water also evens out the temperature and keeps nutrients available.
59839.m: The water in a rice field mainly keeps the weeds in check.

59840.q: Which greenhouse gas is produced in flooded rice fields by microorganisms when there is little oxygen?
59840.e: In the oxygen-poor mud, bacteria break down organic material into methane. Rice fields are therefore among the important human-made sources of methane.
59840.m: Wet rice fields release the greenhouse gas methane.

59841.q: What share of the world's rice production comes from Asia?
59841.e: According to the FAO, about 90 per cent of rice is grown in Asia and also eaten there. The largest producers are China and India.
59841.m: Rice is mainly an Asian staple food.

59842.q: Which country has been the world's largest rice exporter since 2012?
59842.e: India overtook Thailand in 2012 and has since supplied about 40 per cent of rice exports worldwide. Indian export restrictions therefore have a strong effect on world market prices.
59842.m: India is the most important supplier of rice on the world market.

59843.q: What is the traditional method called in which rice seedlings are raised in a seedbed and then planted by hand in the flooded field?
59843.e: The seedlings grow for a few weeks in the seedbed and are then planted in rows in the field. This is labour-intensive, but it gives the plants a head start over weeds.
59843.m: In wet rice farming, the seedlings are often transplanted by hand.

59844.q: Which conditions allow two or three wet rice harvests a year in parts of South and Southeast Asia?
a: High temperatures all year round and enough water
Cold winters with a protective layer of snow
A long dry season with no irrigation at all
59844.e: In the inner tropics there is no cold season that stops growth. Where monsoon rains and irrigation provide enough water, the harvests therefore follow each other closely.
59844.m: Warmth and water all year make several rice harvests possible.

59845.q: Which animals do some farmers in Asia put into flooded rice fields because they eat weeds and pests?
59845.e: Ducks swim between the rice plants, eat weeds and insects and fertilise the field with their droppings. So fewer sprays are needed.
59845.m: Ducks help against weeds and pests in the rice field.

59846.q: How can wet rice farming save water and release less methane at the same time?
a: By alternately flooding the fields and letting them dry out
By keeping the fields deeply flooded all year
By spreading more artificial fertiliser on the fields
By only growing rice in winter
59846.e: When the water drains away from time to time, oxygen gets into the soil and the methane-producing bacteria are slowed down. Yields hardly fall.
59846.m: Alternate flooding and drying makes rice farming more climate-friendly.

59847.q: Which irrigation method brings water through hoses directly to the plant roots and was greatly developed in Israel?
59847.e: In drip irrigation, the water reaches the root drop by drop, so hardly any evaporates. In Israel the technique was spread commercially from the 1960s.
59847.m: Drip irrigation is the most economical way to water fields.

59848.q: What are the traditional irrigation channels in Valais called in German, known as “bisses” in French?
59848.e: Since the Middle Ages, the Suonen have carried glacier water over long distances to the dry meadows and vineyards of Valais. Many are popular walking paths today.
59848.m: In dry Valais, the Suonen bring water to meadows and vines.

59849.q: What are the underground tunnels in Iran called that carry groundwater on a natural slope to fields and settlements?
59849.e: A qanat taps groundwater at the foot of a mountain range and leads it to the surface in a gently sloping tunnel, without a pump. The technique is several thousand years old.
59849.m: Qanats carry groundwater underground without a pump.

59850.q: What share of the world's freshwater withdrawal goes to farming, mainly for irrigation?
59850.e: According to the FAO database AQUASTAT, about 70 per cent of the freshwater withdrawn goes to farming. Industry and households share the rest.
59850.m: Farming is the world's largest user of water.

59851.q: What do you call arable farming that relies only on rainfall without artificial irrigation?
59851.e: In rain-fed farming, the harvest depends entirely on rain, which is a big risk in dry areas. Most of the world's farmland is farmed in this way.
59851.m: Rain-fed farming depends on the weather; irrigated farming less so.

59852.q: What was the effect of the Aswan High Dam, completed in 1970, on farming in the Nile valley?
a: Irrigation all year, but no more fertilising Nile mud
More natural Nile mud, but only one harvest
The end of all irrigation in the Nile valley
An increase in the yearly Nile floods
59852.e: The reservoir makes several harvests a year possible because water is stored. But the fertile mud stays in Lake Nasser, so farmers need more artificial fertiliser.
59852.m: The Aswan High Dam brought water all year, but no more Nile mud.

59853.q: What is the name of the large Libyan project that carries fossil groundwater from the Sahara to the coast through pipelines?
59853.e: Since the 1990s, the project has been pumping water from the Nubian Sandstone Aquifer. It supplies cities and irrigated land on the Libyan coast.
59853.m: With the Great Man-Made River, Libya pumps ancient groundwater from the desert.

59854.q: Why is irrigation with fossil groundwater considered unsustainable?
a: It hardly forms again in today's climate
It contains too much oxygen for plants
It flows back into the sea by itself
59854.e: Fossil groundwater formed thousands of years ago in wetter climate periods. What is pumped out today is practically not replaced.
59854.m: Fossil groundwater is a finite resource.

59855.q: Roughly what share of world palm oil production do Indonesia and Malaysia have together?
59855.e: Indonesia alone supplies more than half of the world's palm oil, Malaysia another quarter. Together they account for about 85 per cent.
59855.m: Almost all of the world's palm oil comes from Indonesia and Malaysia.

59856.q: Which region does the oil palm (Elaeis guineensis) originally come from?
59856.e: The oil palm is native to western and central Africa, which the species name “guineensis” also points to. It was only introduced to Southeast Asia in colonial times.
59856.m: The oil palm came to Southeast Asia from West Africa.

59857.q: Why is the oil palm so attractive economically for producers?
a: It gives the highest oil yield per hectare of all oil crops
It also grows in Europe's temperate climate
It only has to be harvested every ten years
It needs neither light nor water
59857.e: One hectare of oil palms produces several tonnes of oil a year, many times more than rapeseed, soya or sunflowers. The palm also bears fruit for about 25 years.
59857.m: No other oil crop gives as much oil per area as the oil palm.

59858.q: Which ecosystems are drained in Indonesia for oil palm plantations, releasing especially large amounts of CO2?
59858.e: Peat soils store huge amounts of carbon. If they are drained, the peat decomposes or burns, as in the great fires of 2015.
59858.m: Drained peat bogs release enormous amounts of carbon dioxide.

59859.q: Which great apes on Borneo and Sumatra are especially threatened by the spread of oil palm plantations?
59859.e: Orangutans live almost only in the rainforests of Borneo and Sumatra. Turning these forests into plantations destroys and breaks up their habitat.
59859.m: Orangutans are losing their habitat to oil palm plantations.

59860.q: What is a sustainability label for palm oil such as RSPO mainly meant to ensure?
a: That no valuable primary forest was cleared for the plantation
That the oil was pressed in Switzerland
That the palms are genetically modified
That the oil is especially cheap
59860.e: The “Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil” forbids, among other things, clearing primary forest and areas especially worth protecting. Critics complain, however, that the checks are too lax.
59860.m: The RSPO awards a certificate for more sustainable palm oil.

59861.q: What was the result of the Swiss popular vote of 7 March 2021 on the free trade agreement with Indonesia, in which palm oil was the central issue?
59861.e: The agreement was accepted with 51.6 per cent of the votes. Tariff reductions only apply to palm oil that meets certain sustainability requirements.
59861.m: In 2021, voters narrowly said yes to free trade with Indonesia.

59862.q: What does Indonesia increasingly use a large share of its palm oil for in its own country?
a: As a coolant in power stations
As a binder in road building
59862.e: Indonesia requires an ever higher blend of palm oil biodiesel in diesel, about 40 per cent from 2025. This keeps more palm oil in the country.
59862.m: Indonesia increasingly uses palm oil as fuel.

59863.q: From which part of the fruit is palm oil obtained, unlike palm kernel oil?
a: From the flesh of the fruit
59863.e: Palm oil is pressed from the orange-red flesh of the fruit. Palm kernel oil comes from the seed in the middle of the fruit and has a different composition.
59863.m: Palm oil comes from the flesh, palm kernel oil from the kernel.

59864.q: Which country was replaced by Brazil as the world's largest soya producer around 2020?
59864.e: Brazil replaced the USA as the largest soya producer in the 2019/20 season. It is also by far the largest exporter of soya beans.
59864.m: Brazil is the world's most important soya country today.

59865.q: Which Brazilian state harvests the most soya?
59865.e: Mato Grosso in the Centre-West supplies more than a quarter of Brazil's soya harvest. It is grown there on huge, highly mechanised farms.
59865.m: Mato Grosso is the centre of Brazilian soya growing.

59866.q: What is most of the world's soya harvest used for?
59866.e: About three quarters of soya beans are processed into protein-rich soya meal, which is fed to pigs, poultry and cattle. Only a small part is eaten directly by people.
59866.m: Most soya beans end up as animal feed.

59867.q: Which country is the most important buyer of Brazilian soya beans?
59867.e: China buys about three quarters of Brazil's soya exports, mainly as feed for its large pig farming industry. Trade conflicts between China and the USA strengthened this dependence.
59867.m: China is the most important customer for Brazilian soya.

59868.q: What did large agricultural traders commit to with the Soy Moratorium of 2006?
a: Not to buy soya from newly cleared Amazon land
To end soya growing in Brazil completely
To transport soya only by rail
59868.e: The traders promised not to buy soya from land in the Amazon rainforest that was cleared after a cut-off date (now July 2008). This clearly slowed direct deforestation for soya in the Amazon.
59868.m: The Soy Moratorium is meant to protect the Amazon from clearing for soya.

59869.q: Which state research institute made soya growable in Brazil's tropical savannahs through breeding and soil research?
59869.e: Embrapa, founded in 1973, bred soya varieties for tropical day lengths and developed methods to improve the soil. This made Brazil an agricultural superpower.
59869.m: Embrapa's agricultural research opened Brazil's savannahs to soya.

59870.q: How are the very acidic soils of the Brazilian savannahs made usable for soya growing?
59870.e: The old, heavily weathered soils are acidic and contain a lot of aluminium. Lime is used to raise the pH value, and then fertiliser is applied in a targeted way.
59870.m: Lime makes acidic savannah soils fertile for soya.

59871.q: What does the long rainy season allow many soya farmers in Brazil to do?
a: Grow a second crop, usually maize, in the same year
Grow rice under water on every field
59871.e: Because the soya is harvested early, the rainy season is still long enough for a second crop. This second harvest, the safrinha, made Brazil one of the largest maize exporters.
59871.m: Many Brazilian fields produce two harvests a year.

a: All sectors from farm inputs through growing to processing and trade
Only selling farm products directly at the farm
State planning of farming in five-year plans
59872.e: Agribusiness covers the whole chain, from seed, fertiliser and machinery through farming to the food industry and trade. Large companies are often involved at several stages.
59872.m: Agribusiness refers to the whole value chain of food.

59873.q: At which university did John Davis and Ray Goldberg coin the term “agribusiness” in 1957?
59873.e: In 1957, the two economists from Harvard Business School described farming as part of a larger economic system in “A Concept of Agribusiness”.
59873.m: The term agribusiness comes from Harvard Business School.

59874.q: Which agrochemical and seed company based in Basel was taken over by the Chinese state company ChemChina in 2017?
59874.e: ChemChina bought Syngenta for about 43 billion US dollars, at the time the largest takeover by a Chinese company. The headquarters stayed in Basel.
59874.m: Syngenta is a Basel agricultural company in Chinese ownership.

59875.q: Which German company took over the US seed company Monsanto in 2018?
59875.e: Bayer paid about 63 billion US dollars for Monsanto. This created one of the largest suppliers of seed and pesticides in the world.
59875.m: With Monsanto, Bayer became a giant in the seed market.

59876.q: What does the abbreviation “ABCD” stand for in international agricultural trade?
a: Four quality labels for organic meat
59876.e: ABCD stands for ADM, Bunge, Cargill and Louis Dreyfus. These companies handle a large part of the world's trade in grain and oilseeds.
59876.m: A few trading companies control a large part of the grain trade.

59877.q: In agribusiness, what is meant by vertical integration?
a: One company controls several stages of the chain
A farm grows crops on floors stacked above each other
The state takes over all farms
59877.e: A vertically integrated company owns, for example, feed mills, fattening farms, slaughterhouses and distribution all at once. This way it controls costs and quality along the chain.
59877.m: Vertical integration brings several stages of production under one roof.

a: Farmers deliver to a buyer on terms agreed in advance
Farmers rent their land from the state anew every year
Farmers swap their harvest with each other without money
Farmers only sell at weekly markets
59878.e: A processor or trader sets the quantity, quality and often the price in advance and sometimes provides seed or advice. The farmers get a secure market, but become dependent.
59878.m: In contract farming, the buyer is known before sowing.

59879.q: Why do farmers usually have to buy hybrid seed again every year?
a: The offspring lose the yield advantages
Saving seed is banned by law everywhere
59879.e: Hybrid varieties come from crossing two parent lines and grow especially vigorously in the first generation. In the next generation the traits separate and yields fall.
59879.m: Hybrid seed only pays off in the first generation.

59880.q: Which Swiss city is an important international trading centre for agricultural commodities such as grain, oilseeds and sugar?
59880.e: Many large commodity traders have their headquarters or important branches in the Geneva region. A considerable share of world trade in grain and oilseeds is handled from there.
59880.m: Geneva is a hub of the world's agricultural commodity trade.

59881.q: What does the term land grabbing refer to?
a: Large-scale land acquisition by investors at the expense of local users
Dividing up large estates among smallholders
59881.e: In land grabbing, companies, states or funds buy or lease large areas, often in countries of the Global South. The previous users are often pushed out without any say.
59881.m: Land grabbing takes away local people's access to their land.

59882.q: Which crisis triggered a wave of large land deals abroad from 2007/2008?
59882.e: When grain prices rose sharply, countries that depended on imports wanted to secure their supplies. At the same time, investors were looking for safe investments in farmland.
59882.m: Rising food prices made farmland a sought-after investment.

59883.q: Which South Korean company wanted to lease about 1.3 million hectares of land in Madagascar in 2008, leading to fierce protests?
59883.e: The project was mainly meant to supply maize and palm oil for South Korea. The protests against it contributed to the fall of the government in 2009, after which the deal was stopped.
59883.m: The Daewoo deal in Madagascar became a symbol of land grabbing.

59884.q: What is the name of the independent database that records large international land deals worldwide?
59884.e: Since 2012, the Land Matrix has collected information on land deals of 200 hectares or more. Partners include the Centre for Development and Environment at the University of Bern.
59884.m: The Land Matrix makes large land deals publicly visible.

59885.q: Which UN organisation based in Rome works for food security and helped shape guidelines to protect land rights?
59885.e: The FAO is the Food and Agriculture Organization of the UN and is based in Rome. In 2012, voluntary guidelines meant to strengthen the land rights of poor farming families were adopted with its involvement.
59885.m: The FAO also works for fair land rights.

59886.q: Why are smallholders particularly vulnerable to land grabbing?
a: They often only have customary land rights that are not registered
They usually own several plots abroad
They are not allowed by law to sell land
They live almost only in industrialised countries
59886.e: In many countries, land has been used for generations under customary law, without being entered in a land register. Formally it then often belongs to the state, which can hand it to investors.
59886.m: Without registered land rights, smallholders can easily be pushed out.

59887.q: Investors from which region were especially active in looking for farmland abroad after 2008 to secure their food supply despite water shortages?
59887.e: Countries short of water, such as Saudi Arabia or the United Arab Emirates, can hardly grow grain. They therefore leased land in Africa, Asia and Eastern Europe, for example.
59887.m: Gulf States that are short of water secure farmland abroad.

a: Taking land in the name of environmental goals such as CO2 offsetting
Planting greenery on flat roofs in cities
Returning cleared land to the forest
59888.e: Nature reserves, reforestation or CO2 offsetting projects can also claim land that local people used before. If they are pushed out, this is called green grabbing.
59888.m: Environmental projects can also take land away from local people.

59889.q: Where and when was today's common definition of food security set at the World Food Summit?
59889.e: At the FAO's World Food Summit in Rome in 1996, it was defined that all people should have access to enough safe and nutritious food at all times. This definition is still used today.
59889.m: The definition of food security comes from the World Food Summit of 1996.

59890.q: Which four dimensions of food security does the FAO distinguish?
59890.e: Food must be available, people must be able to afford it, the body must be able to use it well, and all of this permanently. If one dimension is missing, food is insecure.
59890.m: Food security needs availability, access, utilisation and stability.

59891.q: Which of the 17 UN Sustainable Development Goals aims to end hunger by 2030?
59891.e: The second goal is called “Zero Hunger” and aims to end hunger, achieve food security and promote sustainable farming. The goals were adopted in 2015.
59891.m: The UN's second Sustainable Development Goal is called “Zero Hunger”.

a: A lack of vitamins and minerals despite enough calories
Hunger that only happens at night
Hunger among animals in factory farming
59892.e: Someone who eats a one-sided diet can be full and still take in too little iron, iodine, zinc or vitamin A. This weakens health and development, especially in children.
59892.m: Even people who are full can suffer from hidden hunger.

59893.q: According to the UN food report SOFI 2025, how many people suffered from hunger in 2024?
59893.e: The report estimates the number of hungry people in 2024 at about 673 million, about 8 per cent of the world's population. Africa and Western Asia are especially affected.
59893.m: About one in twelve people in the world did not have enough to eat in 2024.

59894.q: Which UN organisation received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2020 for its fight against hunger?
59894.e: The World Food Programme (WFP), based in Rome, provides food aid in crisis areas. The Nobel Committee also honoured its contribution to preventing hunger being used as a weapon of war.
59894.m: The World Food Programme received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2020.

59895.q: How high was Switzerland's level of food self-sufficiency in 2024?
59895.e: According to Agristat, domestic production covered about half of food consumption in 2024, a record low. For animal products the figure, at about 93 per cent, was much higher than for plant products at about 31 per cent.
59895.m: Switzerland produces about half of its food itself.

59896.q: What does food sovereignty, a concept of the smallholder movement La Via Campesina, mean?
a: The right of peoples to decide their own farming and food policy
The duty of every country to import all its food
Completely free agricultural trade without tariffs
Feeding the population only with ready meals
59896.e: La Via Campesina presented the concept in 1996. It stresses local production, the rights of smallholders and democratic participation instead of pure market logic.
59896.m: Food sovereignty puts self-determination over the food system at the centre.

59897.q: How do semi-nomads differ from full nomads?
a: They have a fixed home and often do some arable farming
They roam around without any animals
They only move from place to place in cities
59897.e: With semi-nomads, part of the family stays in a fixed settlement with fields while others move on with the herds for a time. Full nomads have no fixed home.
59897.m: Semi-nomads combine moving herds with a fixed place to live.

a: Seasonal movement of herds with herders, while the owners stay settled
Whole families permanently roaming with tents
59898.e: In transhumance, herders move the herds back and forth between summer and winter pastures, for example between mountains and lowlands. The owners of the animals live permanently in the village.
59898.m: In transhumance, only the herds and their herders move.

59899.q: Which people of the Sahara traditionally lived as camel nomads and are known for the blue face veil worn by the men?
59899.e: The Tuareg live in the central Sahara and the Sahel, for example in Niger, Mali and Algeria. Among them, it is the men who wear the indigo-blue veil (tagelmust).
59899.m: The Tuareg are the best-known camel nomads of the Sahara.

59900.q: What is an extreme winter called in Mongolia, in which the nomads' livestock die in huge numbers?
59900.e: In a dzud, deep snow, ice or extreme cold stop the animals from finding food. In the winter of 2009/10, millions of farm animals died this way.
59900.m: A dzud is a threat to the very existence of Mongolian nomads.

59901.q: What effect does settling nomads often have on the pastures around settlements and wells?
59901.e: When large herds stay in the same place all the time, they eat the plants faster than they can grow back. This often creates bare, eroded areas around wells.
59901.m: Without moving, the pastures around settlements are quickly overused.

59902.q: Which herding people in Kenya and Tanzania lost large parts of their grazing land in colonial times and through protected areas such as the Serengeti?
59902.e: The Maasai traditionally keep mainly cattle and move with them between pastures. Colonial treaties and the creation of national parks greatly restricted their access to grazing land.
59902.m: The Maasai have lost a lot of grazing land through colonisation and protected areas.

59903.q: Which animals do the Sami in northern Scandinavia traditionally keep in mobile herding?
59903.e: Reindeer herding is a core part of Sami culture. The herds move between winter pastures in the forest and summer pastures in the mountains or on the coast.
59903.m: The Sami are traditionally reindeer herders.

59904.q: Why is mobile livestock farming in dry areas considered a well-adapted way of life?
a: It makes use of unevenly spread rainfall and pastures
It needs a lot of irrigation and fertiliser
It is only suitable for areas with constant rain
It needs no knowledge of the landscape at all
59904.e: In dry areas, rain falls very unevenly in space and time. Those who move with their herds to where grass is growing can use land that is too dry for arable farming.
59904.m: Nomads make dry areas usable for producing food.

59905.q: According to the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), what share of marine fish stocks is considered overfished?
59905.e: According to the FAO, just under two thirds of the stocks studied are fished sustainably; the rest are overfished. The share of overfished stocks has risen since the 1970s.
59905.m: More than a third of fish stocks in the sea are overfished.

59906.q: In fishing, what does “maximum sustainable yield” (MSY) mean?
a: The largest catch that is possible over time without the stock shrinking
The largest amount of fish a ship can load
The highest price fish fetches on the exchange
The number of days on which fishing is allowed
59906.e: With MSY, only as much is taken as is replaced through reproduction and growth. If more is caught, the stock shrinks.
59906.m: Sustainable fishing takes no more than grows back.

59907.q: What are lost or abandoned fishing nets called that keep catching animals in the sea?
59907.e: Ghost nets drift in the sea for years or get caught on wrecks and reefs. Fish, seals and turtles get tangled in them and die.
59907.m: Ghost nets go on fishing long after they have been lost.

59908.q: Why are deep-sea fish such as orange roughy overfished especially quickly?
a: They grow slowly and reproduce late
They only live in fresh water
They swim in huge shoals at the surface
They die naturally after a year
59908.e: Orange roughy can live for over 100 years. Stocks off New Zealand and Australia collapsed after a few years of intensive fishing because hardly any young fish followed.
59908.m: Slow-growing deep-sea fish are overfished especially quickly.

59909.q: What does the marine biologist Daniel Pauly describe with “fishing down marine food webs”?
a: Fishing switches to ever smaller species lower in the food chain
Fishing takes place in ever deeper layers of water
Fishing moves from rivers to the open sea
Fishing uses ever bigger predatory fish
59909.e: When large predatory fish such as cod or tuna are overfished, more smaller species such as sardines, krill or jellyfish are caught. Pauly described this trend in 1998.
59909.m: Overfishing works its way down the food chain.

59910.q: Which label, founded in 1997 by WWF and Unilever, certifies sustainable wild-caught fish?
59910.e: The Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) is now an independent organisation based in London. Its blue label marks fish from certified fisheries.
59910.m: The blue MSC label stands for certified wild-caught fish.

59911.q: What does the WTO agreement on fisheries subsidies, which came into force in September 2025, ban?
a: Subsidies for illegal fishing and for overfished stocks
All imports of fish from fish farms
59911.e: The agreement forbids state subsidies for illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing and for fishing overfished stocks. It is the first WTO agreement with an environmental goal at its centre.
59911.m: Since 2025, the WTO has banned harmful subsidies for fishing.

59912.q: Which fishing method is especially destructive to habitats on the seabed such as cold-water corals?
59912.e: Heavy bottom trawls are dragged across the seabed and tear away corals, sponges and other organisms. The habitats need decades or longer to recover.
59912.m: Bottom trawls practically plough up the seabed.

59913.q: According to the FAO, since when has aquaculture produced more aquatic animals worldwide than wild catch?
59913.e: In 2022, for the first time, slightly more than half of aquatic animals came from farming rather than wild catch. However, aquaculture only takes pressure off wild stocks if the feed itself is not made from wild fish.
59913.m: Since 2022, more fish has been farmed than caught in seas and rivers.

59914.q: How many countries does the Mekong pass through or along on its way to the sea?
59914.e: The Mekong flows through or along China, Myanmar, Laos, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam. This makes it a typical cross-border river.
59914.m: The Mekong links six countries in Asia.

59915.q: Which lake in Cambodia receives water from the Mekong in the rainy season because its outflow reverses direction?
59915.e: When the Mekong rises sharply in the monsoon, the Tonle Sap River flows backwards into the lake, which grows to many times its size. In the dry season the water flows out again.
59915.m: The Tonle Sap acts as a natural reservoir for the Mekong.

59916.q: Which country on the Mekong is not a full member of the Mekong River Commission, founded in 1995?
59916.e: The full members are Cambodia, Laos, Thailand and Vietnam. China and Myanmar are only dialogue partners, even though China runs numerous dams on the upper course.
59916.m: China controls the upper Mekong but is not a full member of the Mekong River Commission.

59917.q: Which system of waterfalls on the border between Laos and Cambodia prevents continuous shipping on the Mekong?
59917.e: The Khone Falls form a very wide system of rapids and cascades in southern Laos. Even the French colonial rulers failed to get ships past them.
59917.m: The Khone Falls interrupt the Mekong as a shipping route.

59918.q: What is the Mekong Delta called in Vietnamese (translated)?
59918.e: In Vietnamese, the Mekong in the delta is called Cửu Long, meaning “Nine Dragons”. The name refers to its many river mouths.
59918.m: The Vietnamese call the Mekong Delta the land of the nine dragons.

59919.q: Which capital city lies directly on the Mekong, opposite Thai territory?
59919.e: Vientiane, the capital of Laos, lies on the north bank of the Mekong, which forms the border with Thailand here. Bangkok lies on the Chao Phraya, Hanoi on the Red River.
59919.m: Vientiane looks across the Mekong to Thailand.

59920.q: What effect do large dams on the Mekong mainly have on fishing on the lower river?
a: They raise the water temperature sharply
They make the rainy season longer
59920.e: Many Mekong fish migrate upstream to spawn; dams such as the Xayaburi Dam in Laos cut off these routes. The reservoirs also hold back sediments that make the delta fertile.
59920.m: Dams on the Mekong endanger migrating fish and with them the food of millions of people.

59921.q: Which problem is getting worse in the Mekong Delta because of rising sea levels and a lack of sediment?
a: Salt getting into the rice fields
59921.e: Because less sediment arrives and the land is sinking, seawater pushes further into the delta. The salty water harms rice growing in one of the world's most important rice regions.
59921.m: The Mekong Delta becomes salty when the sea pushes further inland.

59922.q: Which is the largest river delta on Earth by area?
59922.e: The Ganges-Brahmaputra Delta covers over 100,000 square kilometres and is the largest delta in the world. It is often also called the Bengal Delta.
59922.m: The largest delta on Earth is in Bengal.

59923.q: Which two countries share the Ganges-Brahmaputra Delta?
59923.e: Most of the delta lies in Bangladesh, the western part in the Indian state of West Bengal.
59923.m: The Bengal Delta is shared by Bangladesh and India.

59924.q: What is the largest mangrove forest on Earth, in the Ganges-Brahmaputra Delta, called?
59924.e: The Sundarbans lie on the coast of the delta and are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The mangroves protect the land behind them from storm surges.
59924.m: The Sundarbans are the largest mangrove forest in the world.

59925.q: Which big cat lives in the mangrove forests of the Ganges-Brahmaputra Delta?
59925.e: One of the best-known tiger populations lives in the Sundarbans. The animals there are adapted to salt water and swimming.
59925.m: The Bengal tiger even hunts while swimming in the mangroves.

59926.q: What is the Ganges called in Bangladesh?
59926.e: After entering Bangladesh, the main arm of the Ganges is called the Padma. The Hooghly, on the other hand, is a distributary in India.
59926.m: In Bangladesh, the Ganges is called the Padma.

59927.q: What is the Brahmaputra called in Bangladesh?
59927.e: The main course of the Brahmaputra is called the Jamuna in Bangladesh. It should not be confused with the Indian Yamuna, a tributary of the Ganges.
59927.m: In Bangladesh, the Brahmaputra is called the Jamuna.

59928.q: Which tropical cyclone killed an estimated 300,000 to 500,000 people in the Ganges-Brahmaputra Delta in 1970?
59928.e: In November 1970, the Bhola cyclone hit the flat coast of what was then East Pakistan with an enormous storm surge. It is considered one of the deadliest cyclones in history.
59928.m: The flat delta is defenceless against storm surges from cyclones.

59929.q: Which natural poison contaminates the groundwater of many wells in Bangladesh?
59929.e: The sediments of the delta contain arsenic, which dissolves in the groundwater. Millions of people therefore drink contaminated well water.
59929.m: In many places, the groundwater in the Bengal Delta is contaminated with arsenic.

59930.q: How high is the Tibetan Plateau on average?
59930.e: The Tibetan Plateau lies at an average of about 4,500 metres above sea level. It is the highest and largest plateau on Earth.
59930.m: The Tibetan Plateau is higher than almost all Alpine peaks.

59931.q: Which nickname is often used for the Tibetan Plateau?
59931.e: Because of its enormous height and size, the Tibetan Plateau is called the “Roof of the World”. The term is also used for the Pamirs.
59931.m: Tibet is called the Roof of the World.

59932.q: Which process lifted up the Tibetan Plateau?
a: The collision of the Indian Plate with the Eurasian Plate
59932.e: For about 50 million years, the Indian Plate has been pushing northwards under Eurasia. This lifted the Himalayas and the plateau, a process that is still going on today.
59932.m: Tibet and the Himalayas were formed by India colliding with Eurasia.

59933.q: Which great river rises in Tibet, breaks through the Himalayas and reaches the sea in Bangladesh?
59933.e: In Tibet, the Brahmaputra flows east as the Yarlung Tsangpo. Then it breaks through the Himalayas in one of the deepest gorges on Earth and joins the Ganges in Bangladesh.
59933.m: The Brahmaputra comes from the Tibetan Plateau.

59934.q: Which city is the capital of the Tibet Autonomous Region?
59934.e: Lhasa lies at about 3,650 metres and, with the Potala Palace, is the traditional centre of Tibet.
59934.m: Lhasa is the capital of Tibet.

59935.q: Which railway line has crossed the Tanggula Pass, about 5,070 metres high, to Lhasa since 2006?
59935.e: The Qinghai-Tibet Railway is one of the highest railway lines in the world. A large part of it runs over permafrost, which is stabilised with cooling pipes.
59935.m: The Qinghai-Tibet Railway runs higher than any railway in the Alps.

59936.q: Why is the Tibetan Plateau also called the “water tower of Asia”?
a: It has the most rainfall in Asia
The tallest water tower stands there
It lies under a huge lake
59936.e: Glaciers and snowfields feed, for example, the Indus, the Yellow River and the Salween. Almost two billion people depend on water from this region.
59936.m: The Tibetan Plateau supplies large parts of Asia with water.

59937.q: Which kind of cattle is especially well adapted to life on the Tibetan Plateau?
59937.e: The yak has a thick coat, large lungs and many red blood cells. It provides herders with milk, wool, meat and fuel.
59937.m: The yak is the farm animal of the Tibetan Plateau.

59938.q: Where does the Yangtze rank among the longest rivers on Earth?
59938.e: At about 6,300 kilometres, the Yangtze is the third-longest river in the world after the Nile and the Amazon. It is the longest river in Asia.
59938.m: The Yangtze is the longest river in Asia.

59939.q: Which crop traditionally dominates farming south of the Yangtze?
59939.e: The Yangtze is seen as a rough boundary between northern and southern China. In the warm, humid south, wet rice is mainly grown, in the drier north it is more often wheat.
59939.m: South of the Yangtze, rice is the most important grain.

59940.q: Which animal of the Yangtze was declared functionally extinct in 2006 after an unsuccessful search?
59940.e: The Chinese river dolphin, also called the baiji, could no longer be found during a large expedition in 2006. Shipping, fishing and pollution are thought to be the causes.
59940.m: The baiji is a victim of the overuse of the Yangtze.

59941.q: Which central Chinese city of millions lies on the middle course of the Yangtze and is divided by it into several districts?
59941.e: Wuhan lies where a large tributary flows into the Yangtze and is an important transport hub. Xi'an and Harbin are in the north, Kunming in the south-west.
59941.m: Wuhan is the largest city on the middle Yangtze.

59942.q: Which big city lies at the upper end of the reservoir behind the Three Gorges Dam?
59942.e: Chongqing lies where the Jialing joins the Yangtze. Thanks to the reservoir, larger ships can sail as far as the city.
59942.m: Chongqing is the most important port on the upper Yangtze.

59943.q: What is the main reason why the Gobi Desert is so dry?
a: The rain shadow of the Himalayas
A cold ocean current off the coast
Constant foehn wind from the Alps
59943.e: The Himalayas and the plateau to the south keep out the moist monsoon winds from the Indian Ocean. In addition, the Gobi is very far from the sea.
59943.m: The Gobi lies in the rain shadow of high mountains.

59944.q: Which finds made the Gobi Desert world-famous in 1923 through Roy Chapman Andrews' expedition?
59944.e: At the “Flaming Cliffs” near Bayanzag, the team found the first dinosaur eggs recognised as such. The Gobi is still one of the richest sites for dinosaur finds today.
59944.m: Famous dinosaur eggs were found in the Gobi in 1923.

59945.q: Which climate is typical of the Gobi Desert?
59945.e: The Gobi is a cold-winter desert with an extreme continental climate. In winter temperatures can fall below minus 30 degrees, and in summer rise above plus 40 degrees.
59945.m: In the Gobi, temperatures vary enormously over the year.

59946.q: With which major project is China trying to slow the spread of the Gobi Desert?
59946.e: Since 1978, huge belts of protective forest have been planted in northern China. They are meant to hold back desertification and sandstorms, but how well they work is disputed.
59946.m: China's Green Wall is meant to stop the Gobi.

59947.q: Which island has the largest population in the world?
59947.e: More than half of Indonesia's population, about 150 million people, lives on Java. The island is fertile thanks to volcanic soils.
59947.m: Java is the most densely populated large island on Earth.

59948.q: Where does Indonesia rank among the most populous countries in the world (as of 2024)?
59948.e: With about 280 million people, Indonesia comes after India, China and the USA. It is also the country with the most Muslims.
59948.m: Indonesia is the fourth most populous country on Earth.

59949.q: What effect did the eruption of Tambora on the island of Sumbawa in 1815 have on Switzerland?
a: A series of earthquakes in Valais
59949.e: The ash and sulphur gases in the stratosphere cooled the climate. In 1816, Switzerland had snow in summer, failed harvests and a famine.
59949.m: A volcanic eruption in Indonesia brought Switzerland cold, failed harvests and hunger in 1816.

59950.q: Which boundary line in animal geography runs between the Indonesian islands of Bali and Lombok?
59950.e: Alfred Russel Wallace noticed that Asian animal species dominate to the west of it and Australian ones to the east. The reason is a deep sea channel that never ran dry, even when sea levels were low.
59950.m: The Wallace Line separates the animal life of Asia from that of Australia.

59951.q: With which country does Indonesia share the island of New Guinea?
59951.e: The western part of New Guinea belongs to Indonesia; the eastern part forms the country of Papua New Guinea. East Timor shares the island of Timor with Indonesia.
59951.m: New Guinea is divided between Indonesia and Papua New Guinea.

59952.q: Which Indonesian province was hit hardest by the tsunami of 26 December 2004?
59952.e: The undersea earthquake off the north-west coast of Sumatra had a magnitude of about 9.1. Well over 100,000 people died in Aceh.
59952.m: The tsunami of 2004 devastated Aceh above all.

59953.q: From which country did Singapore separate in 1965 to become independent?
59953.e: Singapore was part of the Federation of Malaysia from 1963, but left in 1965 after political conflicts. Since then it has been an independent city-state.
59953.m: Singapore has been an independent city-state since 1965.

59954.q: Who founded a British trading post in Singapore in 1819?
59954.e: Thomas Stamford Raffles recognised the favourable location on an important sea route. Singapore then quickly became an important free port.
59954.m: Raffles laid the foundation for modern Singapore in 1819.

59955.q: Roughly how large is Singapore's land area (as of 2023)?
59955.e: At about 730 square kilometres, Singapore is roughly the size of the canton of Glarus. About six million people live on this area.
59955.m: Singapore is smaller than many Swiss cantons.

59956.q: How has Singapore greatly increased its land area since independence?
a: By reclaiming land from the sea
By moving the border into Malaysia
59956.e: For decades, Singapore has been piling sand and soil into the sea and has increased its area by about a quarter in this way. Changi Airport also partly stands on reclaimed land.
59956.m: Singapore is growing out into the sea.

59957.q: Which language is NOT one of Singapore's four official languages?
59957.e: The official languages are English, Malay, Mandarin and Tamil. Malay is also the national language, and English the most important common language.
59957.m: Singapore has four official languages, just as Switzerland has several national languages.

59958.q: What is the treated wastewater called with which Singapore covers part of its water needs?
59958.e: Because Singapore has hardly any water sources of its own, it treats wastewater with membrane filters and UV light to drinking water quality. It also imports water from Malaysia and desalinates seawater.
59958.m: Singapore turns wastewater back into clean water.

59959.q: Who was Singapore's first prime minister?
59959.e: Lee Kuan Yew governed from 1959 to 1990 and turned Singapore into a wealthy centre of trade and finance. Mahathir Mohamad was prime minister of Malaysia.
59959.m: Lee Kuan Yew is seen as the founding father of modern Singapore.

59960.q: Along which line of latitude was Korea divided into a Soviet and an American occupation zone in 1945?
59960.e: In 1945, the USA and the Soviet Union agreed to divide Korea at the 38th parallel. Today's border runs roughly along this line.
59960.m: The 38th parallel stands for the division of Korea.

59961.q: Roughly how wide is the Demilitarised Zone between North and South Korea?
59961.e: The zone extends two kilometres on each side of the demarcation line and is about 250 kilometres long. It is one of the most heavily guarded borders in the world.
59961.m: The Demilitarised Zone separates the two Koreas across a width of about four kilometres.

59963.q: Which volcano, at about 2,744 metres, is the highest mountain on the Korean Peninsula?
59963.e: Paektusan lies on the border between North Korea and China and has a crater lake. Its eruption around the year 946 was one of the most powerful of the last few thousand years.
59963.m: Paektusan is the highest mountain in Korea.

59964.q: Roughly what share of the Korean Peninsula is mountainous?
59964.e: About 70 per cent of the peninsula is mountainous. The population and farming are therefore concentrated on the plains in the west and south.
59964.m: Korea is a mainly mountainous country.

59965.q: Which sea borders the Korean Peninsula to the west?
59965.e: The Yellow Sea lies between Korea and China and is named after the yellow loess that rivers carry into it. To the east lies the Sea of Japan.
59965.m: West of Korea lies the Yellow Sea.

59966.q: Which peninsula is the largest on Earth by area?
59966.e: The Arabian Peninsula covers about three million square kilometres. Saudi Arabia takes up most of it.
59966.m: The Arabian Peninsula is the largest peninsula in the world.

59967.q: What is the largest continuous sand desert on Earth, in the south of the Arabian Peninsula, called?
59967.e: The Rub al Khali, the “Empty Quarter”, is about the size of France. Its dunes reach heights of over 200 metres.
59967.m: The Rub al Khali is the largest sea of sand on Earth.

59968.q: Which strait between Oman and Iran is a bottleneck for oil transport from the Persian Gulf?
59968.e: About a fifth of the world's traded oil is shipped through the Strait of Hormuz. It links the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman.
59968.m: The Strait of Hormuz is the oil gateway of the Persian Gulf.

59969.q: What are the mostly dry river valleys on the Arabian Peninsula called that only carry water after rain?
59969.e: The Arabian Peninsula has no rivers that flow all the time. After rare heavy rain, however, wadis can carry dangerous flash floods.
59969.m: A wadi only carries water after rain.

59970.q: How do the Gulf States cover most of their drinking water needs?
59970.e: Without rivers and with very little rainfall, countries such as Qatar or Kuwait depend on desalination plants. These need a lot of energy.
59970.m: The Gulf States mainly drink desalinated seawater.

59971.q: In which country is the highest mountain on the Arabian Peninsula?
59971.e: Jabal an-Nabi Shuayb in Yemen is over 3,600 metres high. Thanks to the monsoon, the mountains in the south-west get more rain than the rest of the peninsula.
59971.m: The highest mountains in Arabia are in Yemen.

59972.q: Which geological process is separating the Arabian Peninsula from Africa?
a: Sinking under the weight of glaciers
59972.e: The Arabian Plate is drifting away from the African Plate. This created the rift of the Red Sea, which keeps opening further.
59972.m: The Red Sea is getting wider because Arabia is drifting away from Africa.

59973.q: Why is the Caspian Sea geographically considered a lake rather than a sea?
a: It has no connection to the ocean
It is smaller than Lake Constance
59973.e: The Caspian Sea is an inland body of water with no outflow and no natural connection to the world's oceans. At about 371,000 square kilometres, it is the largest lake on Earth.
59973.m: The Caspian Sea is the largest lake in the world.

59974.q: Which river supplies about four fifths of the water flowing into the Caspian Sea?
59974.e: The Volga is Europe's longest river and flows into the sea through a large delta near Astrakhan. It brings most of the water.
59974.m: The Volga is the lifeline of the Caspian Sea.

59975.q: Which country does NOT border the Caspian Sea?
59975.e: The countries on its shores are Russia, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Iran and Azerbaijan. Georgia lies to the west, on the Black Sea.
59975.m: Five countries share the shores of the Caspian Sea.

59976.q: On average, how salty is the Caspian Sea compared with the ocean?
59976.e: The salt content averages about 1.2 per cent, while the ocean has about 3.5 per cent. In the north, near the mouth of the Volga, the water is almost fresh.
59976.m: The Caspian Sea is a brackish lake.

59977.q: Why does salt settle out in shallow, almost cut-off bays on the eastern shore of the Caspian Sea?
a: Strong evaporation in the hot desert climate
The water freezes completely in winter
59977.e: In the Kara-Bogaz-Gol bay in Turkmenistan, more water evaporates in the desert climate than flows in. The salt stays behind and builds up.
59977.m: Strong evaporation makes salt settle out in cut-off bays.

59978.q: Which fish provide the sought-after caviar in the Caspian Sea?
59978.e: Caviar comes from the eggs of sturgeon such as the great sturgeon, also called beluga. Because of overfishing, most sturgeon species are now seriously endangered.

59979.q: To which group of animals does the only mammal living in the Caspian Sea belong?
59979.e: The Caspian seal is the only mammal species in the Caspian Sea and lives nowhere else. It gives birth to its young on the ice in the north in winter.
59979.m: The Caspian seal is endemic to the Caspian Sea.

59980.q: Which sea lies to the west of the Kamchatka Peninsula?
59980.e: Kamchatka separates the Sea of Okhotsk in the west from the Pacific and the Bering Sea in the east. The peninsula belongs to Russia.
59980.m: Kamchatka lies between the Sea of Okhotsk and the Pacific.

59981.q: Which natural wonder on Kamchatka did the geologist Tatiana Ustinova discover in 1941?
59981.e: The Valley of Geysers is one of the largest geyser fields in the world. In 2007, a landslide buried some of the springs.
59981.m: In the Valley of Geysers on Kamchatka, hot water shoots out of the ground.

59982.q: Why are there so many volcanoes on Kamchatka?
a: The Pacific Plate sinks beneath it there
There is a hotspot there like in Hawaii
59982.e: Off the east coast, the Pacific Plate sinks down in the Kuril-Kamchatka Trench. The rising magma feeds about 30 active volcanoes.
59982.m: Kamchatka is part of the Pacific Ring of Fire.

59983.q: What is special about the capital, Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky?
a: It has no road connection to the rest of Russia
It lies on a volcanic crater
It is the northernmost city in the world
It can only be reached by railway
59983.e: Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky can only be reached by plane or ship. The city lies on Avacha Bay on the Pacific.
59983.m: You can only get to Kamchatka by sea or by air.

59984.q: Which fish are the most important food source for the many brown bears on Kamchatka?
59984.e: Every year, millions of salmon swim up the rivers to spawn. The bears eat them to build up fat reserves for the winter.
59984.m: In summer, Kamchatka's bears live on salmon.

59985.q: How strong was the earthquake off Kamchatka in November 1952?
59985.e: The 1952 earthquake is one of the strongest ever measured and triggered a tsunami across the Pacific. In 2025, too, an earthquake of magnitude 8.8 shook the region.
59985.m: Some of the strongest earthquakes in the world happen off Kamchatka.

59986.q: Which navigator in Russian service led the Kamchatka expeditions in the 18th century?
59986.e: The Dane Vitus Bering explored the North Pacific from Kamchatka. The Bering Strait and the Bering Sea are named after him.
59986.m: From Kamchatka, Vitus Bering explored the route to America.

59987.q: For how many years did Britain lease the New Territories from China in 1898?
59987.e: The lease ran out in 1997. Because Hong Kong could hardly survive without the New Territories, Britain gave the whole colony back to China.
59987.m: The lease of the New Territories decided the end of British rule in Hong Kong.

59988.q: Until which year did China guarantee Hong Kong a high degree of autonomy under the principle of “one country, two systems”?
59988.e: The Sino-British Joint Declaration guaranteed Hong Kong its economic and legal system for 50 years after the handover.
59988.m: Hong Kong's special status is guaranteed until 2047.

59989.q: Besides Hong Kong, which area is the second Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China?
59989.e: Macau was a Portuguese colony and was handed back to China in 1999. Shenzhen is a special economic zone, not a special administrative region.
59989.m: China has two special administrative regions: Hong Kong and Macau.

59990.q: At the mouth of which river does Hong Kong lie?
59990.e: Hong Kong lies on the eastern edge of the Pearl River Delta on the South China Sea. The delta, with Guangzhou and Shenzhen, is one of the largest urban regions in the world.
59990.m: Hong Kong lies on the Pearl River Delta.

59991.q: To which currency has the Hong Kong dollar been pegged since 1983?
59991.e: Hong Kong has a currency board that keeps the rate in a narrow band around 7.8 Hong Kong dollars per US dollar. The peg stayed in place after the handover.
59991.m: The Hong Kong dollar is firmly linked to the US dollar.

59992.q: Which language do most people in Hong Kong speak in everyday life?
59992.e: The official languages are Chinese and English, but about nine out of ten people speak Cantonese in everyday life. Mandarin has been gaining importance since the handover.
59992.m: In everyday life, people in Hong Kong mainly speak Cantonese.

59993.q: Through which deep gorge does the upper Yangtze flow in Yunnan province?
59993.e: Tiger Leaping Gorge lies between two mountain massifs over 5,000 metres high and is one of the deepest gorges on Earth. According to legend, a tiger leapt across the river at the narrowest point.
59993.m: On its upper course, the Yangtze squeezes through Tiger Leaping Gorge.

59994.q: Which largest freshwater lake in China is connected to the Yangtze and serves as its overflow basin?
59994.e: Poyang Lake in Jiangxi province fills up a lot when the Yangtze floods and shrinks greatly in dry periods. It is an important wintering area for cranes.
59994.m: Poyang Lake buffers the floods of the Yangtze.

59995.q: Which mountain range extends far into the Mongolian Gobi as an offshoot?
59995.e: The Gobi-Altai is the south-eastern offshoot of the Mongolian Altai. Its bare ranges divide the desert into basins.
59995.m: The Gobi-Altai runs through the Gobi Desert.

59996.q: Which raw materials are mainly mined in the huge Oyu Tolgoi mine in the South Gobi?
59996.e: Oyu Tolgoi is one of the largest copper and gold deposits in the world. Mining is very important for Mongolia's economy.
59996.m: There are huge copper deposits beneath the Gobi.

59997.q: Which Indonesian volcano exploded so violently in 1883 that the bang could be heard thousands of kilometres away?
59997.e: The eruption of Krakatoa in the Sunda Strait triggered huge tsunamis that killed about 36,000 people. The pressure wave was recorded by barometers all over the world.
59997.m: The Krakatoa eruption of 1883 could be measured worldwide.

59998.q: Which largest volcanic lake on Earth is on Sumatra?
59998.e: Lake Toba fills the caldera of a supervolcano that erupted about 74,000 years ago. It was one of the largest volcanic eruptions of the last few million years.
59998.m: Lake Toba is the crater of a supervolcano.

59999.q: What is the causeway called that has linked Singapore with Johor Bahru in Malaysia since 1924?
59999.e: Road, railway and water pipes run across the Johor-Singapore Causeway. It is one of the busiest border crossings in the world.
59999.m: The Causeway links Singapore with Malaysia.

60000.q: Which city in south-east South Korea is the country's largest port?
60000.e: Busan lies on the Korea Strait opposite Japan and is South Korea's second-largest city. Its container port is one of the largest in the world.
60000.m: Busan is South Korea's gateway to the sea.

60001.q: Which strait separates the Korean Peninsula from Japan?
60001.e: The Korea Strait links the Sea of Japan with the East China Sea. The Japanese island of Tsushima lies in it.
60001.m: The Korea Strait lies between Korea and Japan.

60002.q: Which Saudi port city on the Red Sea is the gateway for pilgrims to Mecca?
60002.e: Jeddah lies about 70 kilometres west of Mecca. Dammam is on the Persian Gulf, Riyadh inland and Muscat in Oman.
60002.m: Jeddah is Saudi Arabia's most important port on the Red Sea.

60003.q: What is the monsoon season called in which the Dhofar region in southern Oman turns green in summer?
60003.e: From June to September, the south-west monsoon brings fog and drizzle to the coast near Salalah. Shamal, khamsin and haboob, on the other hand, are dry winds or dust storms.
60003.m: The khareef makes Dhofar the green corner of Arabia.

60004.q: Which raw materials are mainly extracted in and around the Caspian Sea?
60004.e: There are large oil and gas deposits around the Caspian Sea, for example near Baku or in the Kashagan field in the northern Caspian. Production in the shallow, often frozen north is technically difficult.
60004.m: The Caspian Sea is rich in oil and natural gas.

60005.q: Which chain of islands continues Kamchatka's volcanic arc southwards to Japan?
60005.e: The Kuril Islands stretch about 1,200 kilometres from the southern tip of Kamchatka to Hokkaido. They formed above the same subduction zone.
60005.m: The Kuril Islands link Kamchatka with Japan.

60006.q: Which well-known viewpoint mountain on Hong Kong Island can be reached by a historic funicular railway?
60006.e: The Peak Tram has run up Victoria Peak, which is just over 550 metres high, since 1888. However, Hong Kong's highest mountain is Tai Mo Shan in the New Territories at 957 metres.
60006.m: From Victoria Peak you can look out over Hong Kong's skyline.

60007.q: Which extremely densely built settlement in Hong Kong was demolished in 1993 and 1994?
60007.e: At times, over 30,000 people lived in Kowloon Walled City on about 2.6 hectares. Today there is a park there.
60007.m: Kowloon Walled City was one of the most densely populated places in the world.

60008.q: Which facility has lifted ships over the Three Gorges Dam in a water-filled trough since 2016?
60008.e: The ship lift overcomes a height difference of about 113 metres in a few minutes and is the largest of its kind. Larger cargo ships still use the five-step flight of locks.
60008.m: At the Three Gorges Dam, ships travel in a trough like in a lift.

60009.q: Why does China keep experiencing devastating floods on the Yangtze?
a: Heavy monsoon rains hit densely populated lowlands
Tibet's glaciers melt completely every year
Storm surges push the sea as far as Chongqing
60009.e: During the summer monsoon, enormous amounts of rain fall in the river's catchment area. In the flood of 1931, probably millions of people died from drowning, hunger and disease. The Three Gorges Dam is also meant to protect against floods.
60009.m: Monsoon rains make the Yangtze prone to flooding.

60010.q: Which sand desert lies in the Tarim Basin west of the Gobi?
60010.e: The Taklamakan fills the Tarim Basin in Xinjiang and, unlike the Gobi, consists mostly of sand dunes. The Karakum and Kyzylkum are in Central Asia, the Thar in India.
60010.m: West of the Gobi lies the Taklamakan sand desert.

60011.q: Which railway line crosses the Gobi between Ulaanbaatar and Beijing?
60011.e: The Trans-Mongolian Railway branches off the Trans-Siberian Railway in Siberia and runs via Ulaanbaatar right across the Gobi to Beijing. At the Chinese border, the bogies are changed because of different track gauges.
60011.m: The Trans-Mongolian Railway crosses the Gobi.

60012.q: Which Indonesian group of islands was once world-famous as the “Spice Islands”?
60012.e: Cloves and nutmeg originally grew only on the Moluccas. From the 16th century, the Portuguese, Spanish, Dutch and British fought over the trade in them.
60012.m: Nutmeg and cloves originally come from the Moluccas.

60013.q: Which capital city lies on the Taedong River?
60013.e: Pyongyang, the capital of North Korea, lies on both banks of the Taedong, which flows into the Yellow Sea.

60014.q: After the Amazon, which river carries the second-largest volume of water in the world?
60014.e: At its mouth, the Congo carries an average of about 40,000 m³ of water per second. It drains a huge catchment area of about 3.7 million km² in the middle of Africa.
