60244.m: The Northeast Passage is shorter but harder than the route through the Suez Canal.

60245.q: Which cape is the northernmost point of the Eurasian mainland and a key point of the Northeast Passage?
60245.e: Cape Chelyuskin lies on the Taymyr Peninsula on the Vilkitsky Strait. The ice there is often especially stubborn.
60245.m: The northernmost point of the Eurasian mainland is Cape Chelyuskin.

60246.q: Which ships does Russia use to keep the Northeast Passage open even in thick ice?
60246.e: Russia is the only country that operates a fleet of nuclear-powered icebreakers. They can sail for a long time without refuelling and break thick pack ice.
60246.m: Nuclear icebreakers keep the Northeast Passage open for cargo ships.

60247.q: Which seafarer spent the winter of 1596/97 on Novaya Zemlya while searching for a sea route to Asia?
60247.e: Willem Barents' expedition got stuck in the ice and spent the winter in a hut made of driftwood. Barents died on the return journey, and the Barents Sea is named after him.
60247.m: Willem Barents searched for the Northeast Passage in the 16th century.

60248.q: Why has the Northeast Passage become navigable for longer each year in recent decades?
a: Arctic sea ice is shrinking sharply in summer
New canals have been dug through Siberia
The Bering Strait has been widened
60248.e: Because the Arctic is warming, the area of summer sea ice has fallen sharply. This opens the route for longer but brings risks for the environment and climate.
60248.m: The decline of sea ice makes the Northeast Passage navigable for longer.

60249.q: What is the Ilulissat Icefjord, a UNESCO World Heritage Site in Greenland, known for?
a: A very fast glacier calves huge icebergs there
The highest mountain in Greenland is there
The oldest Viking settlement is there
60249.e: The Sermeq Kujalleq glacier pushes huge amounts of ice into the fjord every year. The icebergs then drift out into Disko Bay.
60249.m: In the Ilulissat Icefjord one of the fastest glaciers in the world calves.

60250.q: How did Tasmania become an island?
a: After the last Ice Age the sea level rose and flooded the land bridge
A volcanic eruption blasted it off the mainland
An earthquake made Bass Strait suddenly sink
It drifted away from the mainland as a separate plate
60250.e: During the last Ice Age the sea level was much lower and Tasmania was joined to the mainland. About 10,000 to 12,000 years ago the land bridge was flooded.
60250.m: The rise in sea level after the Ice Age made Tasmania an island.

60251.q: Which disease has seriously threatened the Tasmanian devil since the 1990s?
60251.e: Devil Facial Tumour Disease is passed from animal to animal through bites. As a result, the populations have collapsed.
60251.m: A contagious facial cancer threatens the Tasmanian devil.

60252.q: In which year did the last known thylacine die in a zoo in Hobart?
60252.e: The thylacine, also called the Tasmanian tiger, was wiped out by hunting, loss of habitat and disease. The last animal died in Beaumaris Zoo in 1936.
60252.m: The thylacine has been considered extinct since 1936.

60253.q: What did a large protest movement prevent in the Tasmanian wilderness in 1982/83?
a: The building of a dam on the Franklin River
The building of a nuclear power station
The opening of a gold mine
The building of a bridge to the mainland
60253.e: Thousands protested against the building of a dam on the Franklin River in the World Heritage area, and over 1000 were arrested. In July 1983 the High Court of Australia ruled in favour of the federal government, which stopped the building.
60253.m: The Franklin Dam protest was a milestone of environmental protection in Australia.

60254.q: Which energy source supplies most of the electricity in Tasmania?
60254.e: Lots of rain and mountainous land make Tasmania ideal for reservoirs and hydroelectric power stations. As in Switzerland, hydroelectric power is the most important source of electricity there.
60254.m: Tasmania gets its electricity mainly from hydroelectric power.

60255.q: Which raw material is most important for the economy of New Caledonia?
60255.e: New Caledonia has a large share of the world's known nickel deposits. Nickel is used, among other things, for stainless steel and batteries.
60255.m: New Caledonia is rich in nickel.

60256.q: What was the result of the three independence referendums in New Caledonia in 2018, 2020 and 2021?
a: A no to independence each time
A yes to independence each time
All were cancelled because of unrest
60256.e: In all three votes New Caledonia stayed with France. The last one was boycotted by many Kanak, so the question remains disputed.
60256.m: New Caledonia voted three times against independence from France.

60257.q: Under which special form of rule was Vanuatu, as the New Hebrides, until 1980?
a: Joint administration by Britain and France
60257.e: The New Hebrides were a British-French condominium with two administrations and legal systems. In 1980 Vanuatu became independent.
60257.m: Vanuatu became independent from Britain and France in 1980.

60258.q: What did the people of Bougainville vote for in 2019 with about 98 per cent?
60258.e: The vote was part of the peace agreement after the civil war over the Panguna copper mine. It is not binding, and independence still has to be negotiated.
60258.m: Bougainville voted clearly for independence in 2019.

60259.q: How did Polynesian seafarers find their way to distant islands over thousands of kilometres without a compass?
a: Using stars, wave patterns, birds and clouds
60259.e: Traditional navigation used the rising points of stars, ocean swell, bird flights and clouds over islands. The voyage of the canoe Hōkūleʻa from Hawaii to Tahiti in 1976 proved that this works.
60259.m: Polynesians navigated by stars, waves and birds.

60260.q: Which volcanic eruption in January 2022 triggered a tsunami and a pressure wave that could be measured worldwide?
60260.e: The undersea volcano near Tonga exploded with enormous force. The pressure wave was also recorded by barometers in Switzerland.
60260.m: The eruption of Hunga Tonga-Hunga Haʻapai could be measured worldwide.

60261.q: Why is Kiribati the only country that lies in all four hemispheres?
a: It lies on both sides of the equator and the 180th meridian
It lies on both sides of the prime meridian
It stretches from the North Pole to the equator
It has territory in Europe and Asia
60261.e: Kiribati's islands are spread over a huge area of ocean north and south of the equator and east and west of the 180th meridian. That is why the country moved the date line to the east in 1995.
60261.m: Kiribati lies in all four hemispheres of the Earth.

60262.q: What consequences did phosphate mining have for the island of Nauru?
a: About four fifths of the island is destroyed mining land
The island became twice as large
The island became a nature reserve
60262.e: Phosphate from bird droppings made Nauru very rich for a time. After mining, an uninhabitable plateau of limestone rock remained, and the wealth was lost.
60262.m: Phosphate mining has made most of Nauru uninhabitable.

60263.q: What is special about the traditional stone money (rai) on Yap?
a: The huge stones change owner without being moved
The stones are fired again every year
It is only kept under water
60263.e: The rai stones were brought from Palau and can be several metres across. Ownership is passed on by word of mouth, while the stone stays where it is.
60263.m: With Yap's stone money, ownership counts, not where the stone is.

60264.q: Which ruined city made of basalt columns on Pohnpei has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2016?
60264.e: Nan Madol consists of almost a hundred artificial islands in a lagoon. It was the centre of the Saudeleur dynasty.
60264.m: Nan Madol on Pohnpei is a ruined city in the sea.

60265.q: What were the stick charts of the Marshall Islands used for?
a: They showed wave patterns and the position of islands for navigation
They were calendars for the fishing season
They served as money in trade
They showed the constellations for ceremonies
60265.e: The charts made of palm ribs and shells showed how islands break and bend the ocean swell. Seafarers learned them by heart on land.
60265.m: Stick charts of the Marshall Islands show ocean waves and islands.

60266.q: What is most of the water from the Murray-Darling Basin used for?
60266.e: A large part of Australian farming takes place in the basin, for example rice, cotton, fruit and wine. Irrigation uses most of the water that is taken.
60266.m: The Murray-Darling Basin is Australia's breadbasket.

60267.q: Which strait separates Tasmania from the Australian mainland?
60267.e: Bass Strait is about 240 km wide and relatively shallow. The Torres Strait lies between Australia and New Guinea, Cook Strait in New Zealand.
60267.m: Bass Strait separates Tasmania from the Australian mainland.

60268.q: What is the capital of the Federated States of Micronesia?
60268.e: Palikir lies on the island of Pohnpei and has been the capital since 1989. Majuro is the capital of the Marshall Islands, Ngerulmud that of Palau and Hagåtña that of Guam.
60268.m: Palikir on Pohnpei is the capital of the Federated States of Micronesia.

60269.q: Which UNESCO World Heritage Site on the slopes of the Great Dividing Range protects rainforests with plant lineages dating from the time of the supercontinent Gondwana?
60269.e: The protected areas are scattered across New South Wales and southern Queensland. They contain plant families that already existed when Australia was still joined to Antarctica.
60269.m: The Gondwana Rainforests are living witnesses of an ancient supercontinent.

60270.q: What consequence did the crossing of the Blue Mountains in 1813 have for the British colony?
a: Grazing land in the interior was opened up
Sydney was abandoned as the main town
Large gold finds were made at once
60270.e: West of the mountains the settlers found wide grasslands. A road soon followed, then the town of Bathurst in 1815, and sheep farming spread.
60270.m: After 1813 settlers opened up the pastures west of the Blue Mountains.

60271.q: Which rock is needed for caves with stalactites and stalagmites like those in the Blue Mountains?
60271.e: Rainwater with dissolved carbon dioxide dissolves limestone and creates hollow spaces. When the water drips in the cave, the lime is deposited again and forms stalactites and stalagmites, for example in the Jenolan Caves.
60271.m: Caves with stalactites form in limestone.

60272.q: Who is the train “The Ghan”, which connects Adelaide with Darwin via Alice Springs, named after?
60272.e: In the 19th century camel drivers from Afghanistan and British India carried goods through the Outback. The train remembers them with its name and a camel in its logo.
60272.m: The name “The Ghan” remembers the Afghan camel drivers in the Outback.

60273.q: What made crossing Australia from south to north especially dangerous in the 19th century?
a: Lack of water and great heat
60273.e: Expeditions had to travel hundreds of kilometres without reliable water sources. John McDouall Stuart managed the crossing in 1862 and returned alive; the Stuart Highway follows his route.
60273.m: The Stuart Highway follows the route of the explorer John McDouall Stuart.

60274.q: Which inselberg in the centre of Australia is a sacred place of the Aboriginal people?
60274.e: Uluru, formerly Ayers Rock, rises about 350 m out of the flat plain. It is sacred to the Anangu, and since 2019 it may no longer be climbed.
60274.m: Uluru is a sacred mountain of the Aboriginal people in the Outback.

60275.q: How did the Burke and Wills expedition of 1860/61, which wanted to cross Australia from south to north, end?
a: The leaders died on the way back
They found a large inland lake
They founded the city of Darwin
60275.e: The expedition reached the mangrove swamps on the Gulf of Carpentaria. On the way back Burke and Wills starved to death, even though Aboriginal people gave them food for a time.
60275.m: The Burke and Wills expedition shows how dangerous the Outback was for the unprepared.

60276.q: Why is the Murray regulated with large reservoirs?
a: So that water flows to fields and towns even in the dry summer
So that the river does not freeze in winter
So that ocean-going ships can sail inland
So that the river carries more sand to the sea
60276.e: In Australia river flow varies greatly. Reservoirs such as Lake Hume store water from wet periods and release it in dry periods.
60276.m: Reservoirs even out the changing amount of water in the Murray.

60277.q: Why is the name “Milford Sound” geographically not quite accurate?
a: It is a fjord shaped by glaciers
It is the crater of a volcano
It is a lagoon behind a reef
It is a river delta with sandbanks
60277.e: A “sound” is a river valley flooded by the sea. Milford Sound, however, was carved out by glaciers and is therefore a fjord.
60277.m: Despite its name, Milford Sound is a fjord.

60278.q: What is the name of New Zealand's third largest island, south of the South Island?
60278.e: Stewart Island lies across Foveaux Strait. About 85 per cent of the island belongs to Rakiura National Park, which is known for kiwis.
60278.m: New Zealand's third largest island is Stewart Island.

60279.q: On which main island of New Zealand does the great majority of the population live?
a: On the North Island, about three quarters
On the South Island, about three quarters
On the South Island, about two thirds
60279.e: Auckland, the largest city, and the capital Wellington are on the North Island. The larger South Island is more mountainous and more thinly populated.
60279.m: Most New Zealanders live on the North Island.

60280.q: What were Tuvalu's islands called when they were part of a British colony?
60280.e: Together with the Gilbert Islands, today's Kiribati, Tuvalu formed the colony of the Gilbert and Ellice Islands. Tuvalu became independent in 1978.
60280.m: In colonial times Tuvalu was called the Ellice Islands.

60281.q: What did Tuvalu set down in a change to its constitution in 2023?
a: The state continues to exist even if its land sinks into the sea
Tuvalu becomes part of New Zealand
Only English is an official language
60281.e: The constitution declares Tuvalu's statehood and its maritime borders to be permanent. In this way the country wants to secure its rights even if the islands become uninhabitable.
60281.m: Tuvalu wants to continue existing as a state even without habitable land.

60282.q: In which city has the Secretariat of the Antarctic Treaty been based since 2004?
60282.e: The permanent secretariat organises the annual consultative meetings and manages information. Argentina successfully won the bid to be the host country.
60282.m: The Antarctic Treaty Secretariat is in Buenos Aires.

60283.q: Which 1980 convention in the Antarctic Treaty System regulates fishing, especially for krill?
a: Convention on the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources
International Convention for the Regulation of Whaling
United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea
60283.e: The convention (CCAMLR) looks at the whole ecosystem, not just individual fish species. It is meant to prevent krill being fished so heavily that penguins, seals and whales go hungry.
60283.m: CCAMLR protects the ecosystem of the Southern Ocean from overfishing.

60284.q: Which sea area was declared the largest marine protected area in the world at the time under CCAMLR in 2016?
60284.e: The protected area in the Ross Sea covers more than 1.5 million square kilometres. Commercial fishing is banned in a large part of it.
60284.m: One of the largest marine protected areas in the world is in the Ross Sea.

60285.q: Which large area of Antarctica is not claimed by any country?
60285.e: Marie Byrd Land in West Antarctica is the largest unclaimed land area on Earth. Because of the Antarctic Treaty, no new claim may be made to it either.
60285.m: Marie Byrd Land is the largest area with no territorial claim.

60286.q: What must a country that joined later prove in order to become a consultative party with voting rights?
a: A coast on the Southern Ocean
Membership of the UN Security Council
60286.e: Under Article IX, substantial research activity is needed, such as a station of its own or expeditions. Without this status a country may take part in meetings but not in decisions.
60286.m: Voting rights in the Antarctic Treaty go to those who do serious research there.

60287.q: Roughly how thick is the Antarctic ice sheet on average?
60287.e: On average the ice is about 2 km thick, and much more in the thickest places. That is why Antarctica is the continent with the highest average elevation.
60287.m: The Antarctic ice sheet is about two kilometres thick on average.

60288.q: What are the cold, heavy winds called that flow down from the high ice sheet to the coast?
60288.e: Over the ice the air cools strongly, becomes heavy and flows downhill to the coast. At some coastal places these downslope winds reach hurricane force.
60288.m: Katabatic winds are cold downslope winds from the ice sheet.

60289.q: Under the ice of East Antarctica lies a mountain range about as extensive as the Alps. How was it discovered?
a: By measurements that see through the ice
By finding pieces of rock on the coast
60289.e: The Gamburtsev Mountains lie beneath more than 600 m of ice. They were discovered in 1958 by seismic measurements of a Soviet expedition and later surveyed more precisely with radar.
60289.m: The Gamburtsev Mountains are hidden beneath the ice of East Antarctica.

60290.q: What do you call fast-flowing bands in the ice sheet that carry a large part of the ice to the sea?
60290.e: Ice streams flow much faster than the surrounding ice, often hundreds of metres a year. The ice sheet loses a large part of its mass through them.
60290.m: Ice streams are the motorways of the ice sheet.

60291.q: Why are especially many meteorites found in Antarctica?
a: Flowing ice collects them on blue ice areas at the surface
Antarctica is hit more often than other continents
The magnetic field pulls meteorites towards the South Pole
Meteorites melt into the ice and stay visible
60291.e: The ice carries trapped meteorites to places where wind wears the ice away. On these blue ice areas the dark stones lie clearly visible.
60291.m: Blue ice areas in Antarctica are ideal places to find meteorites.

60292.q: Which raw material is shipped from the Siberian Yamal Peninsula via the Northeast Passage with icebreaking tankers?
60292.e: On the Yamal Peninsula natural gas is extracted, liquefied and taken to Europe and Asia by icebreaking tankers. The port of Sabetta was built especially for this.
60292.m: Liquefied natural gas is shipped from Yamal across the Arctic.

60293.q: When did the Norse settlements in Greenland disappear?
60293.e: The Eastern and Western Settlements were gradually abandoned, the Eastern Settlement last in the 15th century. Cooling, declining trade and isolation are considered the reasons.
60293.m: The Norse settlements in Greenland came to an end in the 15th century.

60294.q: What, among other things, did Greenland receive with the Self-Government Act of 2009?
a: A seat in the EU Commission
60294.e: Since 2009 Greenland has decided for itself about raw materials such as ores and oil. The act also recognises the right of Greenlanders to decide on their independence.
60294.m: Since 2009 Greenland has managed its own mineral resources.

60295.q: What was Camp Century, built in the ice of north-west Greenland in 1959?
a: A US military base in tunnels under the ice
A Danish weather station on a glacier
An Inuit village for seal hunters
60295.e: The USA built tunnels into the ice and ran the station with a small nuclear reactor. After it was abandoned in 1967, waste remained that could be exposed by melting.
60295.m: Camp Century was a military base under the Greenland ice.

60296.q: What did Greenland's parliament decide in 2021 in the dispute over a mining project near Narsaq?
a: The sale of land to China
60296.e: At Kvanefjeld rare earths are found together with uranium. After an election, parliament banned exploring for and mining ores with higher uranium content.
60296.m: In 2021 Greenland put protecting the environment ahead of uranium mining.

60297.q: What is the Isua Greenstone Belt in south-western Greenland known for?
a: Some of the oldest rocks on Earth
The largest diamonds in the world
60297.e: The rocks in the Isua belt are about 3.7 to 3.8 billion years old. They give clues about the early Earth and possibly early life.
60297.m: Some of the oldest rocks on Earth are in the Isua belt.

60298.q: Why does the bedrock beneath the middle of Greenland lie partly below sea level?
a: The weight of the ice pushes the Earth's crust down
There is a deep ocean trench there
The rock was washed out by rivers
60298.e: The kilometres-thick ice sheet weighs down the crust, which sinks into the viscous mantle. If the ice melted, the land would slowly rise again.
60298.m: Heavy ice pushes the Earth's crust down.

60299.q: What is geologically special about Macquarie Island, which belongs to Tasmania?
a: Rock from the Earth's mantle is exposed there above sea level
Australia's only active volcano is there
The oldest granite on Earth is there
There is a glacier reaching the sea there
60299.e: The island was pushed up out of the oceanic crust at a plate boundary. That is why it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1997.
60299.m: On Macquarie Island you can see rock from the Earth's mantle.

60300.q: Which very slow-growing conifer from Tasmania was prized for boatbuilding?
60300.e: The wood of the Huon pine contains an oil that protects it from rot. The trees grow only a few millimetres a year and can become very old.
60300.m: The Huon pine supplies rot-resistant wood from Tasmania.

60301.q: Which exchange system with necklaces and armbands did Bronisław Malinowski describe on the Trobriand Islands?
60301.e: In the Kula ring, necklaces travel clockwise and armbands in the opposite direction from island to island. It is mainly about prestige and relationships, not profit.
60301.m: The Kula ring is an exchange system that strengthens relationships between islands.

60302.q: Which culture with decorated pottery spread out into the Pacific from the Bismarck Archipelago from about 1500 BC?
60302.e: The Lapita people were the first to settle Fiji, Tonga and Samoa from Melanesia. They are considered the ancestors of the Polynesians.
60302.m: The Lapita culture stands at the beginning of the settlement of the remote Pacific.

60303.q: Which almost constantly active volcano on the island of Tanna in Vanuatu attracts many visitors?
60303.e: Yasur has been almost continuously active for centuries and regularly throws out glowing lava. The other volcanoes named are in Papua New Guinea.
60303.m: Yasur on Tanna is one of the most active volcanoes in Melanesia.

60304.q: Which English word comes from the Polynesian languages?
60304.e: James Cook came across the word “tapu” on Tonga; it means something sacred or forbidden. Through his reports it entered English as “taboo”.

60305.q: Which French painter lived and painted in French Polynesia from 1891?
60305.e: Gauguin painted bright pictures of island life on Tahiti and later on the Marquesas. He died in 1903 on the island of Hiva Oa.
60305.m: Paul Gauguin painted his best-known pictures in Polynesia.

60306.q: Which country does the Polynesian island of Tahiti belong to?
60306.e: Tahiti is the largest island of French Polynesia, an overseas territory of France. The capital Papeete is on Tahiti.
60306.m: Tahiti belongs to French Polynesia and therefore to France.

60307.q: What do you call a ring-shaped coral island with a lagoon in the middle, as often found in Polynesia?
60307.e: An atoll forms when a volcano with a coral reef slowly sinks. The reef keeps growing upwards and encloses a lagoon.
60307.m: An atoll is a ring of coral around a lagoon.

60308.q: Who settled the Pitcairn Islands in 1790?
a: Mutineers from the Bounty with people from Tahiti
60308.e: After the mutiny on the Bounty in 1789, some mutineers hid on Pitcairn with Tahitian women and men. Their descendants still live there today.
60308.m: The Pitcairn Islands were settled by mutineers from the Bounty.

60309.q: Which drink made from the root of a pepper plant is drunk at ceremonies in Tonga and Samoa?
60309.e: Kava is made from the ground root of the kava pepper plant mixed with water. At ceremonies it is served according to a fixed order of rank.
60309.m: Kava is a traditional ceremonial drink in Polynesia.

60310.q: Which Micronesian country became the first in 2009 to declare its waters a sanctuary for sharks?
60310.e: Palau banned commercial shark fishing in its entire economic zone. Live sharks bring the country much more through diving tourism than caught ones.
60310.m: In 2009 Palau created the world's first shark sanctuary.

60311.q: What does the “Compact of Free Association” between the USA and several Micronesian countries regulate?
a: The USA takes over defence, and citizens may work in the USA
The USA buys all fishing rights
The countries must abolish the US dollar
60311.e: The Federated States of Micronesia, the Marshall Islands and Palau receive financial aid and defence. In return the USA has special military rights there.
60311.m: Through the Compact of Free Association three Micronesian countries are closely tied to the USA.

60312.q: Why is the Chuuk Lagoon a famous destination for wreck divers?
a: Dozens of Japanese ships sunk in 1944 lie there
The Bounty sank there with its cargo
60312.e: In Operation Hailstone in February 1944, US aircraft attacked the Japanese base. Many ships and aircraft still lie on the bottom of the lagoon today.
60312.m: Chuuk Lagoon is an underwater museum of the Second World War.

60313.q: Which property does the Mercator projection have?
a: It preserves distances from the centre
60313.e: The Mercator projection is a conformal cylindrical projection: angles and small shapes are preserved. In exchange, areas are greatly enlarged towards the poles.
60313.m: The Mercator projection preserves angles but not areas.

60314.q: In which year did Gerardus Mercator publish his world map with the projection named after him?
60314.e: In 1569 Gerardus Mercator published a large world map for navigation in Duisburg. It is considered the origin of the Mercator projection.
60314.m: Mercator published his famous world map in 1569.

60315.q: Why was the Mercator projection especially useful for navigation at sea?
a: Lines of constant compass bearing appear as straight lines
The shortest routes appear as straight lines
The areas of the oceans are correct
The poles appear as single points
60315.e: Lines that cross all meridians at the same angle (rhumb lines) are straight on the Mercator map. A sailor could therefore read the course with a ruler and hold it with a compass.
60315.m: On the Mercator map a constant compass bearing is a straight line.

60316.q: By what factor is an area at 60° latitude enlarged on the Mercator projection compared with the equator?
60316.e: The linear scale grows by 1/cos(φ); at 60° this is 1/0.5 = 2. Since the length is doubled in both directions, the area is enlarged 2 · 2 = 4 times.
60316.m: At 60° latitude areas appear four times too large on the Mercator map.

60317.q: Why can the poles not be shown on the normal Mercator projection?
a: They would lie infinitely far from the equator
They are on the back of the map
60317.e: The north-south stretching grows without limit towards the poles, so the poles would be shown infinitely far away. Mercator maps therefore usually end at about 80 to 85° latitude.
60317.m: The Mercator map cannot show the poles because the distortion becomes infinite there.

60318.q: On the Mercator map Greenland looks about as large as Africa. Roughly how much larger is Africa in reality?
60318.e: Africa measures about 30 million km², Greenland only about 2.2 million km². So Africa is about 14 times larger; Greenland is greatly inflated because of its high latitude.
60318.m: Africa is about fourteen times larger than Greenland, even if the Mercator map suggests otherwise.

60319.q: Which variant of the Mercator projection do many online map services use?
60319.e: Online map services mostly use the Web Mercator projection (also called Pseudo-Mercator). It can easily be divided into square tiles and keeps local shapes when zooming in.
60319.m: Many online maps are based on the Web Mercator projection.

60320.q: Which property is the main focus of the Peters projection?
60320.e: The Peters projection is an equal-area cylindrical projection: areas of the same size appear the same size. In exchange, shapes are heavily distorted.
60320.m: The Peters projection shows the areas of countries in the correct proportion.

60321.q: Why is the Peters projection often also called the Gall-Peters projection?
a: James Gall had already described it in 1855
Peters and Gall developed it together in 1973
Gall was the publisher that printed the map
Gall is the place where Peters lived
60321.e: The Scottish clergyman James Gall had already presented the projection in 1855. Arno Peters made it well known from 1973 without mentioning Gall.
60321.m: The Peters projection goes back to James Gall and is therefore also called the Gall-Peters projection.

60322.q: With which main argument did Arno Peters promote his world map from 1973?
a: The Mercator map made the countries of the South look too small
His map was more accurate for sailors
His map showed the poles as points
60322.e: Peters argued that the widespread Mercator map enlarged Europe and North America and so disadvantaged the countries of the Global South. His map was therefore spread by development organisations and churches.
60322.m: With his map Arno Peters wanted to show the true size of the countries of the South.

60323.q: What do cartographers particularly criticise about the Peters projection?
60323.e: Countries near the equator look greatly stretched on the Peters map, while areas near the poles look squashed. Many cartographers therefore prefer compromise designs such as the Winkel tripel projection.
60323.m: The Peters map preserves area but strongly distorts shapes.

60324.q: A footpath measures exactly 7.4 cm on a 1:50,000 map. How long is it in reality?
60324.m: On a 1:50,000 map one centimetre equals half a kilometre.

60325.q: Two places are 12 km apart; on the map the distance between them is 24 cm. What is the scale of the map?
60325.m: You get the scale number by dividing the real distance by the map distance.

60326.q: Which of these scales is the largest?
60326.e: A large scale has a small scale number: 1:5,000 shows a small area in great detail. 1:1,000,000 is a small scale for large areas.
60326.m: The smaller the scale number, the larger the scale.

60327.q: A square on a 1:50,000 map has sides 2 cm long. What is its area in reality?
60327.e: 2 cm · 50,000 = 100,000 cm = 1 km side length. The area is 1 km · 1 km = 1 km².
60327.m: On maps you work out areas using the real side lengths.

60328.q: What height difference (contour interval) do neighbouring contour lines have on the Swiss national map at 1:25,000?
60328.e: On the 1:25,000 national map the contour lines are 10 m apart; on the 1:50,000 map it is 20 m. The smaller the scale, the larger the contour interval chosen.
60328.m: On the 1:25,000 national map there is a contour line every ten metres of height.

60329.q: An area on a 1:10,000 map measures exactly 3 cm². How large is it in reality?
60329.e: 1 cm corresponds to 100 m, so 1 cm² = 100 m · 100 m = 10,000 m² = 1 ha. 3 cm² is therefore 3 ha.
60329.m: For areas the scale works as a square.

60330.q: Which federal office publishes the official national maps of Switzerland?
60330.e: The Federal Office of Topography (swisstopo) in Wabern near Bern produces the national maps, for example at scales of 1:25,000 and 1:50,000.
60330.m: The Swiss national maps come from the Federal Office of Topography.

60331.q: Which scale indication remains correct when you enlarge a map on a photocopier?
a: The scale in the map title
60331.e: The scale bar is copied along with the map when it is enlarged or reduced and therefore keeps the correct ratio. Figures such as 1:25,000 or “1 cm equals 250 m” are no longer correct afterwards.
60331.m: When a map is copied, only the scale bar stays reliable.

60332.q: Which satellite was launched in 1972 as the first of a long US series of civilian Earth observation satellites?
60332.e: Landsat 1 was launched in July 1972. Since then the Landsat series has provided the longest continuous series of images of the Earth's surface from space.
60332.m: Landsat 1 began civilian Earth observation from space in 1972.

60333.q: Which EU Earth observation programme do the Sentinel satellites belong to?
60333.e: The EU programme Copernicus operates the Sentinel satellites together with ESA. Their data can be used freely by everyone, for example for farming, climate and disaster protection.
60333.m: The Sentinel satellites belong to the Copernicus Earth observation programme.

60334.q: What advantage does synthetic aperture radar (SAR) have over optical sensors?
a: It provides images even through clouds and at night
It provides images in natural colours
60334.e: SAR sends out microwaves itself and receives the echo. Microwaves pass through clouds, and no sunlight is needed.
60334.m: Radar satellites can see through clouds and at night.

60335.q: Which two spectral ranges does the vegetation index NDVI compare?
60335.e: Healthy plants absorb red light for photosynthesis and strongly reflect near infrared. The NDVI calculates (NIR minus Red) divided by (NIR plus Red) from this.
60335.m: The NDVI measures plant health using red and near infrared light.

60336.q: What distinguishes an active from a passive remote sensing system?
a: It sends out radiation itself and measures the echo
It can change its own orbit
It only works during the day
60336.e: Passive sensors measure natural radiation such as reflected sunlight or heat radiation. Active systems such as radar or lidar send out their own signals.
60336.m: Active sensors light up the Earth themselves, passive ones use existing radiation.

60337.q: What is the method called that creates very accurate elevation models of the Earth's surface from an aeroplane using laser pulses?
60337.e: Lidar measures the travel time of reflected laser pulses and produces dense point clouds. Switzerland's digital elevation model is also based on such laser scanning data.
60337.m: Lidar surveys the Earth's surface with laser pulses.

60338.q: What does the spatial resolution of a satellite image indicate?
a: The ground area covered by one pixel
The number of grey levels per pixel
60338.e: At 10 m spatial resolution one pixel corresponds to a ground area of 10 m · 10 m. Smaller objects can no longer be recognised individually.
60338.m: Spatial resolution tells you how large one pixel is on the ground.

60339.q: What usually appears bright red in a classic infrared false-colour image?
60339.e: In an infrared false-colour image, near infrared is shown as red. Healthy plants reflect this light very strongly and therefore glow red.
60339.m: In an infrared false-colour image healthy vegetation is red.

60340.q: What is the name of Russia's satellite navigation system?
60340.e: GLONASS was developed in the Soviet Union and is now operated by Russia. Many smartphones receive GPS and GLONASS at the same time.
60340.m: Russia operates the GLONASS navigation system.

60341.q: What is the minimum number of satellite signals a GPS receiver needs for a three-dimensional position plus exact time?
60341.e: There are four unknowns: three spatial coordinates and the receiver's clock error. This requires at least four satellites.
60341.m: For a GPS position with height you need at least four satellites.

60342.q: At least how many satellites make up the basic GPS constellation?
60342.e: The system is designed for at least 24 satellites in six orbital planes, so that enough satellites are visible everywhere on Earth. There are usually extra reserve satellites in operation too.
60342.m: GPS needs at least 24 satellites for worldwide coverage.

60343.q: What is the method called in which a reference station at a known location sends correction data to GPS receivers?
60343.e: The reference station compares its known position with the measured one and sends the difference. In Switzerland, swipos is such a service for surveying.
60343.m: With correction data from a reference station, GPS becomes accurate to the centimetre.

60344.q: What does a GPS receiver measure to work out the distance to a satellite?
a: The travel time of the signal
The strength of the magnetic field
60344.e: Each satellite also sends its exact time of transmission. The travel time multiplied by the speed of light gives the distance.
60344.m: GPS works out distances from the travel time of the radio signals.

60345.q: Which theory must be taken into account for the running of the atomic clocks in GPS satellites?
60345.e: Because of their motion and the weaker gravitational field, the satellite clocks run about 38 microseconds fast per day according to Einstein's theory of relativity. Without correction the position would be off by kilometres every day.
60345.m: Without the theory of relativity GPS would quickly become inaccurate.

60346.q: Which measure suddenly improved GPS accuracy for civilian users in May 2000?
a: Switching off the deliberate signal degradation
The launch of the first Galileo satellites
60346.e: Until 2 May 2000 the military deliberately degraded the civilian signal (“Selective Availability”). After that, accuracy improved from about 100 m to a few metres.
60346.m: Since the end of deliberate signal degradation in 2000, GPS has been very accurate for civilians too.

60347.q: What is the general term for global satellite navigation systems such as GPS?
60347.e: GNSS stands for Global Navigation Satellite System. Modern receivers often use several such systems at the same time.
60347.m: All global satellite navigation systems are grouped together as GNSS.

60348.q: What distinguishes a thematic map from a topographic map?
a: It always has a larger scale
60348.e: A topographic map shows terrain, water, settlements and transport routes in general. A thematic map shows one subject, such as population density, climate or election results.
60348.m: Thematic maps show a particular subject on a base map.

60349.q: What is a map called in which areas such as cantons are shaded in different colours according to their value?
60349.e: In a choropleth map each administrative unit gets a colour according to its value class. It is common, for example, for maps of Swiss popular votes.
60349.m: A choropleth map colours whole areas according to their value.

60350.q: Which form of thematic map shows, for example, the language shares of each canton as a pie chart directly on the map?
60350.e: In a diagram map, small charts are placed in the respective areas. This allows several values per area to be compared at the same time.
60350.m: Diagram maps show several values per area with small charts.

60351.q: What do isohyets connect on a climate map?
a: Places with the same amount of rainfall
Places with the same air pressure
60351.e: Isohyets are lines of equal rainfall, usually for a year or a month. The part “hyet” comes from the Greek word for rain.
60351.m: Isohyets connect places that get the same amount of rainfall.

60352.q: What is a map called in which the area of each country is distorted in proportion to a value such as population?
60352.e: In an area cartogram, the real shape of countries is distorted in favour of a statistical value. Countries with large populations such as India then look huge.
60352.m: A cartogram distorts areas according to a statistical value.

60353.q: Which doctor showed in 1854, with a map of cholera deaths in London, that a water pump was the source?
60353.e: John Snow marked the deaths in the London district of Soho as dots. They clustered around the pump in Broad Street, after which its handle was removed.
60353.m: In 1854 John Snow proved with a map that cholera was spread by contaminated water.

60354.q: Why should choropleth maps show densities or proportions rather than absolute numbers?
a: Otherwise large areas would look too important
Proportions are always measured more accurately
60354.e: With absolute values a large area stands out just because of its size. Relative values such as inhabitants per km² make areas of different sizes comparable.
60354.m: Area colours should show densities or proportions, not absolute numbers.

60355.q: What is a map called on which each dot represents a fixed amount, for example 1000 inhabitants?
60355.e: In a dot map (dot distribution map) the density of dots shows the spatial distribution. Where there are many dots, the feature is common.
60355.m: A dot map shows distributions with many dots of equal value.

60356.q: Roughly how far apart from north to south are two lines of latitude that are 1° apart?
60356.e: The Earth's circumference over the poles is about 40,000 km. 40,000 km : 360 gives about 111 km per degree of latitude.
60356.m: One degree of latitude equals about 111 kilometres.

60357.q: How many arc seconds are there in one degree?
60357.e: One degree has 60 arc minutes, and each arc minute has 60 arc seconds. 60 · 60 = 3600.
60357.m: One degree is made up of 3600 arc seconds.

60358.q: How many meridians 1° apart are there around the whole Earth?
60358.e: Longitude is counted from 0° to 180° to the east and to the west. Together this gives 360 meridians 1° apart, with 180° E and 180° W being the same meridian.
60358.m: At one-degree intervals, 360 meridians circle the Earth.

60359.q: Which coordinates roughly match the city of Bern?
60359.e: Bern lies at about 46.95° north latitude and 7.45° east longitude. The coordinates 52.5° N, 13.4° E match Berlin.
60359.m: Bern lies at just under 47 degrees north and just over 7 degrees east.

60360.q: By how many degrees does the Earth turn in one hour?
60360.e: The Earth turns 360° in 24 hours. 360° : 24 = 15° per hour.
60360.m: The Earth turns 15 degrees every hour.

60361.q: One place lies at 45° E, another at 30° W. How big is the difference in their local mean time?
60361.e: The difference in longitude is 45° + 30° = 75°. At 15° per hour this gives 75 : 15 = 5 hours.
60361.m: Every 15 degrees of longitude means one hour of difference in local time.

60362.q: In which city did an international conference in 1884 set the meridian through Greenwich as the prime meridian?
60362.e: At the International Meridian Conference in Washington in October 1884, the delegates voted for the meridian through the Greenwich observatory. France abstained and used the Paris meridian for decades afterwards.
60362.m: The prime meridian through Greenwich was set in Washington in 1884.

60363.q: What are the coordinates of the antipode of 47° N, 8° E?
60363.e: At the antipode the latitude switches hemisphere: 47° S. The longitude is 180° minus 8° = 172°, and east becomes west.
60363.m: The antipode lies in the other hemisphere and 180 degrees of longitude away.

60364.q: What distance does one arc minute along a meridian correspond to?
60364.e: From the equator to the pole a meridian measures about 10,000 km and 90 · 60 = 5400 arc minutes; 10,000 km : 5400 ≈ 1.85 km. That is why the nautical mile is set at 1852 m.
60364.m: One nautical mile equals one arc minute on a meridian.

60365.q: Which country skipped a day at the end of 1844 to move to the Asian side of the date line?
60365.e: The Spanish colony had been governed via Mexico and used the American date. To fit in with trade with Asia, 30 December 1844 was followed directly by 1 January 1845.
60365.m: The Philippines moved to the Asian side of the date line in 1844.

60366.q: Which two islands in the Bering Strait are only about 4 km apart but have different calendar days because of the date line?
60366.e: Big Diomede belongs to Russia, Little Diomede to the USA. The national border and the date line run between them, which is why they are also called “Tomorrow Island” and “Yesterday Island”.
60366.m: On the Diomede Islands you can look across from today into tomorrow.

60367.q: Which island nation moved the date line in 1995 so that its whole territory has the same calendar day?
60367.e: Kiribati stretches across both sides of the 180th meridian. Since 1995 the same date has applied throughout the country, which makes the line take a big bend to the east.
60367.m: Kiribati moved the date line to the east in 1995.

60368.q: Which calendar day was skipped in Samoa when it moved to the other side of the date line?
60368.e: Samoa wanted the same date as its trading partners Australia and New Zealand. Thursday 29 December 2011 was followed directly by Saturday 31 December.
60368.m: Samoa skipped a whole day at the end of 2011.

60369.q: On which circumnavigation of the world did the crew first notice in 1522 that a day was missing from the logbook?
60369.e: The survivors of the Magellan and Elcano expedition arrived at Cape Verde in 1522 and found that their date was one day behind the local one. They had sailed west around the world.
60369.m: Even the first circumnavigation showed that you lose a day travelling west.

60370.q: In which novel does Phileas Fogg win his bet only thanks to a day gained by travelling east?
a: Around the World in Eighty Days
Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea
Journey to the Centre of the Earth
60370.e: In Jules Verne's novel Fogg believes he is too late. But because he travelled east, he has gained a day and arrives in time.
60370.m: Phileas Fogg wins his bet because he gains a day travelling east.

60371.q: What is the greatest possible difference in official clock time between two places on Earth?
60371.e: The easternmost time zone is UTC+14, the westernmost UTC-12. Between them there are 14 + 12 = 26 hours.
60371.m: Because of the date line, two places can have a time difference of up to 26 hours.

60372.q: Why does the date line not run exactly along the meridian it roughly follows?
a: So that countries are not split across two calendar days
Because the Earth's magnetic field deflects it
Because it follows the coasts of the continents
60372.e: The line makes bends, for example around Siberia, the Aleutians, Fiji or Tonga. That way every country has the same date everywhere.
60372.m: The date line makes detours so that countries are not divided.

60373.q: In which year did the Kashmir conflict begin with the partition of British India?
60373.e: When British India was divided into India and Pakistan in 1947, it was disputed which country the princely state of Jammu and Kashmir belonged to. The first war broke out in the same year.
60373.m: The Kashmir conflict began in 1947 with the partition of British India.

60374.q: What is the de facto border between the Indian-controlled and the Pakistani-controlled parts of Kashmir called?
60374.e: The ceasefire line of 1949 became the “Line of Control” in the Simla Agreement of 1972. It is not an internationally recognised national border.
60374.m: In Kashmir, India and Pakistan are separated by the Line of Control.

60375.q: Which third country controls part of the Kashmir region with the area of Aksai Chin?
60375.e: Since the 1950s China has controlled Aksai Chin, which India claims. The dispute led to the Sino-Indian border war in 1962.
60375.m: China also controls part of Kashmir.

60376.q: Which ruler signed Jammu and Kashmir's accession to India after armed tribesmen invaded?
60376.e: The Hindu Maharaja Hari Singh ruled a mainly Muslim territory. When armed tribesmen from Pakistan invaded, he signed the Instrument of Accession to India.
60376.m: Maharaja Hari Singh joined Kashmir to India.

60377.q: What did the Indian government abolish for Jammu and Kashmir in August 2019?
60377.e: India abolished the special status under Article 370 of the constitution and divided the state into two union territories. Pakistan protested sharply.
60377.m: In 2019 India ended the special status of Jammu and Kashmir.

60378.q: Which glacier in the Karakoram have India and Pakistan been fighting over since 1984?
60378.e: The Siachen Glacier lies above 5000 m and is considered the highest battlefield in the world. India occupied it in 1984; most of the victims were claimed by cold and avalanches.
60378.m: The Siachen Glacier is considered the highest battlefield in the world.

60379.q: What is the name of the war that India and Pakistan fought in Kashmir in 1999?
60379.e: In 1999 Pakistani troops and fighters occupied heights near Kargil on the Indian side of the Line of Control. India pushed them back; it was one of the few direct wars between two nuclear powers.
60379.m: In the Kargil War of 1999 India and Pakistan fought in Kashmir.

60380.q: What did UN Resolution 47 of 1948 call for in Kashmir?
a: A referendum on which country it should belong to
60380.e: The UN Security Council demanded the withdrawal of troops followed by a plebiscite. The referendum never took place.
60380.m: In 1948 the UN called for a referendum in Kashmir.

60381.q: What is the name of the line with which China claims most of the South China Sea?
60381.e: The nine-dash line covers about 90 per cent of the sea. It goes back to a 1947 map of the Republic of China, which at that time showed eleven dashes.
60381.m: China claims the South China Sea with the nine-dash line.

60382.q: At which institution in The Hague was the arbitration case of the Philippines against China held?
a: International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea
60382.e: The arbitral tribunal under the Convention on the Law of the Sea met under the roof of the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague. The ruling was given in July 2016.
60382.m: The case of the Philippines against China was heard at the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague.

60383.q: What did the arbitral tribunal decide in 2016 about China's claims in the South China Sea?
a: Historic rights have no basis in the law of the sea
China is awarded all the islands
The sea is divided among all neighbouring countries
60383.e: The tribunal ruled that China cannot claim “historic rights” within its line. China does not recognise the ruling.
60383.m: The 2016 ruling rejected China's historic claims, but China does not accept it.

60384.q: Which group of islands is claimed wholly or partly by six parties?
60384.e: China, Taiwan and Vietnam claim all of the Spratly Islands, and the Philippines, Malaysia and Brunei claim part of them.
60384.m: Six parties are in dispute over the Spratly Islands.

60385.q: Which group of islands did China bring completely under its control in 1974 after a battle with South Vietnam?
60385.e: In January 1974 China drove South Vietnamese troops from the Paracel Islands. Vietnam and Taiwan still claim them today.
60385.m: China has controlled the Paracel Islands since 1974.

60386.q: Which reef off the Philippine island of Luzon has been under de facto Chinese control since 2012?
60386.e: After a stand-off between ships of both countries in 2012, China remained present at Scarborough Shoal. It lies about 220 km west of Luzon.
60386.m: Scarborough Shoal has been controlled by China since 2012.

60387.q: How has China been changing many reefs of the Spratly Islands since about 2013?
a: It builds artificial islands with runways and harbours
It places them under UN nature protection
It sells them to private investors
60387.e: By land reclamation China has created more than 10 km² of land and built runways, harbours and radar facilities on it. Other neighbouring countries criticise the militarisation.
60387.m: China builds artificial islands on reefs in the South China Sea.

60388.q: Which strait connects the South China Sea with the Indian Ocean and is one of the busiest in the world?
60388.e: The Strait of Malacca lies between the Malay Peninsula and Sumatra. A large part of the trade between Europe, the Middle East and East Asia passes through it.
60388.m: The Strait of Malacca connects the South China Sea with the Indian Ocean.

60389.q: Which undersea mountain range do Russia, Denmark and Canada claim as part of their continental shelf?
60389.e: The Lomonosov Ridge crosses the Arctic Ocean beneath the North Pole. All three countries argue that it is the natural extension of their continent.
60389.m: Russia, Denmark and Canada are in dispute over the Lomonosov Ridge.

60390.q: What did Russian researchers do at the North Pole in 2007 that caused an international stir?
a: They planted a flag on the seabed
They built a permanent research station
They drilled for oil for the first time
60390.e: Two submersibles placed a Russian titanium flag on the seabed at a depth of over 4000 m. Legally it means nothing, but it was seen as a symbol of territorial claims.
60390.m: In 2007 Russia planted a flag on the seabed at the North Pole.

60391.q: Which small island did Canada and Denmark divide in 2022 after a dispute lasting decades?
60391.e: The dispute over Hans Island between Greenland and Canada became known as the “Whisky War” because both sides left flags and bottles there. In 2022 they agreed on a border across the island.
60391.m: Canada and Denmark divided Hans Island in 2022.

60392.q: How many member states does the Arctic Council have?
60392.e: The members are Canada, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Russia, Sweden and the USA. There are also representatives of indigenous peoples and observers.
60392.m: The Arctic Council has eight member states.

60393.q: What is the name of the shipping route along Russia's Arctic coast for which Russia demands its own rules and permits?
60393.e: The Northern Sea Route greatly shortens the distance between Europe and East Asia. Russia requires ships to register there and sometimes to have an icebreaker escort.
60393.m: The Northern Sea Route runs along Russia's Arctic coast.

60394.q: Which treaty of 1920 gives Norway sovereignty over an Arctic group of islands and also counts Switzerland among its parties?
60394.e: The Svalbard Treaty recognises Norway's sovereignty over Svalbard. Citizens of all the treaty states, including Switzerland, may carry out economic activities there.
60394.m: Norway owns Svalbard, but all treaty states may do business there.

60395.q: Which sea route does Canada regard as internal waters, while the USA regards it as an international strait?
60395.e: The Northwest Passage runs through the Canadian Arctic Archipelago. As the ice melts, the question of whether foreign ships may pass freely becomes more important.
60395.m: Canada and the USA disagree about the status of the Northwest Passage.

60396.q: Which UN body do Arctic countries apply to in order to extend their continental shelf beyond their economic zone?
a: Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf
60396.e: The commission examines geological data and makes recommendations. Russia, Denmark and Canada have submitted overlapping applications there.
60396.m: Extended continental shelves are applied for at a UN expert commission.

60397.q: Which German municipality is completely surrounded by Swiss territory?
60397.e: Büsingen lies near Schaffhausen and belongs to Germany, but it is part of the Swiss customs area. In everyday life people mostly pay in francs.
60397.m: Büsingen is a German exclave in the middle of Switzerland.

60398.q: Which Italian exclave lies on the shore of Lake Lugano?
60398.e: Campione d'Italia is completely surrounded by the canton of Ticino. Since 2020 it has been part of the EU customs area.
60398.m: Campione d'Italia is an Italian exclave in Ticino.

60399.q: How do the terms enclave and exclave differ?
a: In point of view: surrounding country or home country
In the size of the area
In whether the area is by the sea
60399.e: From the point of view of the surrounding country, a foreign territory is an enclave; from the point of view of the country it belongs to, it is an exclave. The former Verenahof near Schaffhausen was thus both a Swiss enclave and a German exclave until 1967.
60399.m: The same area is an enclave for the surrounding country and an exclave for the home country.

60400.q: Which independent country is completely surrounded by South Africa?
60400.e: Lesotho is an enclave in South Africa and lies entirely above 1000 m above sea level. Eswatini, on the other hand, also borders Mozambique.
60400.m: Lesotho lies completely inside South Africa.

60401.q: Which exclave of Azerbaijan is separated from the rest of the country by Armenian territory?
60401.e: The Autonomous Republic of Nakhchivan borders Armenia, Iran and Turkey, but not the rest of Azerbaijan.
60401.m: Nakhchivan is an exclave of Azerbaijan.

60402.q: Which Spanish exclave lies in the French Pyrenees?
60402.e: Llívia was not handed over to France in the Treaty of the Pyrenees in 1659 because it was considered a town and not a village. A French strip only about 1.6 km wide separates it from Spain.
60402.m: Llívia is a Spanish exclave in France.

60403.q: Which two countries exchanged more than 160 enclaves in 2015, including the only third-order enclave?
60403.e: In the border area around Cooch Behar there were enclaves within enclaves. With the 2015 agreement they were exchanged, and the inhabitants could choose their nationality.
60403.m: India and Bangladesh untangled their maze of enclaves in 2015.

60404.q: Which municipality in Belgium consists largely of more than twenty enclaves inside a Dutch municipality?
60404.e: Baarle-Hertog (Belgium) has 22 enclaves in Baarle-Nassau (Netherlands), and there are Dutch enclaves inside these too. The border sometimes runs right through houses.
60404.m: In Baarle the Belgian-Dutch border even runs through houses.

60405.q: What is the maximum width of a country's territorial sea under the Convention on the Law of the Sea?
60405.e: The territorial sea counts as national territory and may be at most 12 nautical miles (about 22 km) wide from the baseline.
60405.m: The territorial sea extends at most 12 nautical miles.

60406.q: How far may the exclusive economic zone (EEZ) extend at most?
60406.e: In the EEZ the coastal state alone may use fishing, raw materials and energy up to 200 nautical miles (about 370 km) from the baseline. Ships of other countries may sail through it freely.
60406.m: The economic zone extends up to 200 nautical miles out to sea.

60407.q: In which place was the Convention on the Law of the Sea opened for signature in 1982?
60407.e: The convention was signed on 10 December 1982 in Montego Bay in Jamaica. That is why it is also called the Montego Bay Convention.
60407.m: The UN Law of the Sea was signed in Montego Bay in 1982.

60408.q: In which year did the Convention on the Law of the Sea come into force?
60408.e: It came into force on 16 November 1994, one year after the 60th ratification. Switzerland is a party to it, while the USA has not ratified it.
60408.m: The Convention on the Law of the Sea has applied since 1994.

60409.q: Which institution issues licences for mining raw materials on the deep seabed outside national jurisdiction?
60409.e: The deep seabed is considered the “common heritage of mankind”. The International Seabed Authority manages it and regulates, for example, the mining of manganese nodules.
60409.m: The deep seabed is managed by the International Seabed Authority.

60410.q: Which right do ships of all countries have in the territorial sea of a foreign country?
a: The right to mine raw materials
The right to anchor without permission
60410.e: Foreign ships may pass quickly through the territorial sea as long as they do not harm the peace, order and security of the coastal state.
60410.m: In a foreign territorial sea the right of innocent passage applies.

60411.q: What is the zone directly beyond the territorial sea called, in which a country may still enforce customs and immigration rules?
60411.e: The contiguous zone extends up to 24 nautical miles from the baseline. There the country may prevent breaches of customs, tax, immigration and health rules.
60411.m: In the contiguous zone the coastal state controls customs and immigration.

60412.q: Which plate tectonic process formed the Pyrenees?
a: Collision of the Iberian plate with the Eurasian plate
Collision of the African plate with the Arabian plate
Drifting apart of the American and Eurasian plates
Rise of a hotspot under the Bay of Biscay
60412.e: The Iberian plate rotated towards Europe and collided with the Eurasian plate. The rocks were folded up in the course of the Alpine mountain building.
60412.m: The Pyrenees formed when Iberia was pushed against Europe.

60413.q: Which mountain is the highest peak of the Pyrenees?
60413.e: Aneto is about 3404 metres high and lies in the Maladeta massif in the Spanish province of Huesca. The largest glacier in the Pyrenees lies on its north side.
60413.m: Aneto is the highest mountain in the Pyrenees.

60414.q: Which small state in the Pyrenees has two heads of state, the French president and a Spanish bishop?
60414.e: Andorra is represented by two co-princes: the President of France and the Bishop of Urgell in Spain. This arrangement goes back to the Middle Ages.
60414.m: Andorra has two co-princes from France and Spain.

60415.q: What is the name of the glacial cirque in the French Pyrenees with one of the highest waterfalls in Europe?
60415.e: The Cirque de Gavarnie is a huge corrie carved out by Ice Age glaciers. The Grande Cascade there plunges over 400 metres.
60415.m: In the Cirque de Gavarnie a waterfall plunges over a huge rock face.

60416.q: Which pass in the French Pyrenees has been climbed most often in the Tour de France?
60416.e: The Col du Tourmalet lies at about 2115 metres and has been part of the Tour de France again and again since 1910. No other pass has been ridden more often.
60416.m: The Tourmalet is the classic Tour de France pass.

60417.q: Which language is spoken in the western Pyrenees on both sides of the border and is unrelated to any other language in Europe?
60417.e: Basque is an isolated language that is older than the Indo-European languages of the region. It is spoken in the Basque Country in Spain and France.
60417.m: Basque is unrelated to any other language in Europe.

60418.q: Which French river rises on the Spanish side of the Pyrenees in the Val d'Aran?
60418.e: The Garonne rises in the Val d'Aran and then flows into France, past Toulouse and Bordeaux. It flows into the Gironde.
60418.m: The Garonne begins its journey in the Spanish Pyrenees.

60419.q: Which treaty in 1659 largely set the border between France and Spain along the Pyrenees?
60419.e: The Treaty of the Pyrenees ended a long war between France and Spain. Among other things, France received Roussillon north of the main ridge.
60419.m: The Treaty of the Pyrenees in 1659 largely made the mountain ridge the national border.

60420.q: On which Pyrenean peak is there a well-known astronomical observatory?
60420.e: Weather and sky research has been carried out on the Pic du Midi de Bigorre since the 19th century. The clear, calm mountain air is well suited to observations.
60420.m: Researchers watch the sky from the Pic du Midi de Bigorre.

60421.q: What is the name of the gorge where the Danube breaks through between the Southern Carpathians and the Balkan Mountains?
60421.e: At the Iron Gates the Danube has cut a narrow valley through the mountains. Today large power stations dam the river there.
60421.m: At the Iron Gates the Danube breaks through the Carpathians.

60422.q: Which mountain in the Eastern Carpathians is the highest mountain in Ukraine?
60422.e: Hoverla is about 2061 metres high and belongs to the Chornohora range. Roman-Kosh, on the other hand, is the highest mountain in Crimea.
60422.m: Hoverla is the roof of Ukraine.

60423.q: Which historical region is enclosed by the arc of the Eastern and Southern Carpathians?
60423.e: Transylvania is an upland region inside the Carpathian arc. Wallachia, on the other hand, lies to the south outside it.
60423.m: Transylvania lies sheltered inside the Carpathian arc.

60424.q: Why were areas of the Carpathians declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2007?
60424.e: The primeval beech forests of the Carpathians in Slovakia and Ukraine were added in 2007. Later, old beech forests from other countries were added, including from Ticino since 2021.
60424.m: The Carpathians preserve some of Europe's last primeval beech forests.

60425.q: Which large lowland lies inside the Carpathian arc?
60425.e: The Pannonian Basin covers large parts of Hungary and neighbouring countries. The Carpathians frame it to the north and east.
60425.m: The Pannonian Basin is framed by the Carpathians.

60426.q: What else are the Southern Carpathians called?
60426.e: The Southern Carpathians are the highest part of the Romanian Carpathians and, with their corries and ridges, are reminiscent of the Alps. That is where the name Transylvanian Alps comes from.
60426.m: Because of their high-mountain character, the Southern Carpathians are also called the Transylvanian Alps.

60427.q: Geologically, which mountain belt do the Carpathians belong to?
60427.e: Like the Alps, the Carpathians were folded up in the Cenozoic era. That makes them young fold mountains.
60427.m: The Carpathians are young fold mountains like the Alps.

60428.q: Which large river rises in the Silesian Beskids of the Western Carpathians?
60428.e: The Vistula rises on the mountain Barania Góra in southern Poland. It flows through Kraków and Warsaw and into the Baltic Sea.
60428.m: The Vistula comes from the Beskids of the Western Carpathians.

60429.q: Which Carpathian range in south-eastern Poland is known for its thinly populated wilderness?
60429.e: The Bieszczady lie where Poland, Slovakia and Ukraine meet. After the Second World War many villages were abandoned; today there are wolves, bears and bison there.
60429.m: The Bieszczady are among the wildest areas of Poland.

60430.q: What does the name of the Norwegian mountain area Jotunheimen mean?
60430.e: Jotunheimen comes from the Jötunn, the giants of Norse mythology. Norway's highest peaks lie in Jotunheimen.
60430.m: Jotunheimen is named after the giants of the Norse sagas.

60431.q: Where is the highest point in Finland?
a: On Halti on the border with Norway
60431.e: Finland's highest point lies at about 1324 metres on the slope of Halti. The summit itself belongs to Norway.
60431.m: Finland's highest point is on Halti in the far north-west.

60432.q: Which two ancient continents collided when the rocks of the Scandinavian Mountains were formed?
60432.e: About 430 to 390 million years ago Laurentia and Baltica collided. This created a mountain range that was later almost completely worn away.
60432.m: The Scandinavian Mountains go back to the collision of Laurentia and Baltica.

60433.q: Why has Scandinavia been rising since the end of the last Ice Age?
a: Because the weight of the ice sheet has gone
Because volcanoes are pushing up magma
Because glaciers are piling up rock
60433.e: The huge ice sheet pressed the Earth's crust down. Since it melted, the crust has been slowly springing back, which is called isostatic or post-glacial rebound.
60433.m: Scandinavia is rising because the heavy ice has gone.

60434.q: What is special about the small Calderone glacier in the Gran Sasso massif?
a: It was long regarded as Europe's southernmost glacier
It is the largest glacier in Italy
It lies on an active volcano
It grows every year despite global warming
60434.e: The Calderone lies in a shady hollow below the Corno Grande in the Abruzzo. Because of warming it has shrunk a lot and split into two ice fields.
60434.m: The Calderone is the remains of a glacier in the Abruzzo.

60435.q: Which town at the foot of the Gran Sasso was hit by a severe earthquake in 2009?
60435.e: The earthquake in April 2009 destroyed large parts of the old town of L'Aquila. More than 300 people died.
60435.m: L'Aquila was shaken by a devastating earthquake in 2009.

60436.q: Which stone is quarried in the Apuan Alps on the north-western edge of the Apennines?
60436.e: White marble has been quarried near Carrara since Roman times. Michelangelo had blocks brought from there for his sculptures.
60436.m: The famous Carrara marble comes from the Apuan Alps.

60437.q: Which mountain range do the Apennines join near Savona in Liguria?
60437.e: The low Colle di Cadibona near Savona is usually seen as the boundary between the Alps and the Apennines. From there the Apennines curve all the way to Calabria.
60437.m: Near Savona the Alps turn into the Apennines.

60438.q: Where do the Dinaric Alps run?
a: Along the Adriatic from Slovenia to Albania
60438.e: The Dinarides run along the eastern coast of the Adriatic through Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Montenegro to Albania. The highest peak is Maja Jezercë in Albania.
60438.m: The Dinaric Alps stretch from Slovenia to Albania.

60439.q: Which mountain are the Dinaric Alps named after?
60439.e: Dinara lies on the border between Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. At about 1831 metres it is the highest mountain in Croatia.
60439.m: The Dinarides take their name from the mountain Dinara.

60440.q: Which landscape does the technical term “karst” come from?
a: The Kras between Slovenia and Trieste
The Jura between Switzerland and France
60440.e: The Kras is a limestone plateau in the border area of Slovenia and Italy. Its German name, Karst, became the technical term for limestone landscapes with caves and sinkholes.
60440.m: The term karst comes from a landscape near Trieste.

60441.q: What is a large, flat basin in karst that is often flooded from time to time called?
60441.e: A polje has a level, fertile floor and steep edges. Many of these technical terms come from the South Slavic languages of the Dinarides.
60441.m: A polje is a flat karst basin with fertile soil.

60442.q: What is an opening in karst where a river disappears underground called?
60442.e: Through a ponor, water drains away into cave systems. It often comes out again elsewhere as a strong karst spring.
60442.m: In a ponor a river sinks into the limestone.

60443.q: Which river has carved one of the deepest gorges in Europe in Montenegro?
60443.e: The Tara gorge is up to about 1300 metres deep and lies in the Durmitor area. The Tara is a headwater of the Drina.
60443.m: The Tara gorge is one of the deepest gorges in Europe.

60444.q: Which cold downslope wind rushes down from the Dinarides to the Adriatic in winter?
60444.e: The bora forms when cold air from inland falls over the coastal mountains. It reaches hurricane force and can close bridges and roads.
60444.m: The bora is an icy downslope wind on the Adriatic coast.

60445.q: What separates the Plitvice Lakes in Croatia from one another like steps?
60445.e: Mosses and algae help limestone to settle out of the water. This makes tufa barriers grow, and the water flows over them in waterfalls from lake to lake.
60445.m: The Plitvice Lakes are dammed by growing tufa barriers.

60446.q: Which coastal mountain range is the largest mountain range in Croatia?
60446.e: Velebit stretches about 145 kilometres along the Adriatic coast. It is a UNESCO biosphere reserve.
60446.m: Velebit is Croatia's longest coastal mountain range.

60447.q: Which depression separates the Greater Caucasus from the Lesser Caucasus?
60447.e: Between the two mountain ranges lies a low zone with the River Rioni in the west and the Kura in the east. Large parts of Georgia and Azerbaijan lie in it.
60447.m: The Transcaucasian Depression lies between the Greater and Lesser Caucasus.

60448.q: Which high mountain region of Georgia is known for its medieval defensive towers?
60448.e: Hundreds of stone tower houses stand in the villages of Upper Svaneti. The region has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996.
60448.m: Svaneti is famous for its old defensive towers.

60449.q: What did Arab geographers call the Caucasus because of its many languages?
60449.e: Dozens of peoples with their own languages live close together in the Caucasus. Many of these languages belong to language families found only there.
60449.m: The Caucasus is one of the regions with the most languages in the world.

60450.q: In which place in the western Caucasus were the Alpine events of the 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics held?
60450.e: Krasnaya Polyana lies in the mountains about 40 kilometres from the Black Sea coast. Ski areas and lifts were built there for the Games.
60450.m: The Sochi 2014 ski races took place in Krasnaya Polyana.

60451.q: Which extinct volcano, at about 5642 metres, is the highest mountain in the Caucasus?
60451.e: Elbrus lies in the west of the Greater Caucasus in Russia. If you count the Caucasus as part of Europe, it is the highest mountain in Europe. Ararat, on the other hand, lies in Turkey, outside the Caucasus.
60451.m: Elbrus is the highest mountain in the Caucasus.

60452.q: Through which countries does the Lesser Caucasus mainly run?
60452.e: The Lesser Caucasus lies south of the Transcaucasian Depression. In the south it merges into the Armenian Highlands.
60452.m: The Lesser Caucasus links Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan.

60453.q: Which Russian republic on the north-eastern edge of the Caucasus is considered especially multilingual?
60453.e: Avars, Dargins, Lezgins and many other peoples live in Dagestan. The name means roughly “land of mountains”.
60453.m: Dagestan is a mountainous land with very many peoples and languages.

60454.q: Roughly how long is the Greater Caucasus?
60454.e: The Greater Caucasus stretches from the Taman Peninsula on the Black Sea to the Absheron Peninsula on the Caspian Sea. That is about 1100 kilometres.
60454.m: The Greater Caucasus is about as long as the Alps.

60455.q: What type of volcano is Elbrus?
60455.e: Elbrus is built up from many layers of lava and ash. Such stratovolcanoes are usually steep and cone-shaped.

60456.q: How long ago did Elbrus last erupt?
60456.e: The last eruption is dated to around AD 50. That is why Elbrus is regarded not as extinct but as a dormant volcano.
60456.m: Elbrus is dormant, but not extinct.

60457.q: What Swiss connection is there to the first ascent of the western summit of Elbrus in 1874?
a: A mountain guide from Valais was there
The Federal Council paid for the expedition
The summit was named after a Swiss person
60457.e: Peter Knubel from St. Niklaus guided the British climbers Gardiner, Grove and Walker to the highest summit. So the first ascent has a Swiss connection.
60457.m: A mountain guide from St. Niklaus was one of the first on top of Elbrus.

60459.q: Why is Elbrus often regarded as the highest mountain in Europe?
a: It lies north of the main Caucasus ridge, which is often taken as the border
It lies in the middle of the Alps
It belongs to the Scandinavian Mountains
The EU has officially declared it so
60459.e: Where the border between Europe and Asia runs in the Caucasus is disputed. If you draw it along the main ridge, the 5642-metre Elbrus lies on the European side and is clearly higher than Mont Blanc.
60459.m: Elbrus is often regarded as Europe's highest mountain.

60460.q: Roughly how many glaciers flow down from Elbrus into the valleys?
a: None, it is free of ice
60460.e: 22 glaciers flow down from Elbrus, together covering about 145 square kilometres. They feed rivers such as the Kuban, Baksan and Malka.
60460.m: Elbrus carries a large ice cap with more than twenty glaciers.

60461.q: Why is climbing Elbrus dangerous for many people, despite the cable car?
a: Because of thin air, cold and sudden changes in the weather
Because of poisonous plants on the summit
Because of avalanches of hot sand
60461.e: Above about 4000 metres there is a risk of altitude sickness, icy wind and thick fog. Climbers die on Elbrus again and again, often because they underestimate the mountain.
60461.m: Elbrus is often underestimated because of height, cold and weather.

60462.q: In which geological feature did the present summit structure of Elbrus form?
60462.e: The present double summit grew up in a caldera measuring about 14 by 17 kilometres. A caldera forms when a volcano collapses after an eruption.
60462.m: Elbrus grew up inside a collapsed volcanic basin.

60463.q: Roughly up to what height does the cable car on Elbrus go?
60463.e: The cable car starts at Polyana Azau at about 2300 metres. The top station, Garabashi, lies at about 3850 metres.
60463.m: On Elbrus a cable car takes climbers up to almost 4000 metres.

60464.e: The name goes back to Muley Hacén, a ruler of the Emirate of Granada in the 15th century. According to legend he was buried on the mountain.
60464.m: Mulhacén recalls a Moorish ruler of Granada.

60465.q: Which peak is the second highest in the Sierra Nevada?
60465.e: Pico del Veleta is just under 3400 metres high and lies near the ski area. Alcazaba follows only a few metres lower.
60465.m: Veleta is the second highest mountain in the Sierra Nevada.

60466.q: Which larger mountain system does the Sierra Nevada in Spain belong to?
60466.e: The Baetic Cordillera runs through southern Spain and formed during the Alpine mountain building. The Sierra Nevada is its highest part.
60466.m: The Sierra Nevada is the highest part of the Baetic Cordillera.

60467.q: What is the area with white mountain villages on the southern slope of the Sierra Nevada called?
60467.e: The Alpujarras were long inhabited by Moors, who built terraces and irrigation channels there. The villages with flat roofs are reminiscent of North Africa.
60467.m: The Alpujarras lie on the sunny southern side of the Sierra Nevada.

60468.q: Why is it remarkable that you can ski in the Sierra Nevada?
a: The ski area is in southern Spain close to the Mediterranean
It has artificial snow in halls all year round
It lies on a Mediterranean island
60468.e: The Sierra Nevada has one of the southernmost ski areas in Europe. In clear weather you can see from the slopes to the Mediterranean and sometimes as far as Africa.
60468.m: In the Sierra Nevada you ski with a view of the Mediterranean.

60469.q: Which rock is dominant in the high areas of the Sierra Nevada?
60469.e: Mica schist is a metamorphic rock formed from other rocks under high pressure and temperature. It weathers into dark, flaky scree.
60469.m: The peaks of the Sierra Nevada are mainly mica schist.

60470.q: Roughly what share of France's area does the Massif Central cover?
60470.e: The Massif Central covers about 85,000 square kilometres. That is about twice the area of Switzerland.
60470.m: The Massif Central covers about a seventh of France.

60471.q: Which volcano of the Chaîne des Puys can be reached by a rack railway?
60471.e: Puy de Dôme is about 1465 metres high and the landmark of Clermont-Ferrand. Since 2012 the “Panoramique des Dômes” has run to the summit.
60471.m: A rack railway goes up Puy de Dôme.

60472.q: What kind of mountain is the Cantal in the Auvergne?
60472.e: The Cantal volcano had a diameter of about 70 kilometres and is regarded as the largest volcano in Europe by area. Today it is heavily eroded, and valleys run outwards from its centre like the points of a star.
60472.m: The Cantal is a huge, eroded volcano in the Auvergne.

60473.q: During which mountain building did the old rock base of the Massif Central form?
60473.e: In the Palaeozoic a large fold mountain range formed there, which was later worn down to a stump. Only in the Cenozoic was the base raised again.
